# ThinnestAI

> This file is very large and may be truncated. For an index of this content, please refer to https://docs.thinnest.ai/llms.txt instead.

> One AI agent that answers on your website, WhatsApp and Telegram — and remembers the same customer across all of them.

# Actions
Source: https://docs.thinnest.ai/agent/actions

Letting the agent do things, not only say them — safely.

An agent that can only talk is a search box with manners. Actions let it look up
an order, check stock, or start something in your own systems.

**The tools we wrote arrive on; anything that reaches outside your business
arrives off.** Knowledge search, lead capture and escalation are what people set
an agent up for, so making you go and find three switches would be a checklist
before the thing works at all. Web search, your own API and every connected
service start off, because those are reachable from a public chat by a stranger
who may be trying to talk the model into using them — and that is a decision
worth making one at a time.

## How the Actions page is laid out

The page has three tabs. The one you have open is kept in the address, so a
reload, or a link you send a colleague, lands on the same tab.

* **Built in** — the tools we wrote, in three cards: **What Agent can do**
  (knowledge search, lead capture, handing over to a person, booking a call back,
  web search), **Reaching the customer elsewhere**, and **Remembering customers
  across channels**.
* **On calls** — **Hand calls to another agent**, **Spam detection**, the
  **Who-is-calling lookup** and **After the call**.
* **Connect a service** — webhooks, a helpdesk, your own API, then calendar,
  spreadsheet, CRM and records, and the directory of other services.

Under the title, one line shows what is on: how many tools are switched on, how
many services are connected, and how many agents a call can be handed to. A tool
you have switched on that is missing something it needs shows an amber **Not in
use yet**, with what is missing, rather than quietly doing nothing.

## Built-in tools

Switchable per agent. Off means the tool is **removed**, not that the model is
asked not to use it.

* **Knowledge search** — your own material, always searched first. **Two
  switches**: one for chat and WhatsApp, one for calls. Both on.
* **Web search** — runs on the model provider's side, so it is only available on
  models that offer it.
* **Capture lead** — see [Leads](/agent/leads).
* **Escalate** — hand the conversation to a person. See [Escalation](/agent/escalation).
* **Hand calls to another agent** — on calls only. Under this heading the agent
  can pass a live call to another of your agents, say sales to support, on the
  same line and in the same conversation. Each agent on the list is handed over
  **warm** (with a short summary and the conversation so far) or **cold** (it
  starts fresh and greets the caller). See
  [Voice](/channels/voice#handing-a-call-on) for the rules.
* **End the call** — on calls only. The agent hangs up once the conversation is
  genuinely finished. See [Voice](/channels/voice#ending-the-call).
* **Book a call back** — somebody asks to be called later and the agent books
  it; your number rings them at that time. See
  [Voice](/channels/voice#booking-a-call-back).

## Spam detection and blocked numbers

On the **On calls** tab. Phone calls only.

**Blocked numbers.** A blocked number cannot reach the agent. Its calls are turned
away before they are answered, so nothing is said and nothing is charged. Type the
number with its country code (`+91 98765 43210`) and click **Block**. Each blocked
number shows how it was blocked (by you, by the agent, or automatically) and how
many of its calls have been stopped. **Unblock** lets it call again.

**Spam detection.** Switch on **Let the agent flag spam callers** and the agent can
flag a call that is not a real enquiry: someone who only wants to chat or pass the
time, keeps asking things that have nothing to do with your business after being
told what the line is for, is drunk, makes no sense or keeps swearing, or is
selling something. The agent then says a short goodbye and ends the call. It never
flags a genuine customer, however angry they are: a complaint, even a heated one,
or a threat to go online or to court, is a complaint.

Choose when a flagged number is blocked: **after 3 spam calls in 7 days** to begin
with, anywhere from 1 to 20 calls and 1 to 90 days. At **1**, the agent's own flag
blocks the number straight away. Numbers flagged but not yet blocked are listed
with how many times, and **Not spam** clears them. Unblocking a number also clears
its flags, so it starts again from zero.

## Booking into your own calendar

Different from **Book a call back** above, and worth keeping straight: that has
your number ring the customer, this puts a real meeting in your diary at a time
you were genuinely free.

Connect Cal.com and the agent can read your availability, offer real times, and
book — with Cal.com sending the confirmation. Twelve switches, all starting off.
See [Calendar](/agent/calendar).

## Filling in your own spreadsheet

The agent takes a caller's details and writes them into a row of your spreadsheet
as it goes, and can look somebody up in the same table to answer from what you
already hold. Connect your own Grist account; two switches, both starting off.
See [Spreadsheet](/agent/spreadsheet).

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Your calendar and spreadsheet switches share one budget: eight on at once.**
> An agent given too many tools gets worse at choosing between them, so we stop
> you at eight rather than let it quietly degrade.

## Reaching the customer on a different channel

A caller needs a link sent to them. A customer on WhatsApp would rather be
phoned. These are the tools for that, and they have their own block on the
Actions page because they share something the others do not: each one reaches
the customer **outside** the conversation the agent is in.

**All four start off**, and three of them cost money each time. Turning one on is
not quite enough on its own — each also needs something only you can give it, and
the row says so when it is missing.

| Tool | You turn it on, and it needs | What it does |
| - | - | - |
| **Ring the customer now** | a number that can dial out, and the customer inside your calling hours | Rings that customer straight away on a number we are allowed to use, and tells them it is coming |
| **Send the customer a WhatsApp** | an approved **utility** template | Sends that template to the customer, blanks filled — never free text, and never while the agent is already on WhatsApp with them |
| **Send the customer an SMS** | your own [SMS provider](/channels/sms) connected, and at least one DLT template | Sends one of your DLT templates by SMS, blanks filled — never free text. Indian mobile numbers only; your provider bills you |
| **Reply to the customer by email** | a connected helpdesk that can send — Zendesk today | Replies on that customer's existing email thread. See [Helpdesk](/workspace/helpdesk) |

> [!NOTE]
>
> **"Ring the customer now" is not the same switch as "Book a call back".** One
> is a customer asking to be rung later; the other is the agent ringing them
> while it is already talking to them somewhere else. You can have either, both,
> or neither.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **The agent never chooses the destination.** It cannot be told "email this to
> another address" or "call this number instead" — there is no such thing to
> say. The number or address is resolved from your records at the moment of
> sending, from the same evidence that
> [links a person across channels](/concepts#how-two-channels-become-one-person).
> So the worst a visitor can talk the agent into is contacting the right person
> at the wrong moment.

A few consequences worth expecting:

* **A WhatsApp template costs money**, the same as any other template send. The
  agent may send **two an hour in one conversation**, so a customer who keeps
  asking — or tries to make it loop — cannot run up your bill.
* **SMS is capped the same way**, two an hour in one conversation, and is billed
  by your own provider, not from your wallet.
* **Emails are capped the same way**, at three an hour in one conversation.
  Enough for the invoice and the corrected invoice, not enough to flood an inbox.
* **The agent will refuse in words** when it has no usable number or address —
  it says so and carries on helping, rather than pretending it sent something.

### Which templates the agent may send

Two separate decisions, both yours:

1. **Whether this agent may send at all** — the switches above, per agent.
2. **Which templates any agent may send** — a tick on each template, once for the
   whole workspace.

Only templates you have ticked **Agents may send this during a call or chat** are
shown to the agent. It picks the one that fits what the customer asked for, and
fills the blanks. It can't send anything you didn't tick, and it can't write its
own words.

| Tool | Where you tick | What can be ticked |
| - | - | - |
| **Send the customer a WhatsApp** | The template's card on [Templates](/whatsapp/templates#letting-an-agent-send-a-template) | Approved **Utility** templates whose link, if any, is fixed |
| **Send the customer an SMS** | The template in [SMS settings](/channels/sms) | Any of your DLT templates |

New templates start **unticked**. A tool with nothing ticked says so on its row,
and isn't given to the agent at all.

The agent is shown at most **ten** ticked templates, the first ten alphabetically,
so every turn stays quick and the same ones appear each time. With more than ten
ticked, untick the ones you don't want it to reach for. The SMS page tells you
when you are over.

> [!NOTE]
>
> Want a message that is always the same one, sent at a known moment? Use
> [After the call](/agent/after-the-call). There you choose the exact template and
> what fills every blank, and no tick is needed.

## A message after the call

Separate from the tools above: the agent can also send the caller a WhatsApp or
an SMS when a call ends — a thank-you with your booking link, or a
sorry-we-missed-you. It's set in the **After the call** card on the same page.
See [After the call](/agent/after-the-call).

## Call your own API

Point the agent at an HTTPS endpoint of yours, describe what it does and what it
takes, and the agent can call it mid-conversation. **[Full guide, including how
to write the endpoint safely](/agent/custom-api).**

* Credentials are encrypted at rest and are not readable from the dashboard.
* The URL is validated **and DNS-resolved** before we fetch it, so an endpoint
  cannot be used to reach inside our network.
* Your header secret is never shown again after you save it.

## Connect a service (MCP)

21 services with addresses read from the official registry and grouped by what
they do, plus any address you want to paste. A further 1,434 services are listed
in the directory.

Sign-in happens in a popup and tokens are sealed and renewed automatically, so
nobody signs in twice.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Asana, Xero and Shopify need a manual step.** Those vendors do not support
> dynamic client registration, so connecting them currently means registering an
> app on their side yourself. It works; it is not one-click, and we would rather
> say so here than have you discover it mid-setup.

## Send what happens somewhere else

Signed outbound webhooks to any HTTPS endpoint. This is the lane that reaches
Google Sheets, Zoho and effectively any CRM through Zapier or Make today. Paste
an address — or an email address, if your helpdesk opens tickets that way — and
pick what it should be told about.

| Event | Fires when |
| - | - |
| A lead was captured | The agent collected a name, email or phone from somebody interested |
| A conversation was escalated | It handed a conversation to a person |
| A conversation was resolved | A teammate marked one done |
| **A call finished** | Any call placed or answered — with the outcome, how long it lasted, and which campaign it belonged to |
| **A call's results are ready** | After a call ends and has been read — its summary, the details it collected, the transcript and a recording link ([shape](/api-reference/calls/get-call)) |
| **A campaign finished** | Everybody on a broadcast or [calling campaign](/channels/voice-campaigns) has been reached or given up on |
| **A caller asked not to be called again** | During a call, somebody asked not to be called again and their number went on your do-not-call list |
| **Something went wrong on a live call** | While a call is going: the agent could not answer, your own model key failed, a reply was very slow, or the voice connection failed. Sent once per kind of problem per call |

A finished call carries whether it was answered, missed or refused, so a missed
call is something your own system can act on rather than something you find out
by opening ours. Want what was *said* as well? Tick **A call's results are
ready** — it arrives a few seconds later, once the summary and details are
written. See [Call leads from your CRM](/guides/leads-from-your-crm).

Every delivery is signed with a secret shown once when you add the endpoint, so
your receiver can prove the request came from us. A delivery that fails is
tried again after 1 minute, 5 minutes, 30 minutes, 2 hours and 6 hours (six
attempts over about 8½ hours). An endpoint is switched off, and says so, only
after five events in a row that each failed every attempt; a failure that a
retry then delivers does not count. What failed can be sent again for 7 days. See
[Webhooks](/api-reference/webhooks) for the headers, the retries and how to
dedupe.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Choose the events you want.** An endpoint with no events chosen receives
> every event — the ones that exist today and any we add later. A receiver built
> for leads should not be woken by a phone call it has never seen the shape of,
> so tick only the events it is built for.

## Two limits worth knowing

**Eight tools per agent.** Every tool's schema is re-sent on every turn, and
models get measurably worse at choosing as the list grows. The cap is a quality
decision, not a licensing one.

**Every discovered tool arrives off.** Enabling is one deliberate act per tool.
A newly connected service does not silently gain the agent thirty new
capabilities.

## Name protection

Third-party tools are namespaced, so nothing you connect can register itself as your own knowledge search and quietly take over your own material.


# After the call
Source: https://docs.thinnest.ai/agent/after-the-call

Send the caller WhatsApp messages or SMS when a call ends — a thank-you, a booking link, a sorry-we-missed-you.

When a call ends, the agent can send the caller messages: WhatsApp, SMS, or
both, up to 3 templates on each, sent in the order you chose them. They're the
same messages every time, from templates you chose, with blanks filled from the
call. Set it in the **After the call** card on the agent's **Actions** page, on
the **On calls** tab.

Things it's good for:

* **Answered calls** — "Thanks for calling, . Book your visit here: …"
* **Missed calls** — "Sorry we missed you, . Reply here or call us back on …"
* **Every call** — your address and opening hours, after anyone rings.

## Set it up

**1. Have a template ready**

* **WhatsApp:** an approved **Utility** template. See [Templates](/channels/whatsapp).
* **SMS:** a DLT template, with your SMS provider connected. See [SMS](/channels/sms).

**2. Choose which calls**

**Send after**: tick *Calls somebody answered*, *Missed calls*, or both for
every call. A call that failed before it rang never gets one.

**3. Choose the templates, and fill their blanks**

Tick up to 3 **WhatsApp templates** and up to 3 **SMS templates**. They're
sent in the order you tick them, and each one you tick shows its text with its
blanks underneath. For each blank, choose what goes in it:

| Choice | Fills with |
| - | - |
| Customer's first name | The caller's first name, or "there" if we don't know it |
| Business name | Your workspace's name |
| Agent's name | This agent's name |
| Date of the call | Like "7 Oct", in your workspace's timezone |
| Fixed text… | Whatever you type, like your booking link |

An SMS blank holds at most 30 characters, so fixed text there is kept short.

**4. Save**

Untick every template on a channel to turn that channel off.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **A WhatsApp template with a blank in its link button can't be used here.** A
> button like `yoursite.com/{{1}}` needs a value for the blank, and nothing can
> fill it after a call. Those templates don't appear in the list, and saving one
> through the API is refused. Use a template whose link is fixed, or put the
> changing part in the message text.

## What keeps it polite

* **Once per call.** A call that ends twice in our records still sends once.
* **Not on a workflow's calls.** When a [workflow](/agent/workflows) places the call, the workflow decides what
  follows it, so these messages are not sent — the caller never gets both.
* **Never to anyone on your do-not-contact list**, including someone who asked
  the agent on the call not to be contacted again.
* **At most once a day to the same number**, per channel. A caller who rings
  three times in a morning gets one set of messages, not three. Your chosen
  templates go out together, as one set.
* **Only to a number we know is theirs**, the one they called from or that we
  called. Never to a number someone said out loud on the call.
* **WhatsApp must be a Utility template.** Marketing templates are refused here.
  They need marketing consent, and Meta pauses them quickly when people don't
  want them.

## What it costs

* **WhatsApp** is charged like any other template you send. See
  [WhatsApp](/channels/whatsapp).
* **SMS** goes through your own provider, which bills you directly. Nothing is
  taken from your wallet here.

## Seeing what went out

Each WhatsApp appears in the customer's WhatsApp conversation, marked as sent by
the agent after the call. Each SMS appears as a note on the call's conversation.
A message that couldn't be sent (no WhatsApp on that number, a template no longer
approved, your SMS provider refused it) is simply not sent. The call itself is
unaffected.

## From the API

The same setting is `followUp` on [Update Post-call
Settings](/api-reference/post-call/update-post-call-settings). It needs a **full**
key, because it makes the agent message customers.

```bash theme={null}
curl -X PATCH https://app.thinnest.ai/api/v1/agents/ag_5cbb2cb9-41aa-4181-9e37-78914bd7b4f9/post-call \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "followUp": {
      "when": "missed",
      "whatsapp": {
        "templateId": "3f1c2b7e-9a41-4f0b-8e2d-5c6a7b8d9e01",
        "values": ["customer_name", "business_name"]
      },
      "sms": {
        "templateId": "8d2e4f6a-1b3c-4d5e-9f70-a1b2c3d4e5f6",
        "values": ["customer_name", "fixed:acme.example/book"]
      }
    }
  }'
```

`values` fill the template's blanks in order, one each. Anything you leave out of
`followUp` keeps what is saved, and a channel set to `null` stops it:

```json theme={null}
{ "followUp": { "sms": null } }
```

To send more than one template on a channel, use `whatsappTemplates` or
`smsTemplates`: a list of up to 3, sent in order. An empty list stops that
channel. `whatsapp` and `sms` still work and mean the first of the list: setting
one replaces the list with that single template.

```json theme={null}
{
  "followUp": {
    "whatsappTemplates": [
      { "templateId": "3f1c2b7e-9a41-4f0b-8e2d-5c6a7b8d9e01", "values": ["customer_name"] },
      { "templateId": "6a0d9c3e-2f4b-4e8a-9b1c-7d5e3f2a1b0c", "values": [] }
    ]
  }
}
```


# Behaviour
Source: https://docs.thinnest.ai/agent/behaviour

Tone, language, opening line, model and when to fetch a human.

## Where to set it

Most of this is on the agent's **Playground**, in four cards: **Language and
model**, **Voice**, **What Agent says** (the opening line and the instructions)
and **Reply length**. Under them are the call settings: how the agent speaks,
listens and ends a call, recording, memory, and call length (see
[Voice](/channels/voice#where-the-call-settings-are)). Nothing changes until you press **Save changes** at the top
right; after that it applies to the next message, including for real customers,
so the Playground is not a sandbox. **Test a call** and a chat panel sit beside
the cards (above them on a narrower screen), so you can try a change straight away.

## Name

Rename an agent from the pencil beside its name at the top of its sidebar, or
under **Settings → Identity**. Customers see the name in the chat.

## Business description

The facts the agent falls back on when a knowledge search finds nothing — what
you sell, to whom, and anything true of the business as a whole.

Keep it factual. This is grounding, not instructions: it is treated as
information to work from, never as commands.

## Instructions

Tone and subject matter. "Be warm but brief." "Never discuss competitors."
"Always mention that delivery is free over ₹2,000."

Tune these in the **Playground**, against a live reply. Guessing at wording and
shipping it is how you find out a week later that the agent has been ending
every message with an emoji.

The box has no character limit — the counter under it shows how many characters
you have used, and the text is sent to the model on every reply, so a longer
prompt costs more on every turn. Through the API, instructions can be up to
**20,000 characters**. Conversation steps are limited separately (up to 12
steps, each with an 80-character title and a 600-character detail) and don't
count toward the instructions.

> [!NOTE]
>
> Your instructions are treated as guidance on tone and subject matter, not as a
> command channel. The platform's own safety rules always win — which is what
> stops a customer talking the agent out of them too.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Your agent never pretends to be a person.** Give it any name and persona you
> like, but if someone asks whether they are talking to an AI, a bot or a real
> person, it says it is an AI assistant — on every channel, in every language,
> whatever your instructions say. On a call, it also answers truthfully whether
> the call is being recorded.

## Opening line

The first thing a visitor reads in the widget. Write it in the business's own
voice; "How can I help you today?" is a wasted sentence.

## Reply language

Choose it when you create the agent, or any time on the **Playground**. Either **\[Auto] Match the customer** — the agent replies in
whatever language the customer speaks in — or tick the languages it speaks: one,
or up to four.

Through the API, send `languages` on Create Agent or Update Agent: a list of
language names. `[]` is auto, one name is that language alone, and two to four are
the languages the agent expects, the first being the one it falls back to, for
example `["Telugu", "English"]`. More than four, a repeat, a name the console does
not offer, or `languages` together with `language` is refused with a `400`. Get
Agent returns `languages` too. Sending `language` (one language) still works and
replaces any list.

In chat (website chat, WhatsApp, Telegram, the Playground and test chat), **Match the
customer** reads the script of the customer's latest message. Write in Telugu, Hindi,
Tamil, Kannada, Malayalam, Bengali, Gujarati, Punjabi or Odia script and the agent
replies in that language, even if its opening line was in another. Once a conversation
is under way, a few words in another script do not move it: the agent switches when the
customer's first message is in that script, or when a later message is a real sentence
in it. Some cases are left to the agent's own judgement: a message written in English
letters (including Telugu or Hindi typed in English letters), a message too short to
tell, and one that is mostly English. A customer can always ask for a different
language and the agent follows.

Pick one language and the agent answers **only** in it. On a phone call that
also tells the speech recogniser which language to listen for. **Match the
customer** leaves the recogniser to work it out afresh for every sentence, and a
short or mixed reply can be heard as the wrong language — a name from another
language is enough. If your callers use one language, choose it.

Pick **several** — Hindi and English, say, or Tamil and English — and the agent
answers in whichever of them the customer is speaking, and in the **first** one
you ticked when they use any other. On a phone call the recogniser still works
out the language for itself, but only among yours: a reply it hears as some
other language is listened to again in the language the call is in. That
second listen adds about half a second, and only to those replies. Up to four
languages; the first one you tick is the one the agent falls back to.

On a phone call the agent is also told which of your languages each sentence the
caller says is in, read from the script it was written in. A full sentence in
another of your languages is answered in that language on the very next reply; a
single word, a yes or a name keeps the language the call was in. When two of your
languages share a script — Hindi and Marathi, say, or English and French — the
script cannot tell them apart, so the agent is left to judge, as it is with
**Match the customer**.

37 languages, including all 22 of the Eighth Schedule, searchable, each in its
own script, so there is no "other languages" section to scroll past.

## Speaking speed

In the **Voice** card, under the voice itself: how fast the agent talks on
calls, on a slider from slower to faster. See
[Speaking speed](/channels/voice#speaking-speed).

## Answer style

Presets rather than a raw temperature number. Precise for policy and pricing
questions; warmer where the conversation is a sales one.

## Model

Every new agent starts on **Prana \[Voice]** — from scratch, from a pre-built agent, or
through the API (`prana-voice`) — and answers chat and calls with it until you choose
another. The choice is checked against your plan at request time, so downgrading a plan
cannot leave a more expensive model quietly running.

If your workspace brings only its own voice key, calls run on Prana, Prana \[Voice],
GPT-OSS 120B or another low-cost model; an agent set to anything else answers its calls
on GPT-OSS 120B. If it brings only its own language model key, your key answers on any model it
offers, and the call is billed like any other call, by the voice. See
[Bring your own keys](/api-reference/bring-your-own-keys).

The model you choose never changes a call's per-minute rate: every call is billed at the
premium rate, or the studio rate with a Studio voice. `GET /api/v1/models` gives the price for
each model: `callTier` (always `premium`) and `callPricePerMinuteMicro`, the price of one call
minute in millionths of `currency` (the currency of the wallet your calls are charged
to). Both cover the model only, with a Premium voice: a Studio voice
raises a call's price, and one call is billed at one rate, never a stacked surcharge. If
your workspace brings its own keys, calls bill at the
[BYOK per-minute rate](/api-reference/bring-your-own-keys) whatever the model, so these
prices apply only to an agent you've set to run on our stack. The exception is a workspace
that brings only its own language model: there the voice plan still applies, set by the voice
alone, and the model you run never raises it. Typical response latency
per model isn't published.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **The agent does not go dark.** If a model provider fails mid-conversation, the
> reply falls through to another model rather than to silence. A customer looking
> at a dead chat window is a worse outcome than a slightly slower answer.

## Conversation budget

A ceiling on what one conversation can cost you in a day, under **Settings →
Conversation budget**. When a single chat or WhatsApp conversation has cost that
much in the last 24 hours, the agent keeps answering on a lighter model until the
day is over. It never stops replying. Leave it blank for no budget; it is in your
balance's currency.

It is for the visitor who will not stop typing, or a loop between two bots. A
regular customer's thread is counted a day at a time, so they are never moved to
the lighter model for good.

## Handing over to a person

One switch, **Actions → Hand over to a person**, with two triggers behind it —
and [Escalation](/agent/escalation) covers what happens when one fires, including
when a custom action fails:

* **When the material does not cover the question.** The honest escalation.
* **When the customer asks for a person**, or is clearly upset.

Turning it off removes the capability entirely rather than asking the model to
refrain — the difference matters, because a model that has a tool will
eventually use it.

> [!TIP]
>
> A business with nobody watching the inbox should turn escalation off. An
> escalation nobody answers is worse than a straight "I don't know", because the
> customer waits.

## Writing your own lead and hand-over rules

Every agent is told, in plain sentences, when to ask for contact details, when to
hand a conversation to a person and what to say when it cannot. If you build on the
API and write those rules yourself, in your own instructions or scripts, set
`ownRules: true` on [Create Agent](/api-reference/agents/create-agent) or
[Update Agent](/api-reference/agents/update-agent) and we leave ours out.

What goes: the sentence about asking for a name, email or number (and the one that
says the business does not collect them), the hand-over rule (and the one that says
nobody can be handed to and that nobody should promise a follow-up), and the "cannot
arrange a call back" sentence. What stays, whatever you send: the boundary (only
this business), the AI disclosure, the reply language, the date, your own
instructions, and how a call is put through to a person.

It is off by default, so no agent's behaviour changes until you set it. The tool
that hands a conversation over still describes when it applies, so an agent keeps
handing over when someone is on duty. `captureLeads` and the escalation switches
keep deciding which tools the agent has; `ownRules` only decides which of our
sentences it reads.


# Calendar
Source: https://docs.thinnest.ai/agent/calendar

Your agent reads your real availability and books meetings into your Cal.com or Calendly.

Someone asks when you are free. The agent reads your actual calendar, offers two
or three real times, takes their name and email, and books it. Your calendar
sends the confirmation itself.

Two calendars are supported: **Cal.com**, connected with an API key, and
**Calendly**, connected by signing in to Calendly. Most of this page is about
Cal.com; [Calendly](#calendly) has its own section below.

It works on every channel — website chat, WhatsApp, Telegram and phone calls.

> [!NOTE]
>
> This is not the same as **Book a call back**. That has your number ring the
> customer at a time they chose. This puts a meeting in your diary at a time you
> were actually free. You can have both on; they do not know about each other.

## Connecting your calendar

You need a Cal.com account. Go to **Actions**, find **Calendar**, and click
**Cal.com**.

**1. Get an API key from Cal.com**

In Cal.com, open **Settings → Developer → API keys** and create one.

It must be a **live** key — one beginning `cal_live_`. Cal.com also issues
test keys, which begin `cal_` and work perfectly against a separate test
world, so a booking made with one never reaches the calendar you are looking
at. We refuse those rather than let you find out from an empty diary.

Leave the expiry off unless you have a reason to set one — a key that
expires will stop your agent booking, and the first sign is usually a
customer who could not get a slot.

**2. Paste it in**

We call Cal.com once to check the key works and to read back which account
it belongs to. If it does not work you are told immediately, rather than
finding out from a missed meeting.

**3. Choose what the agent may do**

Everything starts **off**. Connecting your calendar on its own gives the
agent nothing.

## Choosing what it can do

Twelve things, each its own switch. **Switch on only what the agent needs**: the
fewer it carries, the better it picks the right one.

That eight is shared with anything else the agent connects, so a
[spreadsheet](/agent/spreadsheet) switch and a calendar switch come out of the
same budget.

### What a customer can ask for

| Switch | What happens |
| - | - |
| **See what can be booked** | Reads your meeting types — a 15-minute intro, a demo — so the agent offers real ones instead of inventing them |
| **Check when you are free** | Reads your genuinely open slots and offers a couple of them |
| **Hold a slot while you talk** | Reserves the time for a few minutes so nobody else takes it while the customer is still spelling their email |
| **Book the meeting** | Puts a real booking in your Cal.com. Cal.com emails the confirmation |
| **Find their existing booking** | Looks up what this customer already has, by their email |
| **Move a booking** | Reschedules to a time they picked |
| **Cancel a booking** | Cancels it, with the reason they gave |

Most people want the first four. Add **Find** before **Move** or **Cancel** —
those two need it, because it is where the agent gets the booking to act on.

### Acting as you

Five more decide something on your behalf: accepting or declining a booking that
is waiting on you, marking a no-show, and reading your working hours or time off.

**Three of these need Find their existing booking turned on as well** —
accepting, declining and marking a no-show all act on a specific booking, and
Find is the only thing that can identify one.

Marking a no-show needs one more thing: the person's email address. Cal.com
identifies an attendee by email and by nothing else, so without one the agent
cannot say who failed to turn up.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Leave these off unless the agent only ever talks to your own staff.** A phone
> call has no login, so the agent cannot tell you from a caller who has worked out
> what to say. It is asked to refuse strangers, but the reliable protection is the
> switch being off.

## What your customer experiences

> **Them:** Can I get a demo this week?
> **Agent:** Let me check the diary. I have Tuesday at 11, or Thursday at 3.
> **Them:** Thursday.
> **Agent:** Can I take your name and email?

Then a Cal.com confirmation lands in their inbox, exactly as if they had used
your booking page.

The agent will **not** invent a time. If nothing is free it says so and offers to
look at another week, rather than promising a slot you do not have.

## Things worth knowing

**It always asks for an email.** Cal.com will accept a booking without one; we
will not. A booking with no email gets no confirmation and cannot be found again
if the customer rings back to change it.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Testing in the Playground books for real.** The Playground runs your actual
> agent, not a simulation — so if you ask it to book you a demo, a real meeting
> appears in your Cal.com and a real confirmation email goes out. Cancel it the
> same way, or leave these switches off until you are ready.

**Times are read in your calendar's timezone**, unless the customer says where
they are — then it converts.

**Hidden meeting types are never offered.** If you took something off your public
booking page, the agent will not offer it either.

**Disconnecting leaves your bookings alone.** They are your customers'
appointments, not ours to cancel.

## If it stops working

The card says **Needs attention** and shows what Cal.com said.

Almost always the key expired or was revoked. Create a new one in Cal.com and use
**Replace key** — your switches are remembered, so you do not have to set them up
again.

## Calendly

Go to **Actions**, find **Calendar**, and click **Calendly**.

**1. Sign in to Calendly**

You are sent to Calendly's own page to approve the connection, then brought
back. There is no key to copy, and we never see your Calendly password.

**2. Pick the meeting types**

Click **Find meeting types**. We read the active meeting types on your
account. Tick the ones the agent may book, then **Save meeting types**.

The agent offers only these, by name. Nothing is attached until at least
one is picked.

**3. Choose what the agent may do**

Everything starts **off**, the same as Cal.com.

| Switch | What happens |
| - | - |
| **Check when you are free** | Reads your real open times for a meeting type you picked, a week at a time, and offers a couple of them |
| **Book the meeting** | Books the time the customer chose straight into your Calendly. Calendly emails the confirmation |
| **Send a booking link** | Makes a one-time link to your booking page for a meeting type, so the customer picks a time themselves |

### Booking directly needs a paid Calendly plan

Calendly only lets other apps book a meeting directly on its paid plans
(Standard and above). On a free plan, **Book the meeting** does not fail — it
makes a one-time booking link for the customer instead, and the agent tells them
the meeting is **not** booked until they use it.

The link is also used, on any plan, when a meeting type needs something only
your booking page can collect: required questions you added in Calendly, or a
location the customer has to type in. The card marks those types when you pick
them.

### Sending the link

In a chat — website, WhatsApp, Telegram — the agent gives the link in its reply.

On a phone call it does not read a link out. If the agent can send WhatsApp or
SMS messages, it sends the link that way; if it cannot, it offers to take the
customer's details instead. Turn on **Send a WhatsApp** or **Send an SMS** under
the agent's built-in tools if you want links to reach callers.

### Things worth knowing about Calendly

**It always asks for an email**, as with Cal.com — Calendly needs one for the
confirmation.

**The agent will not invent a time.** It offers only times Calendly returned. If
the customer picks one that has just been taken, the agent checks again and
offers another.

**Times are read in your Calendly account's timezone**, unless the customer says
where they are.

**Disconnecting leaves your bookings alone**, and also removes our access to
your Calendly account.

If the card says **Needs attention**, access was usually removed on Calendly's
side. Click **Connect again** — your meeting types and switches are remembered.

## Deliberately not included

The agent cannot **create, change or delete your meeting types**, in Cal.com
or Calendly. It can book
into them, and that is all. Nobody phoning your business has a good reason to
reshape what your business offers, and the safest way to guarantee that is not to
give the agent the ability at all.


# CRM
Source: https://docs.thinnest.ai/agent/crm

Your agent finds the caller in your HubSpot and writes what it learns into their contact.

Someone rings. The agent looks them up in your CRM by their number, answers from
what you already hold, and writes each new answer into their contact as it
arrives — so a call that ends after two questions still leaves those two answers
behind.

It works on every channel: website chat, WhatsApp, Telegram and phone calls.

Three CRMs can be connected, each its own tile under **Actions → CRM**:
**HubSpot**, **Zoho CRM** and **Zoho Bigin**. This page walks through HubSpot;
the Zoho tiles work the same way, except that you choose a module (usually
Leads or Contacts) and the agent can fill any writable field of it.

> [!NOTE]
>
> This is not the same as **Lead capture**, which stores names and numbers in your
> inbox here. This puts them in **your** CRM, where your team already works. You
> can have both on, and when you do the agent records the details in both places
> rather than choosing between them.

## Connecting HubSpot

Go to **Actions**, find **CRM**, and click **HubSpot**.

**1. Sign in to HubSpot**

You are sent to HubSpot's own page to approve the connection, then brought
back. There is no key to copy.

**2. Choose Contacts**

Click **Find modules** and **Use** Contacts. We read your contact properties
— HubSpot's own and every one you created — and remember them.

**3. Pick the properties the agent fills**

A HubSpot contact has a couple of hundred properties, most of them HubSpot's
own tracking. We start you with the useful ones — name, email, phone,
company, job title, city, lead status and the like — plus every property you
created yourself. Tick or untick, then **Save**. Up to forty.

Read-only and calculated properties are never listed: the agent could not
write them anyway.

**4. Choose what the agent may do**

Everything starts **off**. Connecting HubSpot on its own gives the agent
nothing.

## What the agent may do

| Switch | What happens |
| - | - |
| **Save or update the contact** | Writes what the agent learned into the properties you picked — one contact per conversation, filled in as the call goes |
| **Look someone up** | Finds a contact by phone, email or another picked property, so the agent can answer from what you hold. Reads only |

### Updating the contact you already have

Under **Update an existing record**, pick the property that identifies a person
— usually **Phone Number** or **Email**. When a caller matches it, their answers
go into that contact instead of a new one.

Compare it as a **phone number** and `+91 98018 05137`, `919801805137` and
`9801805137` all count as the same person. On a phone call, the number the call
came from is used when the caller does not say one.

HubSpot keeps one contact per email address. If the agent is about to create a
contact whose email is already in HubSpot, it updates that contact instead.

### When to save

**During the call** writes each answer as it arrives. **After the call** reads
the whole conversation once it ends and writes everything in one go — no pause
mid-call. After-the-call saving is for phone calls; chat and WhatsApp keep
saving as they go, since nothing there ends the way a call does.

### Filling from campaign variables

On a calling campaign the agent may already know things nobody says out loud —
the number it dialled, the lead's name. One per line, `property=variable`, for
example `phone=mobile_no`, fills that property from the campaign.

## Things worth knowing

**Dropdowns take only their own options.** If the caller's answer is not one of
the property's options, the agent is told what the options are rather than
writing something HubSpot would refuse.

**Dates are written as dates.** A date property only takes a real date; an
answer like "next Tuesday" is not saved into it, and the agent is told so.

**Add a property in HubSpot, then find modules again** and use Contacts once
more. Your earlier ticks are kept.

**Disconnecting leaves your contacts alone**, and removes our access to your
HubSpot account.

## If it stops working

The tile says **Last call failed** and the card shows what HubSpot said. Usually
access was removed on HubSpot's side — click **Connect again**. Your properties
and switches are remembered.

## Deliberately not included

The agent works with **contacts only**. It does not create deals, companies,
tickets or tasks, and it cannot delete anything.


# Call your own API
Source: https://docs.thinnest.ai/agent/custom-api

Give the agent one narrow endpoint of yours, and every rule that keeps it safe.

A custom action is an HTTPS endpoint of yours that the agent can call
mid-conversation — an order lookup, a stock check, a booking.

It is the most powerful thing you can give an agent and the one with the
sharpest edges, because it is reachable from a public chat by a stranger who may
be trying to talk the model into using it.

## Defining one

| Field | What it is |
| - | - |
| **Name** | 3–40 characters: lowercase letters, numbers and underscores, starting with a letter |
| **Description** | What the model reads to decide whether to call this at all |
| **Method** | `GET` or `POST` |
| **URL** | Must be `https://`. May contain `{{placeholders}}` |
| **Parameters** | Each with a name and a description |
| **Body template** | For `POST`. JSON, with `{{placeholders}}` |
| **Header secret** | Sent on every call so your endpoint can verify it is us |

### The description is the whole thing

The model has nothing else to go on. It decides whether to call your action, and
with what, entirely from what you write here.

**Weak:**

```
Gets order info
```

**Strong:**

```
Look up a customer's order. Requires BOTH the order number and the email
address on the order — if the customer has given only one, ask for the other
before calling this. Returns found: false when the pair does not match: say you
could not find it and ask them to check both, never say the order does not
exist.
```

The second one tells the model when to call it, when *not* to, what it needs
first, and how to phrase the failure. Every sentence prevents a specific bad
answer.

> [!TIP]
>
> Write the description, then read it back as though you knew nothing about your
> own systems. Anything you had to already know is a sentence that belongs in it.

### Parameters need descriptions too

Every parameter must say what it is, or the model will invent a value. `order_id`
with no description gets filled with something plausible-looking and wrong.

## Placeholders

Use `{{parameter_name}}` in the URL or the body:

```
https://shop.example.com/api/orders/{{order_number}}
```

```json theme={null}
{ "orderNumber": "{{order_number}}", "email": "{{email}}" }
```

Two rules the editor enforces before you can save:

* **Every placeholder must have a parameter behind it.** A `{{order_id}}` with
  no matching parameter would reach your API as the literal text `{{order_id}}`
  — failing in a way that looks like your bug rather than ours.
* **The body must still be valid JSON once the blanks are filled.**

Values are escaped when substituted, so a customer cannot break out of a string
and reshape your request.

## Values the platform fills

Some placeholders are filled by us from the conversation, not by the model, so
a caller cannot talk the agent into sending a different one. They have a dot in
the name, and you do not declare them as parameters.

| Placeholder | Value |
| - | - |
| `{{call.id}}` | The call's id — the same id `GET /api/v1/calls` lists. Empty outside a call |
| `{{call.from}}` | The number the call came from, E.164. Empty outside a call |
| `{{call.to}}` | The number that was dialled, E.164. Empty outside a call |
| `{{call.direction}}` | `inbound` or `outbound`. Empty outside a call |
| `{{conversation.id}}` | The conversation (`conv_…`) |
| `{{contact.id}}` | The contact (`cust_…`) |
| `{{contact.phone}}` | The contact's phone number, E.164, when known |
| `{{agent.id}}` | The agent (`ag_…`) |
| `{{workspace.id}}` | The workspace (`org_…`) — useful when you run customer workspaces |
| `{{test.chat}}` | `true` during a test chat, empty otherwise |

```
https://crm.example.com/calls/{{call.id}}/notes?caller={{call.from}}
```

* They work in the path, the query, the body and in header values. The host
  must be written out in full — a placeholder before the path is refused.
* Header values take only these, never a model parameter.
* An unknown one, such as `{{call.nope}}`, is refused when you save.
* On text chat (WhatsApp chat and web chat) the `call.*` values are empty; the rest still fill.
  Voice calls on every surface, WhatsApp calls and web voice included, fill them.
  A test from the editor or `POST …/actions/{id}/test` has no conversation, so
  only `{{agent.id}}` and `{{workspace.id}}` fill.

Every call also carries `X-Call-Id`, `X-Conversation-Id`, `X-Agent-Id` and
`X-Workspace-Id` headers (each only when known), so you get them without
editing a template. A header you set yourself with the same name wins, whatever its capitalisation
(`x-call-id` replaces `X-Call-Id`).

### During a test chat

A test chat (`POST /api/v1/agents/{id}/test-chat`, or `test_chat` over MCP) runs
your actions for real. So your endpoint can tell, every action request in a test
chat carries an `X-Test-Chat: true` header and `{{test.chat}}` fills as `true`.
There is no call, so `{{call.id}}` and `{{call.from}}` are empty and `X-Call-Id`
is not sent. Check for the header and answer as normal without writing anything
— no order placed, no record created — so testing never changes your real data.
Outside a test chat the header is never sent.

A test chat can also be run **as a call**: send `"mode": "call"` (or `mode` on the
`test_chat` MCP tool). The turn then uses the agent's call prompt, its call rules or
the built-in ones plus the speaking rules, on the model its calls use and, on your
own Gemini key, the thinking level a call uses, with no cards or buttons. It shows the
words a caller will be given, which is how to try Telugu wording before a call. It is
not the voice or the hearing, and not the call's own tools such as transferring or
hanging up. It needs calling set up on the agent.

Only the API's test chat is marked. A chat in the console's **Playground**, a
live conversation and a test of a single action from the editor are not, and the
tools of an MCP server you have connected to the agent are not marked either.

## Reserved names

These clash with the agent's built-in tools and are refused: `search_knowledge`,
`capture_lead`, `escalate_to_human`, `send_media`, `send_link`.

Anything else you connect is namespaced, so no third-party tool can impersonate
one of the agent's own.

## Security

> [accordion] HTTPS only, checked twice
>
> Once when you save it — so you hear about an `http://` address while looking
> at the form — and again at call time.

> [accordion] The URL is resolved before we fetch it
>
> Validated **and DNS-resolved**, so an address cannot be used to reach a
> private network from inside ours.

> [accordion] Your secret is encrypted and shown once
>
> Stored encrypted, not readable from the dashboard, and never displayed again
> after you save it.

> [accordion] Thirty calls per conversation, per hour
>
> Custom actions are the only tool that spends *your* money, so the cap is a
> per-conversation one. A conversation is the unit a visitor controls, so it is
> the unit that gets bounded — a workspace-wide cap would be one a single
> visitor could exhaust for everybody.
>
> Thirty is far above any honest conversation. Checking an order, a booking and
> a balance twice over is under ten.

## Writing the endpoint

Four rules, in order of how much trouble they save.

**1. Check the shared secret first**

Before parsing anything.

```js theme={null}
if (req.get("X-Agent-Secret") !== process.env.AGENT_SECRET) {
  return res.status(401).json({ error: "unauthorised" });
}
```

**2. Require two facts, never one**

An order number alone is guessable — they are usually sequential. Require the
number **and** something only the real customer knows, like the email on the
order.

**3. Fail identically for "not found" and "wrong match"**

```js theme={null}
// Same response either way. A different one for each is an oracle telling a
// stranger which order numbers are real.
if (!order) return res.json({ found: false });
```

**4. Return the smallest useful object**

Everything you return may end up spoken to the customer. Return the status
and the tracking link, not the whole order record with the customer's address
and payment details in it.

```js theme={null}
return res.json({
  found: true,
  status: order.status,
  carrier: order.carrier ?? null,
  trackingUrl: order.trackingUrl ?? null,
});
```

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Never write an action that changes something irreversible.** Cancelling an
> order, issuing a refund, deleting a booking — these should not be one
> conversation away from a stranger who is good at persuasion. Read actions
> first; for writes, [escalate to a person](/agent/escalation) instead.

## When it fails

A timeout, a 500, or an unreachable host does not crash the conversation. The
agent is told the lookup failed and answers accordingly — normally by
[handing over to a person](/agent/escalation) rather than guessing.

Which is the argument for having escalation switched on wherever you have
actions: the failure mode of "I could not check that" is much better when there
is somebody to pass it to.

## Sending leads somewhere

The other direction: signed outbound webhooks to any HTTPS endpoint, fired when
something happens rather than when the model asks. That is the lane that reaches
Google Sheets, Zoho and effectively any CRM through Zapier or Make.

## A full worked example

[Answer "where is my order?"](/guides/order-status) builds one end to end — the
endpoint, the action config, the description text, and the four cases to test.


# Escalation
Source: https://docs.thinnest.ai/agent/escalation

How the agent hands a conversation to a person — including when an action fails.

The counterpart to knowledge search: one finds an answer, this one admits there
isn't one.

Without it the agent's only options are to guess or to apologise into the void,
and you never learn it happened.

## The two triggers

Both behind one switch per agent: **Actions → Hand over to a person**.

| Trigger | Fires when |
| - | - |
| **When the material does not cover it** | A knowledge search found nothing and guessing would be worse than waiting |
| **When the customer asks** | They ask for a person, or are clearly upset |

Turning one off **removes the capability**, rather than asking the model to
refrain. A model that has a tool will eventually use it; a model without one
cannot.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **A business with nobody watching the inbox should turn escalation off
> entirely.** An escalation nobody answers is worse than a straight "I don't
> know", because the customer waits for something that is not coming.

## What happens when it fires

**1. The conversation is flagged**

Status changes to **escalated** and it surfaces in the inbox.

**2. A note is written for whoever picks it up**

One sentence on what the customer wants and what the agent could not find —
written for a colleague, not for a log.

**3. Your integrations fire**

Outbound webhooks are delivered, and if you have connected one, a
[helpdesk ticket](/workspace/helpdesk) opens in Zendesk or Salesforce with
the transcript.

**4. The customer is told**

The agent says a person will follow up. It does not go quiet.

## On a phone call: putting the caller through

With **Call transfer** chosen in **Hand over to a person**, a caller on the phone
is also put through to the number you give. Choose how:

* **Cold** (the default) — the phone rings and the caller is connected as soon as
  someone answers.
* **Warm** — whoever answers first hears a short spoken summary of who is calling
  and what they need, then the caller is connected. The caller hears the phone
  ringing meanwhile. Add **Press 1 to accept** and the caller is connected only
  once that person presses 1, so a voicemail never takes the call; choose
  **Connect after the summary** to connect as soon as it has played.

Press 1 to accept is not available on Telnyx numbers yet. The details are on
[Voice](/channels/voice#handing-a-call-on).

## Escalation from a failed action

The case worth planning for.

When a [custom action](/agent/custom-api) times out, returns a 500, or cannot be
reached, the agent is told the lookup failed. It does **not** invent an answer
and it does not pretend the tool succeeded.

What it does next depends on whether escalation is available:

| Escalation | What the customer gets |
| - | - |
| **On** | "I can't reach our order system right now — I've passed this to the team and someone will come back to you." |
| **Off** | "I can't check that at the moment. Please try again shortly." |

> [!TIP]
>
> **Switch escalation on wherever you have custom actions.** The failure mode of
> "I could not check that" is far better when there is somebody to pass it to —
> and your API will be down at some point, whatever your uptime target says.

The same applies when a customer hits the [per-conversation action
limit](/agent/custom-api#security): the agent stops calling and hands over
rather than continuing without the information.

## Once a person takes over

The agent **stops replying to that thread entirely**. Two voices answering the
same customer, contradicting each other, is worse than a slower answer.

When a teammate replies, the agent later reads that reply as its own prior turn
— so if the conversation returns to it, it does not re-answer something a person
just handled.

## It escalates once

The agent is told to call it once per conversation. Calling it again does not
make anybody arrive sooner, and a thread that escalates four times is four
notifications about one problem.

## If flagging fails

If the escalation cannot be recorded for some reason, the agent still tells the
customer a person will follow up — because the conversation is in the inbox
either way, and promising nothing is worse than promising something you will
honour by reading it.

## Related

> [card] [Inbox](/workspace/inbox)
>
> Where escalations land, and how taking over works.

> [card] [Helpdesk](/workspace/helpdesk)
>
> Escalations as Zendesk or Salesforce tickets, with replies routed back.

> [card] [Custom API](/agent/custom-api)
>
> The actions whose failures escalation catches.

> [card] [Analytics](/workspace/analytics)
>
> "Needed a person" over time — not a failure metric, a working one.


# Find leads
Source: https://docs.thinnest.ai/agent/find-leads

Describe the businesses you want. Your agent finds them and brings back their phone numbers and emails.

Find leads is the first tab on **Leads**. You describe the kind of business you
want to reach — "real-estate developers in Pune", "dental clinics in Bengaluru" —
and an agent finds them and brings back their phone numbers and email addresses. The people who came to *your*
agents are on the second tab, [Inbound leads](/agent/leads).

## Find your first leads

**1. Describe the businesses**

Open **Leads**. Type who you want to reach, or start from one of the
examples. Add a place: "in Pune" finds far better than "developers".

**2. Answer one question, if it asks**

A broad request ("builders") gets one question with a few answers to tick —
which city, what kind. Tick, add your own, or skip it.

**3. Choose how many and start**

The agent shows what it will look for. Pick 25, 50, 100, 250 or 500 leads and
**Start search**. Before it starts you see the most the search can cost.

**4. Watch them arrive**

The chat on the left shows each search the agent runs; the table on the right
fills in as leads are found. You can leave the page — the search carries on —
and **Stop** it whenever you like.

## Ask for more, or something different

After a search, just talk to the agent in the box under the chat.

* **"2 more"**, **"20 more please"**, **"keep going"** — it searches again for
  different businesses and adds them to the same table, up to 500 leads in a
  search. You only pay for the new leads.
* **"Only the ones with an email"**, **"now in Mumbai"**, **"also include
  orthodontists"** — it changes the search and starts the next one in the same chat.
* **"Interior designers in Hyderabad"** — a different search, in the same chat.
* Say how many in the same message — **"10 dentists in Pune"** — and it starts
  straight away.

Your earlier searches stay in the chat, each with a **View leads** button that
brings its table back. **Back to new search** (the arrow beside **Leads**) starts a
fresh chat.

## What you get for each lead

A row in the table: the business, its website, phone, email, location and what
kind of business it is.

* **Only what the website itself prints.** A number or email is included only if
  it is on the business's own page. The link beside the website opens that exact
  page, so you can check any of them.
* **The business's public details, not a person's.** Expect a main line, a sales
  number, a toll-free number or a general address such as `info@` — not the direct
  number of a named person.
* **More than one number or email?** The first is shown, with **+2** or similar;
  hover it to see the rest.

## What it costs

* **₹1 for each lead** (one cent if your workspace is billed in dollars), taken
  from your balance. No GST is added.
* **The first 50 leads are free** — in your workspace's first month of Find leads,
  counted from your first search. They are counted per workspace and per person.
* **You only pay for a lead:** a business with a phone number or email on its own
  website that you don't already have. Sites that were not a match, sites with no
  contact details, businesses already in your contacts and businesses an earlier
  search found are never charged.
* **When the balance runs out,** the search pauses. Add money and press
  **Continue**. A workspace with no balance — the free trial — is asked to choose a
  plan once its free leads are used.

The price is also on each plan card in **Settings → Billing**.

## Do something with them

Tick the leads you want, then:

* **Save to Contacts** — they become contacts in your workspace, and go into a
  [group](/agent/leads#groups) you choose or create.
* **Send WhatsApp** — saves them to a group and opens a
  [broadcast](/whatsapp/broadcasts) already aimed at it.
* **Call with an Agent** — saves them to a group and opens a
  [calling campaign](/channels/voice-campaigns) already aimed at it.

Saving asks you to confirm that **contacting these businesses is your
responsibility**. These businesses have not asked to hear from you, so read the
next section before you send anything.

## Before you contact them

* **Calls.** Calling businesses that have not asked to be called is covered by
  India's telemarketing rules, including Do Not Disturb. Your calling campaign
  still respects calling hours and your do-not-contact list; the rules themselves
  are yours to follow.
* **WhatsApp.** WhatsApp expects people to have opted in. A broadcast to found
  businesses is allowed, but complaints and blocks lower your WhatsApp account's
  quality rating and can get it limited. Send only what they would expect from a
  business like yours.
* **Anyone who says stop is never contacted again,** on any campaign, whichever
  way they were found.

## Save a search, run it again

On a finished search, **Save search** gives it a name and keeps it at the top of
the start screen under **Saved searches**. **History** lists your recent
searches. **Run again** repeats a search: businesses you already have come back as
duplicates and are not charged, so a rerun pays only for new ones.

## Limits

* One search at a time in a workspace, and 30 a day.
* Up to 500 leads a search. A search ends early if it is finding nothing, and says
  so.
* Businesses in India.
* Leads stay in your workspace. They are not in the Contacts download or in the
  contacts API.

## Not available yet

* Workspaces of a white-label client, and customers of a developer: their usage is
  billed through somebody else, and this is not part of that yet.
* Finding leads from the API or the MCP server.
* Repeating a saved search automatically every week.


# Insights
Source: https://docs.thinnest.ai/agent/insights

What your calls came to: how they ended, the objections, why the no's were no's, what is broken on the customer's side, and a follow-up list for the team.

"Calls connected" says a call happened. **Insights** says what it came to, and what to do next.

## Switch it on

Call insights are off until you switch them on, for each agent: **Agents** → the agent → **Voice** → **Call insights**.
After each answered phone or WhatsApp call, the call is read once and noted (Playground, share-link and website
calls are not read, so your own tests are never counted):

* **How it ended** — converted, interested, call back, promise to pay, not interested, no decision, wrong person, do
  not call. *Converted* means the customer agreed to what the call was for: bought, booked, paid, signed up.
* **The objections** — in the customer's own words ("The EMI is too high", "Call me after salary day"), each with its
  kind: price, timing, trust, not a fit, no need, not their decision, uses someone else.
* **Why a no was a no** — price, timing, trust, not a fit, already has one.
* **What is broken on your side** — a payment link that does not open, a double charge, an app login that fails.
* **The next step** — a callback, a promised payment, details to send, a visit, or a lead ready for sales, with the
  day (and time) agreed.

Missed calls and calls where the customer never spoke are not read.

## The Insights page

**Insights** in the sidebar, for the last 7, 30 or 90 days, for every agent or one:

* **Answered calls read**, **Converted** (and its share), and how many are **to follow up**.
* **How calls ended**, **Why the no's were no's**, the **objections** by kind and the ones said most often, and what is
  **broken on the customer's side**, with examples.
* **The follow-up list** — every next step not yet done, the oldest due first, overdue ones in red. **Open** goes to the
  conversation; **Done** takes it off the list for everybody. Each contact shows once, with the step their latest
  call settled: a later call replaces an earlier step.

**Download CSV** on the Insights page saves the range and agent you are looking at, one row a call: when it was
read, the contact, the agent, how it ended, why not, the objections and issues, the next step and its day, and whether
the step is open, done or replaced by a later call.

## On each call

Open a call in **Usage** and its first tab shows the summary and the insight: how it ended, why not, the objections,
problems on the customer's side, and the next step.

Through the API and webhooks, `insights` comes on `call.analysed`, Get Call and Get Call Analysis: `outcome`,
`noReason`, `objections` and `issues` (each `{ text, kind }`), and `nextStep` (`kind`, `at`, `note`, `status`,
`followedUpAt`). `status` is `open` while the step is on the follow-up list, `done` once someone marked it Done, and
`replaced` when a later call with the same contact settled a newer step. `insights` is `null` when the agent's Call
insights is off, or for a call that was not read.

Only what the customer actually said is noted: nothing is guessed, and a date the call did not settle is left empty.
When a call's content is deleted, its insights go with it.


# Knowledge
Source: https://docs.thinnest.ai/agent/knowledge

What the agent answers from, and what it will refuse to guess at.

The agent answers from material you give it. When a search finds nothing, it
says it does not know rather than inventing an answer — that behaviour is the
point, and it is what makes the answers worth trusting.

## Ways to add material

> [accordion] A single page
>
> Paste a URL. Good for a returns policy or a pricing page you want indexed on
> its own.

> [accordion] A whole site crawl
>
> Paste your homepage and choose a depth of 1 to 3 levels. You see the list of
> pages found and **pick which ones to index before anything is ingested** —
> a crawl is a proposal, not a commitment.

> [accordion] A sitemap
>
> Reaches pages a crawl cannot: unlinked pages, pages only reachable from
> search, anything not in your navigation. If a crawl missed something
> important, this is usually why.

> [accordion] Pasted text
>
> For the policies that live in someone's head rather than on a page. Often
> the highest-value thing you will add.

> [accordion] Files
>
> `.txt`, `.md`, `.csv` and PDFs with a text layer.
>
> CSVs are chunked **row by row**, so a price never gets separated from its
> product.

## What is not supported

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Scanned documents do not work.** There is no OCR. A PDF that is really a
> photograph of a page will ingest and contribute nothing, which is worse than
> failing loudly — so check that you can select the text in your PDF before
> uploading it.
>
> Also unsupported: images, video, and Word or Excel files. Export to PDF, CSV
> or text first.

## Getting good answers

**Fewer, better pages.** Four hundred pages of navigation chrome make retrieval
worse, not better. Index the pages that answer questions.

**Write the answer down somewhere.** If three customers a week ask something
your site never states, no amount of crawling will find it. Paste it in as text.

**Check the gaps report.** [Analytics](/workspace/analytics) lists the questions
the agent searched for and found nothing on. Each row is something worth adding
— it is the most directly useful page in the product.

## Knowledge and language

You do not need a knowledge base per language. Keep your material in one
language; the agent translates as it answers, in whichever of the 37 supported
languages the customer is using.


# Leads and contacts
Source: https://docs.thinnest.ai/agent/leads

Ending the conversation with somebody to call, not just a closed ticket.

A support bot answers a question and the visitor leaves. This one answers the
question **and** leaves you a name and a reason to call.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Leads** has two tabs. **Inbound leads** is this page: people who came to your
> agents. **Find leads** goes the other way — your agent finds
> businesses you want to reach. See [Find leads](/agent/find-leads).

## How a lead gets captured

When a visitor shows real interest, the agent asks for their details in the flow
of the conversation and records:

* name
* email
* phone
* **a one-line note on what they actually wanted**

That last field is the one that matters. "Priya, kitchen quote, 12ft run,
budget around ₹4L" is a callback worth making. A bare phone number is not.

## Partial details are still a lead

A phone number on its own is recorded. Later turns add to the same record rather
than starting a new one, so a customer who gives their name first and their
number three messages later ends up as one contact.

## Switching it off

Per agent, on **Actions → Capture leads**. Off removes the capability entirely — the agent has no way to ask
rather than being asked not to.

Worth turning off for a pure support agent, where asking for contact details
reads as a sales tactic and annoys people.

## Contacts

Everyone who has spoken to an agent, **leads first**, with what they asked for.
One click goes from a contact to the conversation that produced them, so
whoever calls back can read what was actually said.

## Groups

A group is a named list of contacts you put together yourself — "Wholesale
buyers", "Pune walk-ins" — so you can send a broadcast or run a voice campaign to
exactly those people.

**1. Create the group**

On **Contacts**, choose **New group** and name it. Names are unique in your
workspace, whatever the capitals.

**2. Add people**

Tick contacts in the list (the box at the top ticks everyone on the page),
then **Add to group** and pick the group. Somebody already in it is left as
they are. A contact can be in any number of groups.

**3. Open it**

Each group is a chip above the list with how many people are in it. Open one
to see only its members; tick people there and **Remove from** the group to
take them out.

The **⋯** beside an open group renames or deletes it. Deleting a group never
deletes its contacts.

A group decides *who you are aiming at*, never *who agreed*. Consent still
applies to everybody in it — see
[narrowing by group](/whatsapp/broadcasts#narrowing-by-tag-or-group).

## Contact language

Each contact can carry a language. Where a WhatsApp template exists in several
languages, the contact's language decides which one they receive.

> [!NOTE]
>
> A contact with no language set gets exactly what they would have got before —
> your default. Setting the field is an improvement, never a prerequisite.

## Consent

Contacts carry a marketing consent state, and it is enforced in the database
rather than in the interface. A campaign audience is computed at send time from
consent — never from a list somebody exported last week.

Businesses you found with [Find leads](/agent/find-leads) have not opted in, and
saving them asks you to confirm that contacting them is your responsibility. They
are the one exception to the opt-in rule for WhatsApp broadcasts; calls and
everything else here still apply, and anyone who says stop is never contacted again.

Somebody who opts out stops receiving **marketing**. Utility and authentication
messages still reach them, and must: an order confirmation is not something
anybody opted out of.


# Spreadsheet
Source: https://docs.thinnest.ai/agent/spreadsheet

Your agent writes what it learns into your spreadsheet while it is still talking, and can look things up in it.

Someone rings and gives their name, their number and what they want. The agent
writes each answer into a row of your spreadsheet as it arrives, so a call that
ends after two questions still leaves those two answers behind. It can also look
somebody up — an order, a booking, a customer record — and answer from what you
already hold.

It works on every channel: website chat, WhatsApp, Telegram and phone calls.

We use **Grist**, a spreadsheet you can sign up for free at
[getgrist.com](https://www.getgrist.com). You connect your own account; we never
put your data in ours.

> [!NOTE]
>
> This is not the same as **Lead capture**, which stores names and numbers in your
> inbox here. This puts them in **your** spreadsheet, in columns you chose, where
> your team already works. You can have both on, and when you do the agent records
> the details in both places rather than choosing between them.

## Connecting your spreadsheet

Go to **Actions**, find **Spreadsheet**, and click **Grist**.

**1. Get an API key from Grist**

In Grist, click your profile picture → **Account settings** → **Developer**,
and create a key in the **API keys** section.

It does not expire until you remove it, so unlike a calendar key there is
nothing here that quietly stops working next year.

**2. Paste it in**

We call Grist once to check the key really belongs to someone. If it does
not work you are told immediately.

**3. Give us the document**

Open the document in Grist, go to **Settings** and find the **API** section.
Copy the **Document ID** from there.

> [!WARNING]
>
> The id in your browser's address bar is a **shorter** one, and the API
> cannot use it. If you paste that, we tell you so rather than letting you
> discover it as "document not found".

**4. Pick the table**

We show you every table in the document with how many fields each has. Pick
one. We then read that table's real column names and remember them.

That is what the agent fills in. It cannot invent a column, and it cannot
reach any other table or any other document.

## What the agent may do

Two switches, both **off** until you turn them on. Connecting your spreadsheet on
its own gives the agent nothing.

| Switch | What happens |
| - | - |
| **Fill in a row** | Writes what it has learned into your table — one row per conversation, filled in as the answers arrive |
| **Look something up** | Finds rows by matching one column exactly, so the agent can answer from what you already hold |

> [!NOTE]
>
> Every switch you turn on — here, on your calendar, anywhere — is described to
> the agent on **every turn of every call**. A handful is sharp and quick. A long
> list is a slower reply from an agent less sure which one you meant. Nothing
> stops you, so the restraint is yours.

## Filling the lead's own row, not a new one

A lead list usually arrives with a row per person already in it — imported from
an ad, a form or a CSV — and the job of the call is to fill in the rest. Left
alone, every call adds a fresh line underneath and the row you already had stays
half empty.

On the spreadsheet card, pick the column that identifies each person under
**Update an existing row**, and how to compare it:

| Comparing as | Use it for | What matches |
| - | - | - |
| **Phone number** | Mobile numbers | The last ten digits, so `+91 98018 05137`, `919801805137` and `98018-05137` are one person |
| **Exact value** | An application id, an email, a name | The same text, ignoring case and spacing |

When a caller matches, their answers go into **that** row. When nobody matches,
a new row is added as before.

> [!NOTE]
>
> We never guess the column. A column called *Contact* might hold an email or a
> phone number, and a wrong guess writes one customer's answers over another's.

### Filling in what the call already knew

On a campaign you already know things the customer is never asked — their name
and number came from your own list. A model told not to repeat those back never
volunteers them either, so they would stay blank.

**Fill from campaign variables** on the same card maps a column to a variable
your campaign supplies, one per line:

```
MOBILE_NO=phone
CANDIDATE_NAME=name
```

Anything the agent did learn wins; this only fills what was left blank.

## When to save: during the call, or after it

A switch on the spreadsheet card, and it only changes **phone calls**.

| | |
| - | - |
| **During the call** | Rows fill in as the customer answers, so the sheet is current while the call is still going. Each save costs the caller a short pause. |
| **After the call** | The agent just asks its questions. The whole conversation is read once it ends and the row is written in one go. |

Reading afterwards is usually the better call, and not only for the pause:

* An answer given in the first minute lands in the right column even if the
  question came in the fourth.
* Someone who corrects themselves — *"sorry, it's 42, not 41"* — is recorded
  once, correctly, instead of twice.
* A call that ends abruptly still leaves everything that was said.

What you give up is liveness: nothing appears until the call is over.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Chat and WhatsApp always save as they go.** Nothing there ends the way a
> call does, so there is no "after" to wait for. The switch is about calls.

## Save in the background

A switch on the same card. With it on, the agent **stops waiting for Grist**.

The answer is kept here the moment the customer gives it, and reaches your
spreadsheet within a minute. Nothing is lost if Grist is slow, and nothing is
lost if you have used up a free plan's calls for the month — the work waits and
goes through when it can.

**Turn it on if your agent answers the phone.** A caller hears every second the
agent spends waiting, and this removes all of them.

**Leave it off if you watch the sheet live** — during a campaign, say — and want
the row to appear as the words are spoken.

Either way the agent never claims something is saved when it is not.

## What your customer experiences

> **Them:** Hi, I'd like a quote for a kitchen.
> **Agent:** Of course. Can I take your name?
> **Them:** Priya Nair.
> **Agent:** Thanks Priya. And the best number to reach you on?

By the end of that call there is one row in your spreadsheet with both answers in
it, plus anything else you have columns for.

## A column for what happened

Make a column called **Summary** — or Notes, Remarks, Comments — and turn on
**Summarise each call** on the Playground, and it fills with two or three
sentences about what the customer said and how the call ended.

It is the one column that is filled even when nothing else could be: somebody
who says only *"not interested, I'm busy"* answers no question on your list, and
that sentence is the whole useful record of the call.

> [!WARNING]
>
