| Yes | Your **GST certificate** |
| No | Your **Certificate of Incorporation**, or your **Udyam certificate** — whichever you hold |

That is the whole form. PDF, JPG or PNG, up to 5 MB.

> [!NOTE]
>
> Send it as registered. The name you type is checked against the certificate you
> attach, so an abbreviation or a trading name is the usual reason an application
> comes back.

#### Following it up

The **KYC** tab shows where the application stands, asked afresh each time you
open the page rather than remembered from last time:

* **Being checked** — sent, usually decided within minutes.
* **Approved** — you can take an Indian number.
* **Not accepted** — the reason is shown with it. **Correct and resend** puts the
  form back up.
* **Suspended** or **Expired** — send your documents again.

Each application has a **reference**. If you ask us to chase one, that is the
thing to quote.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **We keep a copy of the document you sent**, so correcting an application does
> not mean going and finding the file again. You can download it from the same
> tab; that needs an owner or admin.

> [!WARNING]
>
> You cannot buy an Indian number until this is approved — pressing Buy takes you
> to the form instead. Numbers in every other country need none of it.

#### Doing it from the API

If you run a platform with one workspace per customer, each customer's business
is verified in **its own workspace** — the application belongs to the workspace,
not to you. Send the customer's details with the `Thinnest-Workspace` header
(see [Build a platform](/guides/build-a-platform)) and the same form the console
shows is filled in for them.

For each business you need three things: its **legal name**, whether it is
**registered for GST** (yes or no), and **one document** — the GST certificate if
it is, otherwise the Certificate of Incorporation or the Udyam certificate. PDF,
JPG or PNG, up to 5 MB, with a file name of 99 characters or fewer.

```bash theme={null}
curl -X PUT https://app.thinnest.ai/api/v1/phone-numbers/business-details \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $API_KEY" \
  -H "Thinnest-Workspace: org_3f6a9c21-7d4e-4b58-9a1f-0c2e8b7d5a34" \
  -F businessName="Acme Traders Private Limited" \
  -F gstRegistered=true \
  -F document=@gst-certificate.pdf
```

Without GST, send `-F gstRegistered=false` and the certificate you hold, adding
`-F documentKind=udyam` if it is a Udyam certificate (`incorporation` is
assumed). The answer is the application, and the status in it is the same set the
KYC tab shows:

```json theme={null}
{
  "status": "submitted",
  "businessName": "Acme Traders Private Limited",
  "gstRegistered": true,
  "documentKind": "gst",
  "submittedAt": "2026-10-08T09:41:12.380Z",
  "canRent": false
}
```

[Get Business Details](/api-reference/phone-numbers/get-business-details) reads it
back at any time, and checks it afresh each time. The check usually finishes in a
few minutes; when `canRent` turns `true`, [Rent
Phone Number](/api-reference/phone-numbers/rent-phone-number) will issue an Indian
number. If the application comes back `rejected`, `reviewNote` says what to
correct, and sending again corrects that same application. Sending while one is
being checked, or after it was approved, is refused with `409`.

This needs a **full** key and a paid plan: the document goes to India's numbering
authority in your customer's name, so a build or read-only key cannot send it
(any key can read it). We never return the document itself.

### Marketing calls need a different number

Indian rules give every number a purpose, and it is worth knowing before you buy
one rather than after you build a campaign.

| What you are calling about | The number for it |
| - | - |
| Reminders, order updates, renewals, anything the customer is expecting | The numbers on this page — landlines, bought in a few clicks |
| **Marketing** — an offer, a promotion, anything selling | A **140** number, which is applied for in your business's name |

A 140 number is not sold from a list. It is issued to your business after you
register on the DLT portal, so choosing **Promotional (140)** when adding a
number shows you the steps rather than a search.

**1. Register your business on the DLT portal**

As both the *principal entity* and the *telemarketer* — the calls are yours,
so the registration is yours. Two to three working days.

**2. Send us your certificates**

Your GST certificate and both DLT registrations. We apply for the number and
hand you back the approval letter it needs.

**3. Register your header and your script**

On the same portal. Scripts are approved one at a time — a marketing call
says an approved thing, not whatever you type on the day.

Five to ten working days end to end. Get in touch and we will start it.

> [!WARNING]
>
> Check this before anything else: the telemarketer registration has to be in
> **Maharashtra** or **Karnataka**. Registered anywhere else and we cannot get
> you a 140 number today.

> [!NOTE]
>
> Until you hold one, a campaign marked *promotional* is refused rather than
> quietly sent from a landline. That refusal is the rule working — it is the
> number that carries the penalty, not us — and it names the number it is about
> so you know which one to change.

## Using a number you already own

If your number is with **Plivo**, **Vobiz**, **Twilio** or **Telnyx**, you can
point it at your agent and keep it where it is. You go on paying them for the
number and we charge you nothing for it — we only answer it. **Twilio and Telnyx
work a little differently** — we set the number up for you; see
[Numbers from Twilio](#numbers-from-twilio) and
[Numbers from Telnyx](#numbers-from-telnyx) below. The steps here are for Plivo
and Vobiz.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **A Plivo, Twilio or Telnyx number needs your account's credentials before it
> can answer.** Plivo and Twilio sign every call with your Auth Token, and we use
> it to confirm each call really came from your account — without it, calls to
> the number are refused. On Telnyx your API key is how we set the number up at
> all. A Vobiz number answers without them; there, the credentials are only
> needed for outgoing calls.

**1. Open Buy / Import number on the Phone Numbers page**

Choose **Import**, then say which carrier the number is with.

**2. Plivo only: add your account's keys first**

Paste the **Auth ID** and **Auth Token** from your Plivo console. Plivo signs
every call with your Auth Token, and that signature is how we tell a real
call to your number from somebody pretending to be one — so until we have it,
calls to the number are refused. The same keys are what your outgoing calls
go out on. (Vobiz needs nothing here to answer calls.)

**3. Type the number**

Exactly as it is dialled, including the country code.

**4. Point it at us**

Set the address shown as the number's **Answer URL** in your carrier's
console, with the method set to **POST**. Copy the whole thing — everything
after the question mark matters, and a shortened address will not be
recognised.

For one of the two carriers the address is the same for every number and is
shown straight away, so you can set your console up first if you prefer. For
the other it carries a key unique to the number, so it appears once the
number is added. Either way that address belongs to the number, so it keeps
working if you later move the number to a different agent.

**5. Say which agent answers it**

Back on the **Phone Numbers** page, choose the agent under **Inbound**.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **A Plivo number does not answer until its keys are saved.** If you added one
> before the keys were asked for, its row on the **Phone Numbers** page says so —
> open the row's menu, choose **Edit credentials**, and save them.

> [!WARNING]
>
> Until the Answer URL is set, the number rings and nothing picks up. Nothing on
> this page can tell you that has happened, because the call never reaches us —
> so if a test call goes unanswered, check the Answer URL first.

A number on any other carrier cannot be pointed at us. We check that each call
genuinely came from the carrier it claims to, and a call from anywhere else is
refused before it is answered.

### Numbers from Twilio

A Twilio number is set up the other way round from the two above. Instead of you
pasting an address into your carrier's console, **you give us your Twilio account
and we set the number up for you.**

**1. Choose Twilio under Import**

The credentials box comes first, because Twilio is the one carrier where it
is needed before the number.

**2. Add your Account SID and Auth Token**

Both are on your Twilio console's home page. The Account SID starts with
**AC**. We check them with Twilio before saving, and the token is stored
encrypted and never shown again.

**3. Type the number, with its country code**

For example **+1 415 555 0100**. A number typed without a country code is
read as an Indian one, and we will then not find it on your account.

**4. That is it**

We confirm the number is on your Twilio account and point it at us there.
The dialog still shows the two addresses we set, in case you ever want to
check them or set them yourself.

**5. Say which agent answers it**

On the **Phone Numbers** page, choose the agent under **Inbound**.

> [!WARNING]
>
> Pointing a Twilio number at us **replaces whatever it was set to**. If the
> number already runs something of yours — an IVR, a forwarding rule — that stops
> receiving its calls. If it had an address set, the dialog tells you what it was
> so you can put it back, and removing the number here clears the address we set
> and does not restore the old one. Import a number that is free to use.

> [!NOTE]
>
> We need your Auth Token because Twilio signs every call with it, and that
> signature is how we tell a real call to your number from somebody pretending
> to be one. **If you change your Auth Token in Twilio, save the new one** from
> the number's menu (**Edit credentials**) — until you do, calls to the number
> are refused and we tell you so.

> [!NOTE]
>
> A workspace works with **one Twilio account**. If you save a different Account
> SID while Twilio numbers from the first account are still added here, we
> refuse it — those numbers would stop receiving calls. Remove the Twilio numbers
> first, then connect the other account. Saving a new Auth Token for the *same*
> account is always fine.

> [!NOTE]
>
> If we could not set the number up for you — your Twilio account may have
> restricted it — the dialog says so and shows what to set: in Twilio, open the
> number and set **A call comes in** to the Voice URL and **Call status changes**
> to the status callback, both **HTTP POST**.

What a Twilio number does not do yet: **answering-machine detection** (so no
voicemail message) and **transferring a call to a person**. Call recording works
on it — see [Recording calls on a number you brought](#recording-calls-on-a-number-you-brought).

### Numbers from Telnyx

A Telnyx number is set up for you too, and it takes **one API key** rather than
an ID and a token.

**1. Choose Telnyx under Import**

The key comes first, for the same reason as on Twilio: we need it before we
can find the number and set it up.

**2. Paste an API key from your Telnyx portal**

Create one under **API Keys** in the Telnyx portal. We check it with Telnyx
before saving, and it is stored encrypted and never shown again. Saving it
creates an application on your Telnyx account called **ThinnestAI voice
agent** — that is what answers your number and places your outgoing calls, so
leave it in place.

**3. Type the number, with its country code**

For example **+1 415 555 0100**. A number typed without a country code is
read as an Indian one, and we will then not find it on your account.

**4. That is it**

We confirm the number is on your Telnyx account and assign it to that
application. Nothing to paste.

**5. Say which agent answers it**

On the **Phone Numbers** page, choose the agent under **Inbound**.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Telnyx only calls the countries your account allows.** A new Telnyx account
> allows the United States and Canada. To call India — or anywhere else — add the
> country to your **outbound voice profile** in the Telnyx portal (Voice →
> Outbound Voice Profiles) before you place calls; until then Telnyx refuses
> them, and the call shows as failed here. Telnyx may ask you to verify your
> account before it allows some countries.

> [!WARNING]
>
> Assigning a Telnyx number to our application **replaces whatever it was
> connected to**. If it was connected to something else of yours, the dialog
> tells you its name so you can move it back; removing the number here takes it
> off our application and does not restore the old one.

> [!NOTE]
>
> A workspace works with **one Telnyx account**. A key from a different account
> is refused while numbers from the first are still added here — remove those
> numbers first. A new key for the *same* account is always fine, and if you had
> deleted our application in Telnyx, saving a key makes a new one and moves your
> numbers onto it.

> [!NOTE]
>
> If we could not assign the number for you, the dialog says so. In the Telnyx
> portal, open the number and set its connection to the application called
> **ThinnestAI voice agent**.

When we turn a call to a Telnyx number away — no agent set to answer it, or the
workspace out of balance — the caller hears a **busy tone** rather than a
sentence.

A Telnyx number does what a number from us does: it **records**, it **detects
answering machines** (so a campaign can leave a voicemail), and it **transfers a
call to a person**. Telnyx charges your Telnyx account a small fee for each call
it checks for an answering machine, and the call to the person you transfer to
goes on your Telnyx bill like any other call.

### Recording calls on a number you brought

With **Record calls** on, phone calls on a number you brought are recorded too,
whichever company it is with. Your carrier is not asked to record anything — your
agent hears both sides of the call and keeps the recording here, so it plays
with its call in [Usage](/workspace/usage), downloads, and is deleted on your
plan's schedule exactly like any other recording.

### A transferred call on a number you brought

When your agent puts a caller through to a person on a number you brought, **we
stop charging at the moment of the transfer.** From then on the two people talk
on your carrier's line, on your carrier's bill, with no agent involved. (On a
number you took from us the call is billed to its end, because we pay the
carrier for those minutes.)

### Calling out from a number you brought

Outgoing calls go out through the account the number belongs to — and for your
own number, that account is yours, even if your carrier happens to be the same
one we buy numbers from. So there is one more step, and only if you want
outgoing calls: in the same **Import** panel, add the **Auth ID** and **Auth
token** from your carrier's console. (For Plivo, Twilio and Telnyx you have
already done this — it came first.)

We check them against your carrier before saving, so a wrong pair is refused
while you are still looking at the page you copied it from rather than on a call
weeks later. The token is stored encrypted and never shown again.

You can change them later without re-adding the number: the row's menu on the
**Phone Numbers** page has **Edit credentials**. They belong to the carrier
account rather than to one number, so saving applies to every number you brought
from it.

The **Dial-out ready** column on that page says which of your numbers can
already place calls and which are still waiting for their credentials — a number
can answer perfectly while being unable to ring anybody, and that column is where
you would see it.

Once they are saved, calling campaigns and the call API work from that number
exactly as they do from one taken from us.

> [!NOTE]
>
> Answering needs none of this. If the number only ever receives calls, the
> Answer URL above is the whole setup.

> [!NOTE]
>
> A number can answer for **one agent**. Typing a number another agent already
> answers is refused rather than quietly moved — that is almost always a
> mistake. Moving one deliberately is a different act: choose the new agent
> under **Inbound** on the **Phone Numbers** page.
>
> Whenever an agent is about to lose a number — moved to another agent, or set
> back to no agent at all — we ask first and name the agent losing it. Giving a
> number that nobody answers to an agent for the first time takes nothing from
> anybody, so that one just happens.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Getting, moving, renaming, releasing and removing numbers need an owner or
> admin.** Everyone else on the workspace sees the list and what each number is
> doing, which is usually what they came to check.

> [!NOTE]
>
> An agent's **Voice** page shows which number that agent answers, and links here
> to change it. Getting a number and choosing who answers it both happen on this
> page, because a number belongs to the workspace rather than to one agent.

## What you can do to a number

On the **Phone Numbers** page every row has a menu:

* **Edit credentials** — for a number you brought, the API credentials of the
  carrier account its outgoing calls go through. Saving applies to every number
  you brought from that account.
* **Rename** — a name for your own eyes, so a list of numbers reads as
  "Bengaluru showroom" rather than six strings ending in different digits.
  Callers never see it.
* **Forward calls** — send every call to this number to another phone, with
  the agent not answering at all. See [Forwarding a whole
  line](#forwarding-a-whole-line).
* **Move to another workspace…** — only for developers building on the
  [customers API](/api-reference/customers): hand the number to one of your
  customers, or back to your own workspace, keeping its digits. See [Moving a
  number to another workspace](#moving-a-number-to-another-workspace).
* **Release** — only on a number you rent from us. See below; it is permanent.
* **Remove** — only on a number you brought. We forget it; you keep it. For a
  Twilio number we also clear the address we set on it, and a Telnyx number is
  taken off our application, so it stops ringing at us — but only if it still
  points at us, so anything you have since pointed it at yourself is left alone.

You can also search the list, filter it by where the numbers came from, and
export what you are looking at as a spreadsheet.

### Forwarding a whole line

A number can send **every** call straight to another phone — your front desk,
your mobile — without the agent answering. It is meant as a fallback: if an
agent is not working, or the number has no agent at all, point it at a person so
the number never goes quiet, then clear the forward and the agent answers again.

* **It rings for 30 seconds.** If nobody picks up, the caller of a number from
  us, Plivo or Twilio hears that nobody could take the call, and the line ends.
  On a number brought from Telnyx the caller gets no spoken message: the line
  rings out or returns busy, then ends.
* **A forwarded call has a time limit.** On a number you took from us it ends
  when your balance can no longer pay for it, and never later than **20
  minutes**, the longest any call can run. On a number you brought it ends after
  **30 minutes**.
* **Who the phone shows as calling.** On a number from Twilio or Telnyx, the
  original caller's number. On a number from us or from Plivo, your own number —
  those lines may only present a number on the account.
* **It works whether or not an agent answers the number.** If an agent does, the
  forward replaces it. If none does — no agent attached, the agent deleted, or
  its **Answer calls** switched off — the forward answers the call itself. Your
  plan, your call lines and your balance are checked first, as for any call, so
  a workspace that cannot pay for a call, or has every call line busy, does not
  forward it: the caller hears that the number is not answering.
* **What it costs** is what a call put through to a person costs: on a number
  you took from us, every minute the caller is connected, at the voice plan of
  the agent attached to the number — or the Premium voice rate when no agent
  is. If your own keys apply to that agent (or to the workspace, when no agent is
  attached), it is the flat price of that set of keys instead, even though a
  forward uses none of them. On a number you brought, nothing from us — the minutes are on your
  carrier's bill. It is not the carrier-only charge of a call that ends before
  the agent speaks.
* **It is not recorded.** The agent never takes a forwarded call, so there is no
  recording and no transcript: Get Call shows `recording` as `null` and Get
  Recording answers `404`.
* **Not to one of these numbers.** A forward cannot point at the number itself
  or at another number on the platform, which would send calls round in a loop.
* **Not to premium or special numbers.** Premium-rate, shared-cost and toll-free
  numbers, satellite and international-network numbers, and a short list of
  high-cost international destinations are refused
  (`forward_destination_not_allowed`): a forward runs with nobody watching, and
  those numbers charge by the minute to whoever dials them. An ordinary landline
  or mobile is always fine. If you have a real need for one of them, tell us.
* **Nothing is said or sent after a forwarded call.** The agent never took it,
  so there is no summary, no extracted details and no follow-up message — you
  still get the `call.completed` webhook, with `forwardedTo` set, when an agent
  answers the number. When no agent does there is no agent to send it for, so
  the call shows in Usage, Get Call and the call list (with no agent) and not as
  a webhook or an inbox conversation. Get Call and
  the call list carry `forwardedTo` too, and `seconds` is how long the caller was
  connected, even on a number you brought where nothing is billed. A forward
  nobody picked up is reported as `missed`, with a `hangup` of `no_answer`,
  `busy`, `rejected` or `unreachable`, and `seconds` 0. On a Telnyx number
  a caller who hangs up while the phone is still ringing may be reported as a
  completed call instead.
* **Not on Vobiz.** A Vobiz number cannot forward calls, so the setting is
  refused (`number_cannot_forward`).

From the console it is **Forward calls** in the number's menu. From the API it
is `forwardTo` on [Update Phone Number](/api-reference/phone-numbers/update-phone-number):

```json theme={null}
{ "forwardTo": "+919812345678" }
```

Send `"forwardTo": null` to stop. A refusal says which rule stopped it in its
`code`: `forward_loop` or `number_cannot_forward`. A United States number you
rent from us forwards only to US and Canadian numbers (see [United States
numbers](#united-states-numbers)).

### Moving a number to another workspace

If you build on the [developer API](/api-reference/customers), a number can move
between your own workspace and your customers' — **keeping its digits**, so
nobody who has it saved needs a new one.

**In the console**, open the **Phone Numbers** page, open the number's menu, choose **Move to another workspace…** and
pick where it goes: your own workspace or one of your customers. The option is
there only for developers, and only on a number that can be moved. A refusal
says why (the number is on a call, an Indian number whose new workspace has no
approved business details, and so on).

**Through the API** (or the `move_phone_number` [MCP tool](/mcp/tools)):

```bash theme={null}
curl -X POST https://app.thinnest.ai/api/v1/phone-numbers/918041234567/move \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" \
  -H "Thinnest-Workspace: org_…the customer that has it now…" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "toWorkspace": "org_…the workspace it goes to…" }'
```

Leave the `Thinnest-Workspace` header out when the number is in your own
workspace. What happens:

* The number stops being any agent's line, and leaves every agent's spare
  numbers, in the workspace it leaves.
* It arrives in the other workspace **answered by nobody**. Point it at an agent
  there, as with a number you have just rented.
* **Rent** carries on from the next month in the new workspace. The month
  already paid is not charged again — and since your customers are billed to
  you, no money moves either way.
* **An Indian number** is held in the name of the business using it, so the
  workspace it moves to must have its own business details approved first (see
  [India needs your business verified first](#india-needs-your-business-verified-first)).
  The move registers the number to that business.
* **A number you rent from us** moves only to a workspace billed in the same
  region: a United States number stays with workspaces billed outside India, an
  Indian number with workspaces billed in India (`number_move_other_region`).
* **A number you brought** moves only when both workspaces have the same
  carrier account's keys saved. A Telnyx number set up for one workspace cannot
  move this way: remove it and add it again in the other workspace.
* It is refused while the number is on a call, or while the same number is
  already being moved.
* Any call forwarding set on the number is cleared: it was the old workspace's
  choice.
* If the phone network cannot take the move, the number stays where it was,
  answered by nobody, and you can try again shortly (`number_move_unavailable`).
* Repeating a move that already succeeded, to the same workspace, gives the same
  result, so a lost response is safe to retry.
* A few long-held numbers were set up before workspace-level phone accounts
  existed and cannot be moved this way; write to us for those.

Only workspaces of one developer can trade numbers. A key you gave one customer
cannot move its numbers anywhere.

## Inbound and outbound are separate

Every number has two pickers on the **Phone Numbers** page, and they are
independent:

| | What it decides |
| - | - |
| **Inbound** | Which agent **answers** when somebody rings the number. One agent, or nobody. |
| **Outbound** | Which agent **calls out** from the number — in campaigns, test calls and the call API. |

They can be the same agent, which is the ordinary case, or different ones.
Some things that is useful for:

* **A receptionist and a caller on one number.** One agent answers; a different
  one makes the outbound calls, and the people it rings see your usual number.
* **A number that only calls out.** Leave **Inbound** empty and choose an agent
  under **Outbound**. Nobody answers when it is rung, but the agent can place
  calls from it.
* **An agent that only calls out.** It does not need a number of its own at all.
  Give it a number under **Outbound** and it can run campaigns and test calls
  straight away — we switch its phone on for you when you do.

**Inbound empty means nobody answers.** Whoever rings the number hears that it is
not taking calls — including somebody ringing back after a campaign call. A
number that is only lent out for calling is never answered by the agent calling
from it. If you want a number to answer, choose an agent under **Inbound**.

When you let a different agent call out on a number that another agent answers,
we ask first, because of exactly that: a customer ringing it back will reach the
agent that **answers** it, not the one that rang them.

A number is lent to one agent at a time on this page. Lending it to a second
agent takes it out of the first one's list, and **ends no call**: one that is
ringing or being answered carries on from that number to its end.

**Several agents can call from one number at once through the API.** A call placed
with [Place Call](/api-reference) can name, as its `from`, **any number the
workspace holds and can call from** — lent to that agent or not. So one agent can
answer the number while two others call out from it, with no lending at all. A call
waiting to be placed that named a number rings from it as long as the workspace
still holds it; one that named no number rings from the agent's own number, or its
first lent one.

**A ring-back can reach the agent that called.** When several agents call out from
one number, a person ringing it back normally reaches the agent that **answers**
it. Set the number's `ringBack` to `last_caller` with
[Update a Phone Number](/api-reference) and they reach the agent that called them
from that number in the last 30 days instead. If no agent called them, or that
agent is not answering phone calls, the number answers as usual. It is off unless
you turn it on.

### Numbers from different phone companies on one agent

An agent can call out from numbers on **different phone companies** — a
ThinnestAI number and one you imported from Twilio, say — like a phone with two
SIM cards. Each call goes out through **its own number's** company, on its own
account, and hangs up there too.

* **In the Playground**, **Call from** lists every number the agent can call
  from, each with its company's logo. A number that cannot call yet (one you
  imported without saving its credentials) is shown but greyed out.
* **Campaigns** spread their calls across all of them.
* **Some features depend on the company.** Transferring a call to a person and
  leaving a voicemail work on ThinnestAI numbers and numbers from Plivo or
  Telnyx, but not on Vobiz or Twilio numbers. Recording works on every number. A
  call from a number that can't do one of these still goes out — that feature is
  simply off for it, and the Playground and the campaign builder tell you before
  you call.

One limit to know about: **a number you brought needs its credentials saved**
before an agent can call from it, the same as any number of yours that places
calls.

## Spare numbers for calling out

A calling campaign goes out from your agent's number. That is fine for a few
hundred calls and starts to hurt at a few thousand: phone companies and phones
themselves watch for a line that makes a burst of calls, and once a number is
marked as one, **everything it does afterwards suffers** — including a customer
ringing you back and seeing a warning on their screen.

Spare numbers spread that out. Give an agent several numbers under **Outbound**,
and campaigns share their calls across the agent's own number, if it has one, and
the others.

**1. Have a spare**

Any number on the page — one you bought and have not pointed anywhere, one
you brought and have not used yet, or one another agent answers.

**2. Lend it**

Under **Outbound**, choose the agent. That is the whole setup.

**What it does not do.** A spare does not become the agent's number. Nothing
about who answers changes, the number you gave your customers stays the number
they ring, and you can take a spare back at any time by choosing the agent that
answers it, or **Nobody** if none does.

**One person always sees the same number.** Whichever of your numbers rings a
customer is the one that rings them again — including a second attempt days
later. Three attempts from three different numbers is what a nuisance call looks
like, and avoiding that is half the point, so it does not happen.

> [!NOTE]
>
> A spare can be on a different phone company from the agent's other numbers. A
> spare you brought needs its carrier credentials saved, the same as any number of
> yours that places calls. The page says which of these is missing
> rather than letting you find out on a campaign.

> [!NOTE]
>
> Changing who answers a number does not change who calls out on it. Moving or
> clearing **Inbound** leaves **Outbound** exactly as it was.

> [!WARNING]
>
> A spare must be licensed for the same kind of calling as the campaign. In
> India promotional calls need a 140-series number, so a campaign marked
> promotional is refused if **any** of the numbers it would use is not one — and
> it names which. It is the number that carries the penalty.

## Disconnecting, giving up, and removing

Three different things and only one of them is permanent.

**Disconnect** takes the number off the agent so it stops answering. The number
stays yours either way — your own number stays with your carrier, and one you
rent from us stays rented and still charged. It shows on the **Phone Numbers**
page with nothing under **Inbound**, ready to point at another agent. An agent
you had chosen under **Outbound** keeps calling out on it.

**Give up** hands a number you rent from us back to the phone company. The
monthly charge stops and the number goes back to the pool.

**Remove** applies only to a number you brought. It takes our record of it away,
so we stop answering it and stop listing it — the line stays yours and your
carrier keeps billing you for it exactly as before. Remember to unset its Answer
URL in your own console afterwards, or calls to it will still reach us and be
declined. Bringing it back later is the same three fields.

> [!WARNING]
>
> Releasing is permanent. The number goes back to the phone company and somebody
> else can take it — we cannot get it back for you, even a minute later. If it
> is printed anywhere, or anybody has it saved, keep it.

## What callers hear when nothing is set up

* **Answer calls off** — the agent does not answer. A caller on a Plivo, Vobiz or Twilio
  number hears a short spoken message and the call ends; a Telnyx caller hears a busy tone.
  You can write the message yourself ([When Answer calls is off](/channels/voice#when-answer-calls-is-off)).
* **Answer calls on, Phone number switched off** — the same: the agent does not answer. You
  have switched voice on without telling it to pick up the phone.
* **Everything on, no greeting** — the agent waits for the caller to speak
  first. That is a real choice, and some lines are better that way, but it
  surprises people who expected a greeting.

## Things worth knowing

> [accordion] One number, one answering agent
>
> Two agents cannot both **answer** one number. If you want different behaviour
> for different callers — sales and support, say — that is one agent with
> instructions covering both, or two agents on two numbers.
>
> Who *calls out* on a number is a separate choice, and an agent can call out
> on several numbers — see **Inbound and outbound are separate** above.
> Answering is still one to one.

> [accordion] Trying it on a real phone
>
> The **Playground** has a **Try it on a real phone** box under the browser
> call. Type your own number and press **Place call**: the agent rings you from
> its number, so you hear exactly what a customer hears — a phone line, not a
> browser. If the agent can call out on more than one number, a **Call from**
> list lets you choose which, so you can hear a spare as well.
>
> It is a real call and costs the same per minute as any other. The browser
> call beside it is free and instant, which is the one to use while you are
> editing what the agent says; this one is for hearing how it sounds.

> [accordion] Which number do calls out use?
>
> When your agent rings somebody, it calls from its own number, or from one you
> have given it under **Outbound**. That is what they see, and what they will
> ring back — and it is answered by whichever agent is under **Inbound** on that
> number, which may not be the one that rang them. See **Inbound and outbound
> are separate** above.
>
> How long those calls ring before they count as not answered is a setting of
> the agent, not of the number: **Playground → Ending calls → Ring time** in the console, or
> `voice.ringSeconds` in the API (and `ringSeconds` on a single call). See
> [How long it rings](/channels/voice#how-long-it-rings).

> [accordion] Promotional calling in India needs a different kind of number
>
> A normal business number is licensed for service and transactional calls.
> Promotional calling in India needs a 140-series number, and using an
> ordinary one for it can get the number blocked. See [Calling
> campaigns](/channels/voice-campaigns).

> [accordion] Test before you print it
>
> Ring your own number and ask the hardest question you get — not "what are
> your hours". The awkward one, with a condition attached, where the honest
> answer is "it depends". That is the answer worth hearing out loud before a
> customer does.


# SMS
Source: https://docs.thinnest.ai/channels/sms

Let your agent text customers in India — through your own SMS provider, under your own DLT sender ID.

Your agent can send a customer an SMS **while it is talking to them** (a booking
link mid-call, an address they asked for) and **after the call ends** (a thank-you
with your booking link, or a "sorry we missed you"). See
[Actions](/agent/actions#reaching-the-customer-on-a-different-channel) and
[After the call](/agent/after-the-call).

**SMS goes through your own provider account.** You connect your SMS provider, it
sends under your own sender ID, and **it bills you directly**. Nothing for SMS is
taken from your wallet here.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **SMS reaches Indian mobile numbers only.** Every business SMS in India has to
> follow the DLT rules below, and those apply to Indian numbers. For customers
> elsewhere, use [WhatsApp](/channels/whatsapp).

## What DLT asks of you first

India's telecom rules (TRAI's DLT) mean an operator only delivers a business SMS
that matches what you registered in advance. You register once on any one DLT
portal (Jio, Airtel, Vi, BSNL…), and it works on every network. If your business
already sends OTPs or order updates, you probably have all of this.

| You need | What it is | Where it comes from |
| - | - | - |
| **Entity (PE) ID** | Your business's registration on DLT, usually 19 digits | Your DLT portal, once your business is approved |
| **Sender ID (header)** | The six letters the message shows as coming from, like `ACMEIN` | Registered on your DLT portal |
| **Templates** | The exact words of each message, with `{#var#}` wherever the text changes | Registered and approved on your DLT portal; each gets a **DLT template ID** |
| **Your provider in your PE–TM chain** | Telling DLT which provider sends for you | Your DLT portal — add your provider's telemarketer ID |

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Do the PE–TM chain step, or every message is dropped.** Since 2024 operators
> reject a message unless your DLT registration names the provider that delivered
> it. Your provider's support team will give you their telemarketer ID if it is
> not below.

## Providers you can connect

| Provider | You'll need | Templates also need | Telemarketer ID |
| - | - | - | - |
| **MSG91** | Auth key | MSG91's own template ID (from its dashboard) | `1302157225275643280` |
| **Exotel** | Account SID, API key, API token, region (`in` or `sg`) | — | ask Exotel |
| **Gupshup Enterprise SMS** | User ID, password | — | ask Gupshup |
| **Infobip** | Your API base URL (like `xxxxx.api.infobip.com`), API key | — | `110200001152` |
| **Vonage** | API key, API secret | — | ask Vonage |
| **Fast2SMS** | API key | Fast2SMS's own message ID (from its DLT manager) | ask Fast2SMS |

MSG91 and Fast2SMS send by **their own** copy of each template, so you add the
template on their dashboard too and paste their ID here. The others send your
template's text along with your DLT IDs.

Using a different provider? Tell us which one. We add a provider once we can test
its DLT sending API against its own documentation.

## Connect

**1. Open Settings → SMS provider**

Only owners and admins can change it.

**2. Choose your provider and paste its keys**

Then enter your **DLT sender ID (header)** and your **DLT entity (PE) ID**.
Keys are sealed as soon as they arrive and never shown again. To change one
field later, leave the secret blank and the saved one is kept.

**3. Add your templates**

Under **DLT templates**, add each template you want the agent to use:

* **Name** — your own, like `booking_link`. The agent sees it, so make it say what the message is for.
* **Text** — copied from your DLT portal **exactly**, with `{#var#}` where it varies.
* **DLT template ID** — the number your DLT portal gave it.
* **Category** — Transactional, or Service (implicit or explicit). Promotional templates can't be sent by an agent.
* **Agent may send this during a call or chat** — tick it for the templates you want the agent to be able to use mid-call. New templates start unticked. The **after the call** message doesn't need the tick.
* **MSG91 template ID / Fast2SMS message ID** — only with those two providers.

The page shows how many blanks the template has and how many SMS it will be
sent as.

**4. Send a test**

Under **Send a test**, send one template to your own mobile. A success marks
the provider **Working**; a refusal shows the provider's reason, so you can fix
it before a customer is waiting.

## Writing templates the agent can use well

Each `{#var#}` takes **at most 30 characters** when it is sent, so keep the
moving parts short: a first name, a date, a short link.

```text Good theme={null}
Hi {#var#}, thanks for calling Acme Clinic. Book your visit here: {#var#}
```

```text Good theme={null}
Your appointment at Acme Clinic is on {#var#} at {#var#}. Reply on WhatsApp to change it.
```

```text Won't work well theme={null}
{#var#}
```

A template that is nothing but a blank was never going to pass DLT, and the agent
cannot write free text into an SMS anyway. Every message is one of your approved
templates, with only the blanks filled in.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Plain English fits 160 characters in one SMS.** Hindi, other Indian scripts
> and emoji fit 70, so the same message may be sent as two or three SMS, and your
> provider charges for each one.

## Using it

* **During a call or chat** — tick the templates the agent may use, then turn on
  **Send the customer an SMS** on the agent's **Actions** page. See [Actions](/agent/actions#reaching-the-customer-on-a-different-channel).
* **After a call** — choose an SMS template in the **After the call** card on the
  same page. See [After the call](/agent/after-the-call).

Every SMS the agent sends shows up as a note in that conversation, so your team can
see what went out.

## When something goes wrong

| What you see | Usually means |
| - | - |
| The provider's test fails with a DLT or template error | The text here doesn't match the DLT template word for word, or the DLT template ID is wrong |
| The test succeeds but nothing arrives | Your provider isn't in your PE–TM chain yet, or the sender ID isn't approved for that template |
| "SMS can only be sent to an Indian mobile number" | The customer's number is a landline or outside India |
| "MSG91 needs the MSG91 template ID" | Add the template on MSG91's dashboard too, and paste its ID |
| Can't change a template's text | An agent sends it after calls and fills a different number of blanks. Change that agent's **After the call** first |

## From the API

Everything above is also in the API: [SMS](/api-reference/sms/get-sms-provider).

```bash theme={null}
curl -X POST https://app.thinnest.ai/api/v1/sms/templates \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "name": "booking_link",
    "body": "Hi {#var#}, thanks for calling Acme Clinic. Book your visit here: {#var#}",
    "dltTemplateId": "1207169876543210987",
    "category": "service_implicit"
  }'
```


# Telegram
Source: https://docs.thinnest.ai/channels/telegram

The quickest channel to connect — no approvals, no templates, no waiting.

Telegram is the one channel you can connect entirely by yourself, in about two
minutes. There is no business verification, no template approval and no 24-hour
window.

## Connect

**1. Create a bot**

Message [@BotFather](https://t.me/BotFather) on Telegram and send
`/newbot`. Choose a display name and a username ending in `bot`.

BotFather replies with a token that looks like
`123456789:AAF-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx`.

**2. Paste the token**

On the agent's **Channels** page, open Telegram and paste it.

> [!WARNING]
>
> That token controls the bot completely. Treat it like a password — anyone
> holding it can read and send everything your bot does. It is sealed on
> arrival and never shown again.

**3. Say hello**

Open your bot in Telegram and press **Start**. The agent answers with the
same knowledge and instructions it uses everywhere else.

## What it can do

Text, buttons and images. Cards degrade to text with the buttons preserved.

Long replies are split across messages rather than truncated — Telegram rejects
a message over 4,096 characters outright, so splitting is the only behaviour
that does not silently lose the end of an answer.

## Opting out

A customer who asks the agent to stop is recorded as withdrawn, exactly as on
WhatsApp, and the agent stops replying to them.

## Two things it does not do

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Telegram does not join a customer's identity.** There is no phone number
> unless the user volunteers a contact card, and matching on display name would
> merge two different people called Priya into one memory. Telegram threads are
> read once a customer has been linked by other means — they never do the
> linking.
>
> **Broadcasts do not send on Telegram.** A bot may message anyone who has
> pressed Start, so this is buildable; it is simply not built. Only WhatsApp
> carries a campaign today.

## Why start here

If you are evaluating the platform and do not yet have WhatsApp connected,
Telegram gives you a real, external channel to test against in minutes — a
proper end-to-end run rather than the Playground.

## Disconnecting

Disconnecting the bot stops it reaching you and frees the connection, so you can
put a different bot on the same agent afterwards.

> [!TIP]
>
> **Your Telegram conversations and their messages stay.** Disconnecting removes
> the connection, not the history — the transcripts remain in your
> [inbox](/workspace/inbox) and in the record of what your customers were told.


# Voice
Source: https://docs.thinnest.ai/channels/voice

Your agent answers the phone — with the same memory of each customer it has everywhere else.

Voice is your agent picking up a call and holding a conversation out loud. It
listens, thinks and speaks, and the person on the line can interrupt it.

It is the same agent. The same knowledge, the same instructions, the same memory
of the same customer. Somebody who messaged you on WhatsApp last week and rings
you today is one person with one history.

> [!NOTE]
>
> Voice has its own page in the agent sidebar, under **Deploy**: whether the
> agent answers and where. How it speaks, listens and ends a call is on the
> agent's **Playground**, under its other settings.

## Turn it on

**1. Open Voice**

In the agent sidebar, choose **Voice**.

**2. Switch on Answer calls**

Off means the number does not answer at all. Nothing on the page runs until
this is on.

You can set everything up first and turn it on last. The settings are never
greyed out, because the worst version of this is a real caller reaching a
half-configured agent.

**3. Choose where it answers**

Open **Website** and switch on **Answer here**, and your agent answers calls
from the chat widget straight away — no number needed, on any plan.

To answer a number people dial, go to **Phone Numbers** in the main sidebar —
the Voice page links there too.
Take one from us — that needs a paid plan — or bring one you own with Plivo,
Vobiz, Twilio or Telnyx, which works on every plan including the free one. A
Plivo or Twilio number also needs your account's Auth ID and Auth Token before
it answers, and a Telnyx number your account's API key. Then choose this agent beside the number, and it starts answering.
See [Phone numbers](/channels/phone-numbers).

**4. Call it**

Ring the number. You should hear your greeting, then the agent.

Through the API: `voice.surfaces`, a list of `"web"`, `"whatsapp"` and `"phone"`. A new agent starts with
`["web", "whatsapp"]`, and `phone` is added when a number is attached. Adding `phone` while the agent answers
calls and has no number is refused (`phone_number_required`); with calls off you can set it first; while a number is attached, `phone` stays on — to stop it
ringing, switch off `answersCalls` or take the number off. Whether a WhatsApp number takes calls is its own
**Calls** switch on Connect WhatsApp.

## Where the call settings are

The **Voice** page holds one section:

| Section | What is in it |
| - | - |
| **Calls** | Whether the agent answers, the message callers hear when it is off, and where it answers |

Everything else about a call is on the agent's **Playground**, as cards under the
model, voice and instructions:

| Card | What is in it |
| - | - |
| **How Agent speaks** | The rules it speaks by, and the lines it says while it works something out |
| **Listening** | Noise cancellation, turn detection (how it decides a caller has finished), and when a caller can cut in |
| **Sound and recording** | Background sound and recording |
| **Ending calls** | Voicemail, do-not-call, how long an outbound call rings, hanging up when done |
| **Memory** | What it remembers from earlier conversations, and the summary after each call |
| **Call length and silence** | The longest call, and what happens when nobody speaks |

On the Playground, the one **Save changes** at the top right saves these cards
and the rest of the page together, and what you save applies from the next call.
**Test a call** sits beside the settings and saves any unsaved change before it
dials, so a test call always uses what is on the screen. On the Voice page,
**Save changes** stays at the bottom of the screen and **Test a call** sits beside
the Calls section.

## The settings

### Replies use

Which model does the thinking. Leave this on the recommendation unless you have
a reason to change it.

The list here is deliberately shorter than the one for chat. A model is only
offered if it can answer fast enough to hold a conversation — one that pauses to
think reads as a dropped call, not as a careful answer.

> [!NOTE]
>
> Your chat model is not used on calls. Voice is its own choice, because what
> makes a good writer and what makes a good speaker are not the same thing.

### Speech to speech: OpenAI GPT-Live-1

For a call that feels more like talking to a person, an agent can run on **OpenAI GPT-Live-1**. One model
hears the caller and answers in its own voice, and it listens while it speaks, so a caller can talk over it and
it carries on naturally.

> [!NOTE]
>
> OpenAI GPT-Live-1 and [OpenAI GPT-Realtime Mini](#speech-to-speech-openai-gpt-realtime-mini) are on the
> **Enterprise plan** only, for now. They are not in the Model picker or in
> [List Models](/api-reference/models/list-models): we set them up on your agents. Talk to us to use them.

**Your agent stays in charge.** GPT-Live-1 hands every question about your
business and every action to your agent, then says the answer in its own words.
Your instructions, knowledge, actions, transfers and hang-up all work as they do
on any other model, and the call shows up in Usage and the inbox as usual.

**Its own voices.** GPT-Live-1 speaks in its own voices, listed under **Voice** on
the Playground with the Indian voices first: a woman and a man for each of Hindi,
Bengali, Tamil, Telugu, Marathi, Gujarati, Kannada, Malayalam and Punjabi. Each
is shown with its language, and searching a language finds its two. Press play
beside a voice to hear it. Every voice speaks whatever language the agent is set
to; its language is the accent it speaks with. The Standard, Premium and Studio tabs do not apply to it. Switching the agent to another model brings back the
voice you had.

**Settings that do not apply.** On a GPT-Live-1 agent these are shown greyed out
with the reason in a tooltip, and the values you saved are kept for when the
agent goes back to another model:

* **Fillers before tool run**, because it keeps talking while it looks something up.
* **Speaking speed**, which it does not let you change.
* **Ear mode** and **Turn detection**, because it takes
  turns itself.
* **Early answers**, because it starts answering as soon as the caller stops.
* **Digit hold**. GPT-Live-1 is told to wait for a whole number and read it back.
* **The interruption settings** (words needed to cut the agent off, never interrupt, answer what was
  said over the agent, let the greeting finish), because it decides itself when to stop talking and when
  to carry on.
* **The silence prompts** (ask again, "are you still there?", end after silence): a call that stays
  quiet for five minutes ends.
* **End phrases**, because it may not pass a goodbye to your agent.

**In the Model picker.** On an agent we have set up on GPT-Live-1, the picker shows it as the agent's model, with
its price per minute for your workspace's currency; hovering over it lists its price, why it was chosen and what
to know. Picking another model moves the agent off it, and only we can move it back.

**How many at once.** The number of GPT-Live-1 calls that can run at the same time follows your plan's
concurrent-call limit, the same as any other call.

**Billing.** A call on GPT-Live-1 is billed at its own flat rate a minute, with the phone line included: per
second on web calls and in 30-second blocks on phone calls (whole minutes on a workspace billed outside India). There is no voice plan for it. [Usage](/workspace/usage) shows each call's charge, and a workspace needs a balance for the start of
a call as for any other.

**Testing it.** Test Chat cannot run a speech-to-speech model, so it answers with
your chat model. Use a **web call** on the Playground to hear GPT-Live-1.

**Through the API.** An agent we have set up on it reads back `model: "openai-gpt-live-1"`. The API does not set
a realtime model as a new choice yet; it refuses one with "… is not available yet." On such an agent you can
change `voice.realtimeVoice` to another of the model's voices, or `null` for its default, an Indian voice. The
agent's `voice` is left as it is. A call's
[`billing`](/api-reference/calls/get-call) carries `billedOn: "usage"` and the
charge in `chargedMicro`.

### Speech to speech: OpenAI GPT-Realtime Mini

**OpenAI GPT-Realtime Mini** is a second speech-to-speech model, at a lower rate a minute than GPT-Live-1. Like
GPT-Live-1 it is on the **Enterprise plan** only for now, set up on your agents by us.

**How it differs from GPT-Live-1.** It takes turns: a caller can cut in, but it does not listen while it is
speaking. It answers simple things itself, like a greeting, small talk or a question it has already answered.
When the caller needs something only your agent knows or does, it uses your agent: a fact from your knowledge,
or an action such as a booking, a transfer or ending the call. It never states a fact your agent has not given
it. A turn that needs your agent takes a moment longer to answer than one it handles itself.

**Its voices.** Ten voices, listed under **Voice** on the Playground, each marked **All Languages Supported**:
every one speaks whatever language the agent is set to. Press play beside a voice to hear it.

**Its own call settings: Realtime session.** On the Playground, under its voice, **Realtime session** holds the
settings the model uses to hear the caller. They replace the fillers and listening settings in the Playground's call cards, which
are hidden on this model, with a note pointing here.

| Setting | What it does | Default |
| - | - | - |
| Noise reduction | Cleans the caller's audio first: close microphone (phone, headset), far microphone (laptop, room), or off | Automatic: close on phone calls, far on web calls |
| Turn detection | How it knows the caller has finished: **by silence** or **by meaning** | By silence |
| Speech threshold | By silence: how loud speech must be to count, 0 to 1 | 0.50 |
| Prefix padding | By silence: audio kept from just before speech starts | 300 ms |
| Silence | By silence: the quiet that ends the caller's turn | 500 ms |
| Idle timeout | By silence: after this much quiet the agent speaks up, 5 to 60 seconds | Off |
| Eagerness | By meaning: how soon it decides the caller has finished | Automatic |
| Callers can interrupt | Whether a caller speaking cuts the agent off | On |
| Caller transcript | Fast, most accurate, or classic | Fast |
| Words to expect | Names and brand words the transcript should get right | None |
| Longest reply | The most a single reply may say, in tokens | Unlimited |
| Speaking speed | 0.25x to 1.5x | 1.00x |
| Long calls | How much of a long conversation is kept when it is trimmed | Automatic |

A call that stays quiet for five minutes ends, as on any other model. The agent speaking up after an idle
timeout does not count as the caller speaking.

**Billing, testing and limits** work as for GPT-Live-1: its own flat rate a minute, per second on web calls and
in 30-second blocks on phone calls (whole minutes outside India). Test Chat answers with your chat model, so use a **web call** to hear it.
Calls at once follow your plan's limit.

**Through the API.** An agent we have set up on it reads back `model: "openai-gpt-realtime-mini"`; as with
GPT-Live-1, the API does not set it as a new choice yet. On such an agent you can change `voice.realtimeVoice` to
another of its voices. Its session settings are `voice.realtimeSession`:
send only the fields you change, and the rest keep their values. `null` puts them all back to the defaults.
Values outside a range are brought into it. A wrong type or an unknown field is refused, naming the field.

```json theme={null}
{
  "voice": {
    "realtimeVoice": "marin",
    "realtimeSession": {
      "noiseReduction": "near_field",
      "turnDetection": "server_vad",
      "silenceDurationMs": 700,
      "transcriptionPrompt": "Sunrise Clinics, Dr Mehta"
    }
  }
}
```

The fields: `noiseReduction` (`auto`, `near_field`, `far_field`, `off`), `turnDetection` (`server_vad` by
silence, `semantic_vad` by meaning), `vadThreshold`, `prefixPaddingMs`, `silenceDurationMs`, `idleTimeoutMs`
(or `null`), `eagerness` (`auto`, `low`, `medium`, `high`), `interruptResponse`, `transcriptionModel`
(`gpt-4o-mini-transcribe` fast, `gpt-4o-transcribe` most accurate, `whisper-1` classic), `transcriptionPrompt`
(or `null`), `maxOutputTokens` (1 to 4096, or `null` for unlimited), `speed`, and `truncationRetention` (0.1 to
0.9, or `null` for automatic). [Get Agent](/api-reference/agents/get-agent) returns all of them.

### Voice

Which voice your customers hear. Press play on a Standard or Premium voice to listen. Studio voices have no
sample: pick one and use **Test a call** to hear it.

On an agent that uses [OpenAI GPT-Live-1](#speech-to-speech-openai-gpt-live-1) or
[OpenAI GPT-Realtime Mini](#speech-to-speech-openai-gpt-realtime-mini) these tabs do not apply: it
speaks in its own voices. Otherwise voices come in three tiers, on their own tabs:

> [card] Standard
>
> Natural voices that read all eleven Indian languages, at the lowest
> per-minute rate. The rate is lower again on a number you imported and on
> web calls, since no line of ours is used. For workspaces billed in rupees.

> [card] Premium
>
> Warm and expressive, and what a new agent starts on (Kavya).

> [card] Studio
>
> The largest catalogue we offer — hundreds of voices, each speaking many
> languages — plus [your own cloned ones](/channels/voice-clone). A higher
> per-minute rate, on **every plan**.

**The per-minute price sits on each tab**, so you can see what a choice costs
before you make it, and again beside **Voice** once you have chosen. A call is
billed at the rate of the voice answering it.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Premium is open on every plan, including the free trial.** Standard voices
> were retired on 23 October 2026: an agent that was on one was moved to a
> similar Premium voice automatically.

**Studio is open on every plan**, including the free trial: pick any Studio voice and put it on your agent.
Only [cloning your own voice](/channels/voice-clone) needs the Pro plan or above.

> [card] [Clone your own voice](/channels/voice-clone)
>
> On the Pro plan and above, record a short sample and your agent can speak
> in it — a founder's own voice, or someone from your team. Up to 10 on Pro
> and 20 on Scale. Full details on its own page.

#### Studio voices and languages

Every Studio voice speaks all 63 languages Studio supports, in whatever language your agent is set to, or the one
the caller speaks on **Match the customer**. Since November 14, 2026 the Studio catalogue is one set of voices in
every market.

* **In the voice list.** Open **Browse voices**. Every voice shows its own accent and flag; filter by language,
  accent, gender, age and tag. Choosing a language puts the voices native to it first (for an Indian language, the
  Indian-accented voices).
* **No sample to play.** Studio voices have no preview, so there is no play button. Pick one and use **Test a call**
  to hear it.
* **A voice chosen before November 14, 2026.** If an agent's Studio voice is no longer in the list, its calls answer
  in a Studio voice of the same gender until you choose a new one. Your own [cloned voices](/channels/voice-clone)
  were moved over and sound as before.

Through the API, [`GET /voices`](/api-reference/voices/list-voices) lists each Studio voice with `languages`.

> [!NOTE]
>
> If your workspace uses its own voice account, the voice comes from that
> account instead, and a Cartesia voice can be tuned per agent: speed, volume,
> emotion, the Sonic model and a pronunciation dictionary. See [Tune a Cartesia
> voice](/api-reference/bring-your-own-keys#tune-a-cartesia-voice).

#### Speaking speed

How fast the agent talks, set on the agent's **Playground**, right under the
voice, with a **slider** from 0.7× (slower) to 1.3× (faster); the middle is
**Normal**, the voice's own pace, and **Reset to Normal** puts it back. If
callers say the agent rushes, or many of them are listening in a second language
or on a poor phone line, a little under Normal (0.9×) is usually enough — it
changes the pace, not the voice.

Every voice follows it: Premium, Studio, and the voices you clone here — so a
clone that sounds slow can be sped up without recording it again. A voice from
your own voice account follows it too, wherever that provider has a speed
setting (Mistral and Speechify have none, and Rime only on its Mist models). If
you set a speed in a Cartesia voice's own settings, that one is used instead.
A Cartesia Professional Voice Clone keeps its recording's pace: Cartesia does
not let a speed change it.

Through the API: `voice.speakingSpeed` (0.7 to 1.3, as a multiple of the voice's
own pace; `null` for normal).

Every voice speaks every language we support. The tier changes how a voice
*sounds*, never what it can say — which language it uses comes from your agent's
setting, covered below.

Through the API, `PATCH /api/v1/agents/{id}` with `"voice": { "voice": null }`
puts the agent back on the voice a new agent starts with (currently Kavya, a
Premium voice), and `"model": null` puts it back on the default model (Prana
\[Voice]). An empty string is refused: `null` is the way back.

### How Agent should speak

The rules the agent follows on calls, and only on calls. Your chat and WhatsApp
replies are untouched.

It comes filled in, so you are editing real sentences rather than facing an
empty box. Change what you like; clear the box entirely to go back to the
supplied wording.

> [!WARNING]
>
> Two of the supplied lines are not style, and are worth keeping.
>
> **Write titles and abbreviations in full.** Speech is produced one sentence at
> a time, and a full stop inside a name ends a sentence early — an agent that
> writes "Dr. Iyer" can be heard stopping halfway through the name.
>
> **No brackets or bullet points.** Nothing pronounces a bracket. An aside in
> brackets is either read out as though it were the main sentence or lost. If
> your agent writes one anyway, such as `[pause]` or `(waiting for the caller)`,
> it is left out of what is spoken and of the transcript. Only short notes in
> square brackets are left out: a figure such as `[1]` or `[Rs 500]` is kept,
> and a link written as `[label](address)` is spoken as its label.

It replaces the supplied wording rather than adding to it, and on a call it is
read after your agent's own instructions. Up to 4,000 characters, counted
separately from the agent's instructions; a longer box is refused, never cut.

Through the API: `voice.callInstructions` (a string, or `null` to go back to the
supplied wording). The name must be exactly that; `voice.instruction` is refused.

### Opening line

The first thing a caller hears, in your agent's own voice, the moment the call
connects. It is set on the agent's **Playground**, under **What Agent says**, and
it is also the first message in the chat. Leave it empty and the agent waits to
be spoken to.

Keep it short. It is spoken, and a caller who hears a paragraph before they can
speak will talk over it.

### Earlier conversations

What happens when somebody who has spoken with your agent before calls again,
or is called — whether that was an earlier call from the same number, or a chat
on WhatsApp or your website.

* **Remember quietly** — the default. Your agent knows what was said before and
  uses it, without mentioning it. Nobody has to repeat themselves.
* **Remember and recap** — your agent opens by saying you have spoken before and
  what it was about, then asks whether they would like to carry on or talk about
  something else. On a call you placed, it answers what they say first and
  recaps right after.
* **Start fresh** — every call starts clean. Your agent is given nothing from
  earlier calls or other channels, and never greets anyone as a returning
  caller.

A [call back](#booking-a-call-back) the customer asked for is the exception:
it always carries on from the conversation they booked it in, whichever you
choose, and its opening line already says why it is calling, so it is never
recapped on top.

The recap is in your agent's own words and in the language of the call — there
is nothing to write. It names what you talked about, never what they told you:
no amounts, dates or addresses until they bring them up, because anyone can
pick up a phone. A WhatsApp conversation that is kept hidden until the
caller is confirmed (the **Remembering the customer across channels** setting
on the Actions page, see [how two channels become one person](/concepts#how-two-channels-become-one-person))
stays hidden — your agent only says you have been in touch there.

It only happens when there is something to recap, and only once per call. A
first-time caller is greeted as one.

### Who is calling

When somebody rings from a number that is in your **Contacts** — one you
imported, or sent through the API — your agent is told their name. It can use
it in the greeting and the instructions as `{{name}}` and `{{first_name}}`
(and `{{phone}}`), the same placeholders a campaign fills, and it is told in a
sentence that the caller is probably that person.

*Probably*, because the number a call arrives from can be faked. So the agent
is asked to confirm who it is talking to before discussing their account, the
caller's **email is never given to the agent**, and the call is kept on its
own line in your inbox rather than being filed into the contact's record. If
the agent is set to remember people across channels only once they are
verified, it is not given the name either.

On a call your agent **places** — through the API, a campaign or a call back —
none of that caution is needed: you chose the number. The call is filed on the
contact, and their name, phone and email fill the placeholders. Anything you
send in a call's own `variables` wins over the contact's fields.

### Who-is-calling lookup

Give this an https address of your own and, when somebody rings this agent,
we ask your system who it is **before the agent answers** — so you can hand
it the caller's name, their last order, their plan, whatever your CRM knows.
It is the inbound counterpart of the `variables` you send when you place a
call.

We `POST` this, signed exactly like a [webhook](/api-reference/webhooks):

```json theme={null}
{
  "event": "call.started",
  "callId": "CA0c7c…",
  "surface": "phone",
  "agentId": "ag_…",
  "from": "+919876543210",
  "to": "+918000000000",
  "direction": "inbound",
  "contact": { "id": "cust_…", "name": "Asha Menon", "phone": "+919876543210", "email": "asha@example.com", "externalId": "CRM-1183" },
  "sentAt": "2026-10-09T10:30:00.000Z"
}
```

`surface` is `phone` or `whatsapp`. `to` is the agent's voice line, on a
WhatsApp call too. `contact` is the person in your Contacts with the caller's
number, or `null`. Answer within **two seconds** with:

```json theme={null}
{ "variables": { "name": "Asha", "plan": "Gold", "last_order": "A-1183 delivered Tuesday" } }
```

Up to 20 values, each cut to 150 characters, names lower-cased with spaces
turned into `_` — the same rules as a call's `variables`. They fill
`{{plan}}`, `{{last_order}}` and the rest in the greeting and the agent's
instructions, and they win over the contact's own fields.

If your system does not answer in two seconds, answers with an error, or sends
anything else, the call goes ahead without them. We never retry it, and the
caller only ever hears a little more ringing. A phone provider that repeats its
own request to us (it does, when it did not get our answer in time) asks your
system again **with the same `callId`**, so treat `callId` as the key and ignore
one you have already answered.

It is asked only for a call your agent is going to answer. A number you have set
to forward calls to a person is not announced to your system.

Set it on the agent's **Actions** page, in the **Who-is-calling lookup** card, or with
`voice.callStartUrl` on [Update Agent](/api-reference/agents/update-agent).
Saving a new address shows a **signing secret once** — copy it into your
receiver then, it is not shown again. Verify `x-thinnest-signature-v2` with it
as you would a webhook. Clearing the address switches the lookup off.

To replace the secret without changing the address, press **New secret** on the
Actions page, or send `"callStartSecret": "rotate"` in `voice`. The old secret
stops working at once, and the new one is shown once.

The address must be https, must not carry a username or password, and must not
point inside a private network. If signing is not available at that moment the
API answers `503` with the code `signing_unavailable` and saves nothing; try
again shortly.

**Duplicating an agent does not copy this address.** The copy gets no signing
secret of its own, so it opens with the lookup switched off and the Agents page
tells you to set it again on the copy. Do that on the copy's Actions page, and it
gets its own secret.

> [!WARNING]
>
> The lookup runs for phone and WhatsApp calls, and only on inbound calls. Treat
> what it is sent like caller ID: `from` is the number the call claims to come
> from. Before your system hands the agent anything sensitive, decide whether a
> matching number is enough.

### Fillers before tool run

On, and worth leaving on. Checking your documents or calling one of your tools
takes a second or two, and this is what the caller hears instead of silence.

Leave **What Agent says** blank and the agent says it in whichever language it is
speaking — if you have not fixed a language, it works that out from the caller,
so somebody who rings you in Tamil is answered in Tamil from the first word.

Fill it in and it says exactly that, every time, in whatever language you wrote
it. Keep it to a few words: it is covering a pause of a second or two, and
something longer just leaves a new silence after it.

Turn it off if you would rather the line stayed quiet.

You can write up to eight lines, one per line, each up to 60 characters. The
agent picks among them, and only uses lines written in the caller's script — so
a Hindi line is said on Hindi calls and an English line on English ones. Words
of an Indian language typed in Roman letters are converted to that language's
script when you save.

Through the API: `voice.thinking` (on or off, on unless set) and
`voice.thinkingLines` (a list of up to 8 lines of 60 characters; `null` or `[]`
for the built-in lines in the caller's language). The name must be exactly that;
`voice.thinkingPhrase` is refused.

#### When it speaks

When your agent decides to look something up or run one of your tools, it says
its line **straight away**, while the lookup runs, rather than going quiet
first. If the answer still has not started a little later, it says one more
line, then waits for the answer. It never says more than that for one question.

With **Fillers before tool run** off, the agent says nothing extra while it
works, however long the lookup takes.

Two boxes under it set the timing. Leave either blank to use the standard.

| Setting | What it controls | Standard | Range |
| - | - | - | - |
| **How long Agent waits first** | Quiet time before the agent speaks on a slow reply | 900 ms | 200–5,000 ms |
| **How long before Agent says another** | The gap before a second line, and how long a lookup that is still running waits for it | 2,500 ms | 1,000–10,000 ms |

Set the second one longer if your lines take a while to say, so the second
never lands on top of the first. A value outside the range is pulled back into
it when you save.

Through the API: `voice.thinkingDelayMs` and `voice.thinkingRepeatMs` (whole
milliseconds; `null` for the standard). The API refuses a value outside the
range instead of pulling it in.

#### Fillers after the customer stops speaking

Off unless you turn it on. When on, the agent says a short acknowledgement
("Okay.") the moment the caller stops, before **every** reply, rather than only
when a reply is slow. It suits a slower model; on a quick one it puts a syllable
in front of everything.

Through the API: `voice.thinkingAtTurnEnd` (`false` unless set).

## What language it speaks

Voice follows the language on your agent — set it on the **Playground**. Set the agent to Marathi and it answers calls in Marathi
**only**, and the speech recogniser listens for Marathi too.

Leave it on **\[Auto] Match the customer** and it works out what they are
speaking and answers in that. The recogniser then has to decide the language
afresh for every sentence, so a short or mixed reply can be heard as the wrong
one. On a line where people open in English, Hindi or a mix of both, this is
usually the right setting; if your callers all use one language, fix it.

An agent has one language. There is no "second language" setting: to serve two,
leave the agent on **Match the customer**.

## Where calls appear

Each call is its own conversation in the inbox, with its transcript, alongside
that customer's chats. One customer record, one memory, one history.

A call is genuinely a different thing from a message thread — it has a start, an
end and a duration — so it reads as its own entry rather than being appended to
a chat.

### The call log

**Usage → Calls** lists every call the workspace has made or taken, newest
first, with the transcript and the recording behind each row. Each one says how
it actually ended rather than just whether it finished:

| Outcome | What happened |
| - | - |
| Answered | A person picked up |
| No answer | It rang out — the commonest by far, and what retries are for |
| Line busy | Engaged. Worth trying later; they are near their phone |
| Declined | They pressed decline. Never called again automatically |
| Not reachable | No such number, barred, or out of service |
| Answering machine | Voicemail took it — see [Hang up on voicemail](#hang-up-on-voicemail) |
| Ended before the agent spoke | Something picked up, but the call ended before your agent started — usually somebody who hung up while the voicemail check was listening, or a caller who put the phone down straight away |

On an outbound call the row also shows **which of your numbers placed it**,
which is the question worth asking once an agent has spare numbers to call from.
Export gives you all of it as a spreadsheet.

> [!NOTE]
>
> A lot of *Not reachable* usually means a stale list. A lot of *Declined*
> usually means the wrong audience or the wrong opening. A lot of *No answer* is
> usually the wrong time of day. That is the whole reason the reason is shown.

Open a call to see **How the call went** — how long the caller waited for
each reply, silences, interruptions, and any turns the agent could not answer
or that a backup answered — and **Problems on this call**, if anything went
wrong while it was live. The same figures come through the API as `quality` on
[Get Call](/api-reference/calls/get-call), and each problem is sent as a
`call.problem` [webhook](/api-reference/webhooks#problems-on-a-live-call) while
the call is still going on. See [Usage](/workspace/usage#how-a-call-went).

### Call summaries

Off unless you turn it on, under **Summarise each call** on the Playground.
With it on, two or three sentences are written once a call ends — what the
customer said and how it finished — and they appear as a **Summary** tab on the
call in **Usage → Calls**, beside the recording and the transcript.

The transcript was always there and always free. What this buys is the time:
forty calls to get through is forty transcripts to open, or forty pairs of
sentences to skim.

It is written from the transcript afterwards by a small model, so it is a
reading of the call rather than a record of it. The transcript is what was
actually said, and it is still there underneath.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **A summary covers one call, not the customer.** Somebody rung three times
> has three calls in the log and three separate summaries. The whole history
> with that person is the conversation in the inbox.

If your agent writes into a [spreadsheet](/agent/spreadsheet) and you have made
a column called **Summary** — or Notes, or Remarks — the same switch fills that
too. Nothing is summarised anywhere while it is off, including into that
column: making the column does not start it.

## Your knowledge on calls

Your agent searches your knowledge base on calls, the same as it does in chat.
Both are on by default.

They are **two switches**, on the **Actions** page, because looking something up
costs a little more on a call than on a page — the agent has to find the answer
before it can start speaking, so the caller hears a short pause. It is a pause,
not a wait, and for most businesses being right is worth it.

Turn the calls one off if you want the quickest possible line and your callers
mostly ask things your instructions already cover. Changing one switch does not
change the other.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **The agent says something while it looks.** When it has to check your
> documents — or reach any of your connected tools — it says a short "one
> moment" first rather than going quiet. A caller cannot see an agent thinking,
> and a few seconds of silence on a phone line reads as a dropped call.
>
> It is on to begin with, and it is yours to change under **Fillers Before Tool
> Run** on the Playground.

## Booking a call back

"Can you call me after five?" — the agent books it, and your number rings them
at that time. It works on calls and in WhatsApp chats, because that is where
people ask.

Say it however you like: *in half an hour*, *after five*, *tomorrow morning*.
The agent repeats back the time it booked, so nobody is left guessing.

**It only promises what it can keep.** If it cannot book one it says so plainly
instead — and there are a few reasons it might:

| Why | What the agent says |
| - | - |
