  sounded robotic on a first call. Change it any time from the voice picker. Calls
  on a new agent are billed at the Premium rate until you do.
  [Voice](/channels/voice#voice)
* **New agents start on the Prana \[Voice] model.**
  [Model](/agent/behaviour#model)
* **Replies start sooner after a caller stops speaking,** and the agent is better
  at telling a finished sentence from a pause.
  [Voice](/channels/voice)
* **The call's cost is on its result in the API.**
  [Get Call](/api-reference/calls/get-call)

**Oct 6, 2026**

Build on the API, white label on every paid plan

**New**

* **Build your own product on ThinnestAI.** Create a workspace for each of your
  customers, reach all of them with one key and a `Thinnest-Workspace` header, and
  receive one webhook for every customer.
  [Customers](/api-reference/customers) and
  [Build a platform](/guides/build-a-platform)
* **White label on every paid plan.** Resell the console under your own brand and
  domain: 3 clients on Pay As You Go, 20 on Pro and 100 on Scale. Each client has
  its own plan and call lines, and starts on a free trial that you set and pay for.
  A reseller with no domain yet gets a free preview address.

# Broadcasts
Source: https://docs.thinnest.ai/whatsapp/broadcasts

One approved template, to everybody who agreed to hear from you.

**Broadcasts** in the sidebar sends an approved
[template](/whatsapp/templates) to an audience computed **at send time from
consent** — never from a list somebody exported last week.

> [!NOTE]
>
> The WhatsApp Business App calls this a broadcast too, and caps it at 256
> contacts, reaches only people who saved your number, and gives you no
> scheduling, no personalisation and no delivery reports. This is the same job
> without any of that: no cap beyond [Meta's own messaging
> tier](/meta/overview), no requirement that anybody saved you, and you can see
> what arrived.

## It belongs to the workspace, not to an agent

A broadcast is sent from your WhatsApp number, using a template that belongs to
your WhatsApp Business Account, to your workspace's contacts. None of those is
one agent's, so neither is the list: **every broadcast appears here**, whichever
agent answers it.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Looking for calling campaigns?** They are **Voice Campaigns** in the main
> sidebar, listed the same way this page lists broadcasts. The difference is
> what you choose when you build one: a call goes out from a particular agent's
> number and is opened in its own words, so the builder asks which agent does
> the calling. See [Calling campaigns](/channels/voice-campaigns).

## Before you can send

In this order: WhatsApp connected, an approved template, and contacts who have
consented. Each screen in the chain says what the next one needs, and the
**Send broadcast** button says which one is missing before you start rather than
after you have filled the form in.

## How marketing broadcasts are sent

A broadcast on a **marketing** template goes out through Meta's **Marketing
Messages API**, which Meta optimises for delivery. Meta reports up to 9% more
marketing messages delivered in India than the standard API, for messages people
engage with. There's nothing to switch on: if your account isn't eligible yet,
Meta sends it the standard way instead. The price is the same.

WhatsApp still limits how many marketing messages each person receives, on
every platform. If some aren't delivered, see
[When a message isn't delivered](/whatsapp/not-delivered).

## Writing one

**New broadcast** opens a page, not a dialog — five decisions with a live
preview of what arrives between them:

**1. Name it**

For you, not the customer. Nobody receiving it sees this.

**2. Choose who it goes to**

See below — the lists overlap, and the page says which one it settles on.

**3. Pick an approved template**

Only approved ones appear. Meta refuses anything else at the moment of
sending, so an unapproved template is not an option you can pick and regret.

**4. Fill the blanks**

Each one takes a contact field or a fixed value. The preview updates as you
type, so you read the message a real recipient gets rather than a row of
braces.

**5. Say when**

Now, or a time. Scheduling needs nothing left open — see **Sending** below.

The page does not scroll. The two side columns do, and the preview between them
stays put, because it is the thing you are checking the other two against.

> [!TIP]
>
> **From a template you just got approved**, press **Send broadcast** on its card
> on the [Templates](/whatsapp/templates) page. It opens this page with that
> template already chosen.

## Who answers the replies

A broadcast produces conversations — people reply to it. **Who answers the
replies** on the send form picks the agent that handles them, and defaults to
the one your number already answers on.

It is a real choice rather than a formality: you may want a different agent on a
sale than on a delivery notice. Replies land in your [inbox](/workspace/inbox)
whichever you pick, so nothing is lost if you change your mind afterwards — only
who drafts the first answer.

## Choosing an audience

> [!WARNING]
>
> **A broadcast only reaches people who opted in.** That is WhatsApp's rule, not
> ours: Meta allows a business to message someone only if they gave you their
> number **and** agreed to hear from you. Contacts who never opted in are left
> out of every broadcast, whichever list you choose.

Three lists, each showing its count **before** you commit:

| Audience | Who |
| - | - |
| Imported contacts | Contacts from a spreadsheet you uploaded, whose opt-in you confirmed when uploading |
| Opted in on WhatsApp | Opted in, and reached you via WhatsApp |
| Everyone who opted in | Everyone who opted in, however they arrived |

You can tick more than one. The lists overlap — everybody who opted in on
WhatsApp is also in *Everyone who opted in* — so ticking two sends to *Everyone
who opted in*, and the page says so and shows that count as soon as you pick a
second list.

### Uploading a list for this broadcast

You don't need to import a spreadsheet on **Contacts** first. Under **Select
audience**, choose **Upload a CSV** and drop the file in:

**1. Map the columns**

Say which column holds the phone number, and optionally the name and email.
A number without a country code is read in the country you pick.

**2. Check the rows**

The people the file turned into are shown beside the form. Rows that are
not a usable number are listed by line; tick **Leave them out and send to
the rest** to go ahead without them.

**3. Confirm consent**

Tick **These people agreed to get WhatsApp messages from you**. It is
required: WhatsApp only reaches people who agreed, so an unticked list
would reach nobody. Only tick it if they did.

The broadcast goes to exactly the people in the file. They are also added to
**Contacts**, with their consent and today's date recorded, so later broadcasts
can reach them too. Anyone who has already told you to stop is left out, even
if they are in the file.

## Getting people opted in

Consent is collected out in the world — on your website, a form, at your counter,
in a shop, over the phone — as long as what they agreed to names your business
and says you will message them on WhatsApp. What the console does is **record**
it. There are four ways, and they all write the same thing: the answer, the date,
and where it came from.

| | How |
| - | - |
| **A customer agrees in the conversation** | Automatic. Your agent records it when somebody says yes, in their own words, and records the opposite when they say stop. |
| **Importing a spreadsheet** | Tick *These people agreed to hear from us* on the import. Only tick it if they did. |
| **People already in your contacts** | The **Contacts** page says how many have not been asked, with a **Record consent** button beside it. |
| **From your own system** | Our [Contacts API](/api-reference/contacts/create-contact) takes a consent status and source with each contact, so a CRM or billing system can keep it in step. |

> [!WARNING]
>
> **If your contacts show as not asked, broadcasts reach nobody.** Importing a
> spreadsheet without ticking the box is the usual reason: the contacts save
> fine, and every broadcast and sequence then leaves them out, because WhatsApp
> only allows marketing to people who agreed. The banner on **Contacts** is
> there to say so before you build an audience and find it empty.

### Recording it for people already in your contacts

An admin can record consent for everyone nobody has asked yet, in one go. You
confirm that they agreed and say how — in writing, in person or by phone, or on
your website — and that answer is stored beside each contact with today's date.
It is what you would show WhatsApp if they ever ask, so it is worth being
accurate about.

It never touches anybody who opted out. Somebody who replied STOP stays opted
out, and no bulk action can undo that.

> [!NOTE]
>
> Contacts with no phone number are left alone too — a WhatsApp consent needs a
> WhatsApp number to apply to — and so are the people your agent spoke to, who
> live on [Leads](/agent/leads) and arrived by a different promise.

Consent is enforced in the database. There is exactly one way an audience gets
built, and it is not the interface — so a bug in a screen cannot message
somebody who did not opt in, or who opted out.

### The do-not-contact list

Separate from consent, and it applies to broadcasts as well as calls.

Consent is about a customer you already have: they replied STOP, or they never
opted in. The **do-not-contact list** is a list of *numbers* — the file you get
from a regulator, a complaint, a lawyer's letter, or the CRM you used before.
Most of those numbers are not in your contacts at all, so there is nothing to
set a consent flag on.

Add them on the **Contacts** page, with the **Do not contact** button at the top — paste them or upload
a file. Nothing on that list is ever messaged or called again, on any channel.

**Finding the numbers to add.** Filter your contacts by what happened to their last
WhatsApp message (for example *Failed* or *Not delivered*), then choose **Export
CSV**. You get exactly the people that filter shows, every page of them, with a
**Do not contact** column saying who is on the list already. The file opens in
Excel and Google Sheets, including names written in Telugu, Hindi or any other
script. Only owners and admins can export.

> [!NOTE]
>
> It is checked **at the moment each message is sent**, not when the audience was
> built. So a list you upload at eleven stops a broadcast that is already part
> way through. It also survives an import: bringing in a spreadsheet that happens
> to contain one of those numbers updates the contact, but it does not take the
> number off the list. Only removing it does that, and that needs an admin.

### Narrowing by tag or group

Tags filter *within* the list you chose — they never reach past it. Picking two
tags means **either**, not both.

**Groups** work the same way, under **Narrow it by group**: pick one or more of
the [groups you made on Contacts](/agent/leads#groups) and the broadcast goes
only to people in them who are also on the list you chose. Tags and groups
together mean either: anyone carrying one of the tags *or* in one of the groups.

The exact number after tagging is worked out when the broadcast sends, against
consent as it stands then, so the summary shows the list's own size and says the
tags will narrow it. That is deliberate: somebody who withdraws consent between
your writing it and its going out is not messaged.

## Variables

Each blank binds to a contact field or one fixed string. A template with a
placeholder cannot go out with it empty.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **You cannot edit the message here**, and that is not an omission. Meta
> approved a specific wording; changing it means submitting a new template and
> waiting for review. What is yours per-send is what goes in the blanks, which
> is what this asks for.

## Retargeting and split tests

Both optional, both at the foot of the form.

**Only people from an earlier broadcast** `broadcast + outcome`

Sends only to people who did something — or nothing — with a broadcast that
has already gone out. *Did not reply* is the usual one and usually the one
worth sending.

Both halves or neither: an earlier broadcast **and** what those people did.
Half-filled, it would quietly mean everybody, so the page refuses it.

**Test a second template against it** `template`

Splits the audience in half by a hash of the contact, so the two sides never
overlap and nobody gets both. It makes **two broadcasts**, named (A) and (B),
which you compare on the list.

Press **Send broadcast** and both go out. Press **Save as draft** and you get
two drafts to start when you are ready.

## Sending

> [!WARNING]
>
> **A send started from the console runs from your browser, so that tab must stay
> open to finish.** It is the same client-driven loop the site crawl uses.
>
> A **scheduled** send has no tab and does not need one — it runs on our side.
> It also picks up any broadcast a closed tab left half-sent.

Sends are resumable. Each recipient is its own row, so a crash or a closed tab
**pauses** rather than loses, and nobody is messaged twice.

## Watching it

The broadcast's own page shows the message as sent, every recipient with their
state, the refusal reasons grouped, and a timeline.

**On the Contacts page**, every contact shows what became of their last WhatsApp
campaign message, and the menu above the list filters by it — the same states,
plus *Never messaged*. The filter stays in the address, so a page, a reload or a
shared link keeps it.

**On a broadcast's own page, filter its list by what happened** — the menu above
it, beside the search:
Delivered, Read, Replied, Not delivered, Failed, Not contacted, Sent with no
receipt yet, and Waiting, each with how many are in it. "Delivered" includes the
people who went on to read or reply. It combines with the search, so you can
look for one person among the undelivered.

**Export CSV**, beside the search, downloads exactly the people that filter
shows, every page of them. Each row has the name, the number, the status, the
reason where there is one, and when the message was sent, delivered, read and
replied to, on your workspace's clock. A calling campaign also gets how each
call ended, the talk time and the number of dials. The file opens in Excel and
Google Sheets, including names written in Telugu, Hindi or any other script.
Only owners and admins can export.

**Sent, delivered, read and refused are four different facts**, each carrying
Meta's own reason where one applies. "Sent" means WhatsApp accepted it — not
that it arrived.

## Cost

The summary beside the form shows the per-message rate and what the audience
would cost at it, **before** you send. It is an estimate and it lands high
rather than low: Meta charges per *delivered* message, so anything that does not
deliver is not charged.

See [Windows and what gets charged](/meta/windows-and-pricing).
Marketing templates are charged by Meta on **every** send, unlike replies inside
the 24-hour window.

A **utility** broadcast is different: any recipient who is still inside their
own 24-hour window receives it free. So the same broadcast can cost less than
its estimate, and the [usage](/workspace/usage) breakdown is what tells you
which sends were actually charged.

Calling campaigns are priced separately — see [Calling
campaigns](/channels/voice-campaigns).

Both appear line by line in [Usage](/workspace/usage), where you can also open
any call from a calling campaign and read what was said.

## What is not built

> [!WARNING]
>
> * **Broadcasting on any other channel.** A broadcast is WhatsApp. Instagram and
>   Messenger cannot carry marketing outside the 24-hour window at all — Meta
>   forbids promotional content there explicitly — Telegram does not send one yet,
>   and website chat never will: a broadcast reaches somebody who is not there.
> * **Sending to people who never opted in.** Not a missing feature — buying a
>   list and messaging it is the fastest way to lose a WhatsApp number.


# WhatsApp calls
Source: https://docs.thinnest.ai/whatsapp/calls

Customers call your business from WhatsApp, and your agent answers.

A customer taps the call button in your WhatsApp chat, and your agent picks up —
the same agent, with the same voice, knowledge and tools, that answers your phone
line and your website. No phone number to rent, and nothing for the customer to
install: they are already in the chat.

## Turning it on

1. On **Connect WhatsApp**, press **Calls** on the number.
2. Switch on **WhatsApp calls** and save.

That is all. Switching it on also turns on **Answer calls** for the agent on that
number, and gives it a voice if it had none. Its **WhatsApp** row on the Voice page
shows **On** — it follows this switch, and every agent has it on by default.

> [!NOTE]
>
> The **WhatsApp calls** switch is the one that decides. While it is off, this
> number answers no calls — even if the same setting is on in Meta's WhatsApp
> Manager. Switching it off turns the agent's WhatsApp row off too, and leaves the
> website and phone as they are.

## The settings

| Setting | What it does |
| - | - |
| **WhatsApp calls** | On or off for this number. |
| **Show the call button** | Whether customers see a call button in your chat. They can still call from a message that has a call button. |
| **Allow callback requests** | After a customer calls (answered or missed), WhatsApp asks them whether your business may call them back. Their answer appears in the inbox as a message — for example *Allowed you to call them back on WhatsApp, for the next 7 days*. Calling them back over WhatsApp from ThinnestAI is coming next. |
| **Call hours** | When customers can call. Outside them, WhatsApp offers to chat or request a callback instead. Off means always available. |
| **Closed days** | Up to 20 dates — holidays, events — when calls aren't taken. |

The settings are read from WhatsApp each time you open them, so a change made in
Meta's WhatsApp Manager shows up here too.

Pick each time from the list, or type it however you like — `09:00`, `9 am`, `18:00` and `6 pm` all work.
Switching call hours off really
turns them off at WhatsApp, even if you cleared the days first.

Call hours are edited one range a day here. WhatsApp allows two a day; a second
range set in WhatsApp Manager is kept as it is unless you edit that day.

**Customers don't see your hours listed anywhere** — not on your profile, not in
the chat. They meet them when they call outside them: WhatsApp offers to chat or
to request a callback, and shows when you're next available. WhatsApp applies a
change straight away, but a customer's phone can take **up to 7 days** to pick
it up; opening your business's chat info page on that phone refreshes it at once.
To test your hours, call from another phone at a time they're closed.

## Who can use it

WhatsApp only enables calling for businesses with a **daily messaging limit of at
least 2,000 people** — unique people you start conversations with in a rolling
24 hours, counted across your whole business, not per number. Every new business
starts lower. The quickest way up is [verifying your business](/meta/verification);
otherwise Meta raises it as you send messages people engage with
([how limits rise](/meta/quality-and-limits#climbing)).

The Calls window states your business's limit. If it is under 2,000, it says so
over its settings and holds the Save button until it is.

> [!NOTE]
>
> WhatsApp Manager may show an older **per-number** limit, often 250. That figure
> does not decide calling — the business-wide one does, and it is often already
> 2,000.

While **WhatsApp calls** is off, the other settings in the window are greyed out.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **A number that is also in the WhatsApp Business app cannot take WhatsApp calls.**
> WhatsApp does not allow voice or video calls on a number used in the app and over
> the API at once. See [Keeping the WhatsApp Business
> app](/channels/whatsapp#keeping-the-whatsapp-business-app).

## What it costs

A WhatsApp call is billed at your **voice per-minute rate** — the same as a phone
call — for the time your agent is on it, rounded up to the next whole minute.
Calls your customers make to you cost nothing from Meta.

## Not here yet

* **Your agent calling customers on WhatsApp.** Coming next: callbacks, "ring the
  customer now", voice campaigns and the call API will be able to use WhatsApp, for
  customers who have allowed calls from your business.
* Video calls.

If a call doesn't connect, the reason is shown in WhatsApp's words with what it
means — see [WhatsApp error codes](https://thinnest.ai/whatsapp-error-codes).


# Connect External Agent/CRM
Source: https://docs.thinnest.ai/whatsapp/external-agents

Answer WhatsApp customers from your own CRM or agent platform. ThinnestAI runs the WhatsApp side — the number, the inbox, templates and opt-outs.

**Connect WhatsApp → your number → Connect External Agent/CRM.**

You already have a CRM or an agent platform of your own — your own prompts, your
own voice and chat stack — and you want it on WhatsApp without building a
WhatsApp integration. Switch on
**Connect External Agent/CRM** for a number and ThinnestAI stops answering it. Every
message a customer sends is passed to your external agent, and its replies go back to the
customer through us.

What stays with ThinnestAI: the connected number, the shared
[inbox](/workspace/inbox) where your team sees every thread and can take one
over, [templates](/whatsapp/templates), [forms](/whatsapp/templates#forms), opt-outs
("STOP") and Meta's 24-hour rule.

## How a message travels

1. A customer writes to your WhatsApp number.
2. We store it in the inbox and post it to your platform's address as `message.received`.
3. Your agent decides what to say.
4. Your platform calls `POST /api/v1/conversations/{conversationId}/reply`.
5. We send it on WhatsApp and add it to the thread as the agent's reply.

Your agent can take as long as it needs — nothing waits on it. A reply sent
after the customer's [24-hour window](/meta/windows-and-pricing) has closed
must be an approved template.

## Only want the WhatsApp API?

If nothing of ours should answer — your own software does all of it — pick
**WhatsApp API** from the use-case dropdown in the top bar, before you connect a
number. You land on **WhatsApp** instead of Agents, and **every number you connect
starts with Connect External Agent/CRM already on**. There is no agent to set up and no
toggle to find; follow the steps under the number. Changed your mind — want voice or
our AI agent too? Pick another use case from the same dropdown; your
connected numbers keep answering through your software until you change them.

* **Start a conversation** with an approved template:
  [`POST /api/v1/messages`](/api-reference/messages/send-message). WhatsApp only lets a
  business message someone first with a template.
* **Reply** once they write back, with text, media, a form or a template:
  [`POST /api/v1/conversations/{id}/reply`](/api-reference/conversations/reply-to-conversation).
* **Read** threads and catch up on anything missed:
  [conversations](/api-reference/conversations/list-conversations).

You pay Meta's fee to Meta and 10% of it to us, per message. Nothing for AI —
no agent of ours runs. On the **Free plan**, your first **200 messages**
(one time) carry none of our charges; after that, switch to Pay as you go (no
monthly fee) to keep sending.

## Set it up

**1. Connect your WhatsApp number**

On **WhatsApp**, connect your own WhatsApp Business Account — a new one or
one you already have.

**2. Switch on Connect External Agent/CRM**

Under the number, switch on **Connect External Agent/CRM**. Our agent picker
moves to **Not assigned** and locks — nothing of ours answers this number.
The number then shows these same steps. Only admins can change it; switching
it off hands the number back, and you choose one of our agents again.

**3. Create an API key**

**Settings → API keys.** Send it on every call as
`Authorization: Bearer ta_live_…`. See [authentication](/api-reference/authentication).

**4. Give us your external agent's address**

Under the number, paste the HTTPS address customer messages should be posted
to and press **Save**. The **signing secret** is shown once — keep it. Saving
again mints a new one.

**5. Reply**

Call [`POST /api/v1/conversations/{id}/reply`](/api-reference/conversations/reply-to-conversation)
with the `conversationId` from the event.

> [!WARNING]
>
> Until you save an address, customer messages go nowhere and nobody answers
> them. The WhatsApp page shows a red warning under the number when that is the
> case, and again if your platform starts refusing deliveries.

## What your webhook receives

```json theme={null}
{
  "event": "message.received",
  "sentAt": "2026-09-21T10:15:02Z",
  "data": {
    "conversationId": "conv_e0829641-…",
    "messageId": "msg_91c2…",
    "channel": "whatsapp",
    "from": "919876543210",
    "name": "Priya",
    "text": "Has my order shipped?",
    "media": null,
    "form": null,
    "receivedAt": "2026-09-21T10:15:01Z"
  }
}
```

* **`media`** — when the customer sent a photo, voice note, video or document:
  `{ "kind": "image" | "audio" | "video" | "file", "mimeType", "filename" }`.
  The file itself is not in the event — read the conversation's
  [messages](/api-reference/conversations/list-conversations) for a download link.
* **`form`** — when the customer submitted a WhatsApp form: `{ "answers": { "field": "value" } }`.
* **`text`** — the message, or a media message's caption.
* **`messageId`** — the same id the [messages API](/api-reference/conversations/list-conversations)
  returns, so you can tell a message you already handled from a new one.

Every delivery carries `x-thinnest-signature: sha256=…`, an HMAC-SHA256 of the
raw body under your signing secret. Check it before trusting the body.

Every message is sent, not just the last one in a burst. If a customer sends
three messages quickly, your platform gets three events.

## What your agent can send

| Send | When | Body |
| - | - | - |
| Text | Window open | `{ "text": "…" }` |
| A photo, video, audio or document | Window open | `{ "media": { "type": "image", "url": "https://…", "caption": "…" } }` |
| A WhatsApp form | Window open | `{ "form": "Delivery address" }` — its name on the Forms page |
| An approved template | Any time | `{ "template": { "name": "…", "variables": ["…"] } }` |

One kind per call. The full reference, with every refusal, is on
[Reply to a conversation](/api-reference/conversations/reply-to-conversation).

## When a person takes over

If a teammate takes a conversation over in the inbox, your agent's replies to
it are refused, and its new messages are not sent to your webhook, until the
conversation is handed back. That way the customer never has two voices
answering at once. The teammate's exchange can be read through the
[conversations API](/api-reference/conversations/list-conversations).

"STOP" and other opt-outs are handled before anything reaches you. The
customer is unsubscribed from marketing whatever your agent does.

## Pricing

Meta bills your WhatsApp Business Account directly for its fee on each message,
at [Meta's rates](/meta/windows-and-pricing). ThinnestAI charges **10% of Meta's
rate** per message, from your wallet — pay as you go, with no monthly
subscription. A message Meta does not charge for costs nothing from us either.
Replies your teammates send from the inbox or a connected helpdesk on these
numbers are charged the same way.

There is no AI usage to pay for on these numbers, because your agent does the
answering.

## If your endpoint misses a message

Each message is sent once. One your endpoint does not accept is not retried, and
the WhatsApp page shows the last failure under the number. Nothing is lost:
[read back what you missed](/api-reference/conversations/list-conversations)
with the conversations API.

## Not available yet

* **No typing indicator or read receipts** from your agent.
* **WhatsApp only.** Website chat, Telegram and voice are answered by
  ThinnestAI agents.


# When a message isn't delivered
Source: https://docs.thinnest.ai/whatsapp/not-delivered

What WhatsApp said, what it means, and what to do about it.

When WhatsApp doesn't deliver a message, you'll see it in two places: on the
message in your [inbox](/workspace/inbox), and against the person in a
[broadcast's](/whatsapp/broadcasts) results.

Each one shows **Meta's own message first**, exactly as WhatsApp sent it, and
then **what it means** in plain words. Meta's wording is kept so you can see the
refusal came from WhatsApp, search for it, or quote it to Meta's support.

A broadcast also groups its failures, so forty people refused for the same
reason are one line with a count, not forty.

## The marketing limit

The one you'll see most is this:

> This message was not delivered to maintain healthy ecosystem engagement. (131049)

**This isn't a fault with your account, your template or us.** WhatsApp limits
how many *marketing* messages each person receives from **all businesses
combined**, and refuses the rest. It does this on every WhatsApp platform, not
just this one. It decides per person, based on things like how often they read
marketing messages and how busy their inbox is.

What helps:

* **Wait at least 24 hours** before sending that person marketing again. Meta
  warns that resending sooner can keep them blocked for longer.
* **Space your campaigns out.** Several offers in a few days to the same list is
  exactly what triggers it.
* **Replies reset it.** When someone messages you, marketing you send them in
  the next 24 hours doesn't count toward the limit.
* **Use utility templates for transactional messages.** Order confirmations,
  delivery updates and tickets aren't subject to the limit — as long as the
  template is honestly utility and not a promotion.
* **Testing on your own phone counts too.** A marketing template tried several
  times in a day on your own number hits the limit like any other, and the
  later tests come back with 131049. Message your business first (that opens
  the 24 hours), or test on another phone.

**You can see who it applies to.** For 24 hours after WhatsApp holds back a
marketing message to someone, they show **Marketing paused until** a time, on the
Contacts page and next to their name in the Inbox. Replies in an open
conversation still reach them; it's only marketing templates that wait.

> [!NOTE]
>
> To protect your customers, a marketing broadcast **holds back** anyone WhatsApp
> limited in the last 24 hours, rather than sending again and extending the
> block. They're listed as *Not contacted*, with the reason. Utility templates
> are never held back.

## Other reasons

| Meta's code | What it means | What to do |
| - | - | - |
| **131050** | The person turned off marketing messages from you in WhatsApp. | Don't send them marketing unless they turn it back on. |
| **131026** | The number can't receive the message — usually not on WhatsApp, or on a very old version. | Check the number with them. |
| **131053** | WhatsApp couldn't fetch the picture, video or document. | Upload the file to the template again, then resend. |
| **131047** | It's been over 24 hours since they last messaged you. | Send an approved [template](/whatsapp/templates) instead. |
| **131056** | Too many messages to the same person in a short time. | Wait a little before messaging them again. |
| **131042** | Meta couldn't charge your WhatsApp Business account's payment method. | Add a working card in Meta: [step by step](/whatsapp/payment-method). |
| **131048** | Messages from your number were blocked or reported as spam. | Check your quality rating in WhatsApp Manager; send fewer, more relevant messages. |
| **132015** | Meta paused the template after people blocked or reported it. | Edit it and resubmit. |
| **132001** | The template isn't approved, or doesn't exist in that language. | Check its status on the Templates page. |
| **130472** | WhatsApp held a marketing message back for its own experiment. | Nothing — it isn't something you can fix. |

Every code has its own page in
[WhatsApp error codes, explained](https://thinnest.ai/whatsapp-error-codes) — what
it means, whose problem it is, how to fix it and whether to retry.

A message WhatsApp didn't deliver isn't charged.

If you see a code that isn't here and its explanation is missing, or the same
failure keeps happening, tell us and include Meta's message.


# One-time codes
Source: https://docs.thinnest.ai/whatsapp/one-time-codes

OTP over WhatsApp — Meta writes the message, you choose how it behaves.

**One-Time Codes** in the sidebar is where you set up the template a login code
goes out on. It is deliberately not part of Templates, because almost nothing on
that page applies here.

## You do not write this one

An authentication template is the one kind whose words are not yours. Meta
writes them:

> **394812** is your verification code. For your security, do not share this code.
>
> *Expires in 10 minutes.*

You cannot change that wording, add your brand to it, or explain anything in it.
That is a mercy rather than a restriction — OTP is the one message where wording
is a liability, and Meta has already argued with every phishing pattern there
is.

What you choose is three things, and the preview beside them updates as you do.

**Expires after** `1–90 minutes`

Ten by default: long enough to find your phone, short enough that a screenshot
in a group chat is worthless by the time it matters. WhatsApp says this line
in the customer's own language, so it costs you no words.

**Warn against sharing it** `on / off`

Appends *"For your security, do not share this code."* On by default.

**How they get it into your app** `Copy code / One-tap`

* **Copy code** — they tap, then paste. Works everywhere, needs no
  integration, and is the right answer for almost everyone.
* **One-tap autofill** — hands the code straight to your Android app. Needs
  your app's **package name and signing hash**, which the form asks for. Meta
  refuses the template without them, so you would otherwise find out at review
  rather than at login.

There is no "no button" option, and that is Meta's rule rather than ours: a
code template must carry exactly one button, of one of these two kinds.

## Getting it approved

On the new-template page, press **Save & submit for review** to save it and send
it to Meta in one step. Or press **Save as draft** — a draft is ours, not
Meta's, and it cannot send anything — then open it later and press **Submit for
review**. Authentication templates are usually approved within minutes, because
Meta wrote the content and has little to argue with.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Submit needs a connected number.** Meta reviews a template against your
> WhatsApp Business Account, so until one is connected there is nothing to
> submit it to — the button says so on hover.

Once submitted, the settings lock. Meta reviewed a specific configuration and
the API offers no way to change it underneath them. To use different settings,
delete it and make another.

## Sending a code

From your own website's server, through the API. On any code template, press
**View embed code** — on the template's page, or in the **⋯** menu of its row in
the list. A window opens with the four steps (get an API key, make the code on
your server, send it, check it when the customer types it in) and code you can
copy in cURL, Node.js, Python and PHP, with your template's name already filled
in. See also [Send a one-time code](/api-reference/one-time-codes/send-one-time-code). The short
version:

```json theme={null}
POST /api/v1/codes
{ "to": "919876543210", "code": "394812" }
```

We do not generate, store, expire or check the code. That stays yours.

## Deleting one

Either from the row's **⋯** menu in the list, or from **Delete** on the
template's own page.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **This removes it from Meta as well as from here**, and there are two
> consequences worth knowing before you click:
>
> * Anything calling the API with that template's name **stops working**.
> * Meta will **not let the name be used again for 30 days**. If you are
>   replacing a template, give the new one a different name.

A draft that never reached Meta has neither consequence — nothing is using it,
and the name stays free.

## What this costs

Authentication is priced separately from marketing and utility, and a code sent
to another country costs many times a domestic one — on Meta's Indian card, more
than twentyfold. Your own figures are on the [usage page](/workspace/usage),
split by category and country, which is the only way anyone notices a login flow
that has quietly gone international.


# Adding a payment method in Meta
Source: https://docs.thinnest.ai/whatsapp/payment-method

Why Meta blocks your number for a payment method, where to add a card, which cards work, and what happens next.

If you connected **your own WhatsApp Business Account**, Meta charges WhatsApp's
message fees to a card on your Meta account. Until that card works, Meta blocks
the messages your business starts. You may see this on Connect WhatsApp:

> There is an error with the payment method. This will block business initiated
> conversations. Please add a new payment method to the account.

It's quick to fix, and nothing in ThinnestAI needs to change.

## Why it happens

Meta and ThinnestAI send separate bills ([how the two bills work](/meta/windows-and-pricing)):

| What | Who charges it | Paid from |
| - | - | - |
| WhatsApp's per-message fee | Meta | The card on your **Meta** account |
| Our 10% platform fee | ThinnestAI | Your ThinnestAI balance |

Your ThinnestAI balance can't pay Meta. With no working card, Meta blocks the
conversations **you start**: templates and broadcasts. Replies to customers who
messaged you first, inside the 24-hour window, keep working.

## Which account to add it to

The card goes on the **Meta business** that owns your WhatsApp Business Account,
not on your personal Facebook profile.

* The business is usually named after you or your company. It's the one you
  chose, or created, in Meta's popup when you connected WhatsApp.
* If you manage several businesses in Meta, the card must be on the one that
  holds this WhatsApp account. A card on another business doesn't count.

## Where to add it

1. Open **[business.facebook.com/latest/billing_hub/payment_methods](https://business.facebook.com/latest/billing_hub/payment_methods)**,
   signed in with the Facebook account you used to connect WhatsApp.
2. At the top left, check that the **business that owns your WhatsApp account** is
   selected. Switch to it if not.
3. Click **Add payment method**.
4. Choose your country and currency (for India: India, INR), then enter your card
   and business details.
5. Save. If Meta asks which payment method your WhatsApp account should use,
   choose this card.

## Which payment methods work

* A **credit or debit card**. Visa and Mastercard work most reliably.
* The card must allow **online and international transactions**. Many Indian
  cards have these switched off by default; turn them on in your bank's app or
  net banking before adding the card. A card with them off is accepted at first,
  then fails when Meta charges it, and the block comes back.
* Meta lists the options available for your country when you click **Add**.

## What happens next

* Once Meta accepts the card, the block usually lifts **within minutes**.
* Then **open or reload Connect WhatsApp** in ThinnestAI. That's when we ask Meta
  for your account's status: the warning clears straight away, and your
  messages go out normally.
* You don't need to reconnect your number or change anything in ThinnestAI.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **"I've added it" on Connect WhatsApp is a reminder, not a check.** We can't see
> your Meta payment details, so ticking it only stops us asking. Whether Meta can
> actually charge your card is what decides if messages go out, and if it can't,
> the warning comes back on its own.

## Also worth doing: business verification

Meta may also show your business as **not yet verified**. That doesn't block
you, but until it's done Meta limits how many new people you can message each
day. Start it in Meta Business Settings → **Security Centre** → **Start
verification**; you'll need your business documents. See
[Business verification](/meta/verification) for what Meta asks for.

## Still blocked?

If the warning is still there when you reload Connect WhatsApp **an hour** after
adding a working card,
use **Contact support** (the help icon at the top of the app) and we'll check your
account's status with Meta.


# Your products in the chat
Source: https://docs.thinnest.ai/whatsapp/products

The agent can show what you sell, with your real prices and pictures, without the customer leaving WhatsApp.

When a customer asks "what do you have?" or "do you sell the 5-litre one?", the
agent can answer with the products themselves rather than a paragraph about them.
WhatsApp draws them from your own catalogue — your photographs, your prices, your
descriptions — and the customer can tap through, add to a cart and send the order
back into the same conversation.

## What you need first

**A product catalogue linked to your WhatsApp Business Account**, in Meta's
[Commerce Manager](https://business.facebook.com/commerce). This is the one part
we cannot do for you: Meta only lets the business that owns the catalogue link
it.

If you sell on Shopify or WooCommerce you very likely have a catalogue already —
those platforms publish one to Meta for you, and linking it is a setting rather
than a piece of work.

> [!NOTE]
>
> We never copy your catalogue. Prices and pictures are rendered by WhatsApp from
> your catalogue at the moment the message is opened, so a customer cannot be
> shown a price you changed last week.

## Turning it on

On the agent's **Channels** page, under the WhatsApp number, switch on **Show
products from your catalogue**.

With the switch on and no catalogue linked, nothing happens — the agent is simply
never offered the ability, rather than trying and failing in front of a customer.

## What the customer sees

| When the agent | They get |
| - | - |
| Knows which product they mean | That one product, with its price, picture and an **Add to cart** button |
| Has a few that fit | A list they can scroll, each tappable |
| Has nothing specific to show | Your whole catalogue, opened inside the chat |

All three carry the agent's own words above them, so it still sounds like a
conversation rather than a brochure.

## Naming particular products

To show *specific* products rather than the whole catalogue, the agent needs to
know your product codes — the SKUs as they appear in your catalogue — and what
each one is. Meta does not let us read the contents of your catalogue, only the
fact that you have one, so this short list is something you tell us.

Send us the codes and names and we will set them against your agent. Until then
the agent opens the whole catalogue, which is the useful half and needs nothing
from you.

> [!WARNING]
>
> A code that does not exist in your catalogue makes WhatsApp refuse the entire
> message, so the agent only ever names codes from your list and quietly skips
> anything else. If a product never appears when it should, the code we have is
> probably not the one in Commerce Manager.

## Orders

An order the customer sends back arrives in your [inbox](/workspace/inbox) as part
of the conversation, listing what they chose as `2 x SKU-CODE` — the codes from
your own catalogue, since Meta does not let us read the names against them.

Nothing is charged and nothing is reserved: a catalogue order is the customer
saying what they want, not a sale. It is yours to price, confirm and fulfil,
exactly as if they had typed it out.

## Where this is charged

A product message is an ordinary WhatsApp message inside the customer's
[24-hour window](/meta/windows-and-pricing) — the same price as any other reply,
with no surcharge for the products in it. Starting a conversation with products
is not possible: outside the window WhatsApp carries only an approved
[template](/whatsapp/templates).


# Send a message
Source: https://docs.thinnest.ai/whatsapp/send

One approved template, to a handful of numbers, without building a campaign.

**Workspace → WhatsApp → Send.**

Some messages are not a campaign. Telling four people their slot moved, or
sending yourself a test before a launch, does not need an audience, a schedule
and a spend — it needs one template and a phone number.

## Sending one

1. **Pick a template.** Only [templates](/whatsapp/templates) Meta has approved
   appear. An unapproved one cannot be sent, so listing it would only waste your
   time.
2. **Add the numbers.** Type one and press Enter to turn it into a tag. Up to
   **ten** at a time. Country code, spaces and dashes are all fine — the number
   is read the same way an imported contact is.
3. **Fill the values.** Each `{{1}}`, `{{2}}` in the template gets a box,
   pre-filled with the sample you wrote. Edit or leave them.
4. **Add the picture, if the template has one.** A template with an image, video
   or document header needs that file on **every** send — WhatsApp does not
   reuse the one it was approved with. The box is pre-filled with the template's
   own, and WhatsApp fetches it itself, so it has to be a public address.
5. **Fill the link, if a button has one.** A button whose link ends in a
   placeholder — an order number, a booking reference — gets its own box.
6. **Check the preview**, which shows the message as the customer will read it.
7. **Send.**

A **carousel** template can be sent here too. Its cards go out with the pictures
and links they were approved with — there is nothing to fill per card.

Each number is sent to one at a time, and each gets its own result — so if one
is refused and three go, you are told exactly that rather than "failed".

> [!NOTE]
>
> The same number typed twice in different formats — `+91 98765 43210` and
> `919876543210` — is one person, and gets one message.

## The handler

Before sending you can choose **which agent manages the chat**.

Left alone, the chat is handled by the agent that owns the number. Choose a
different one and that agent answers when the customer replies — not just for
this message, but for the conversation that follows.

This is how a chat reaches an agent that has no number of its own: a specialist
that handles bookings, say, while the number itself belongs to your main agent.

## Who you have messaged

The panel beside the composer lists **every WhatsApp number you have a
conversation with**, newest first. Open one to read the thread without leaving
the page, or jump straight to it in the [inbox](/workspace/inbox) to reply, take
over or see the contact's details.

A message you send appears there immediately, and replies land in your inbox
like any other conversation.

## What it will refuse

* **A customer who has opted out**, when the template is marketing. Utility and
  authentication still reach them, and must — see [Opting
  out](/channels/whatsapp#opting-out).
* **A template Meta has not approved.**
* **A media template with no picture**, saying so by name. WhatsApp refuses
  those outright, so it is better caught here than reported as a failed send.
* **Anything at all**, if no number is connected. The page says so at the top and
  links to [Connect WhatsApp](/channels/whatsapp#connecting), which is where you fix
  it.

## When to use a campaign instead

| | Send | [Broadcasts](/whatsapp/broadcasts) |
| - | - | - |
| Who | Up to ten numbers you type | An audience you define |
| When | Now | Now or scheduled |
| Cost known first | No | Yes, priced before it runs |
| Retries a failure | No | Yes, per person |
| Record of who got what | The conversation | A full report |

Ten is a deliberate ceiling. Past that you want the things a campaign gives you,
and the most expensive mistake in messaging is sending to more people than you
meant to.


# Sequences
Source: https://docs.thinnest.ai/whatsapp/sequences

A series of messages triggered by something that happened, not by a date.

A campaign is one message to a list. A **sequence** is a series of messages
triggered by an event — somebody abandoned a cart, placed an order, or asked
about a product and never came back.

## How it works

**1. Something happens**

An event arrives — from your systems via the API, or from something the
customer did.

**2. A matching contact is enrolled**

Consent is checked at enrolment, and again at each send.

**3. Steps run on their own delays**

"Immediately", "after 2 days", "after a week". Each step is an approved
template.

**4. It completes, or stops early**

A customer who replies, converts or opts out leaves the sequence.

## Sending events

Events come in through the API. See the [API reference](/api-reference/introduction).

## Variables

Each step's template blanks bind to contact fields or values carried on the
enrolment — so an abandoned-cart message can name the actual product.

## Consent, again

WhatsApp only allows messages to people who opted in, so who can be enrolled
depends on how they arrive:

| How they are enrolled | Who can be |
| - | - |
| Enrolling a list from the console | Only people who opted in |
| A tag that triggers the sequence | Only people who opted in |
| An event or enrolment from your systems, [via the API](/api-reference/events/report-event) | Anyone you send — the call is you confirming they opted in |

Opting out always wins, on every route: somebody who opted out is never enrolled,
and opting out is re-checked at each send. A customer who opts out on day one of a
seven-day sequence does not receive day three.

## Metering

Sequence sends are metered like any other template send.

Most are charged. A **utility** step is the exception: until 1 October 2026, if
it reaches somebody who is still inside their own 24-hour window — which a drip
step often does, since it goes out to people who replied recently — Meta gives
it away, and so do we.

> [!NOTE]
>
> Sequences run on our side, not from a browser tab — unlike a campaign started
> in the console. Nothing needs to stay open for a sequence to keep sending.


# Templates
Source: https://docs.thinnest.ai/whatsapp/templates

The only thing that reaches a customer outside the 24-hour window.

Outside the [24-hour window](/meta/windows-and-pricing) WhatsApp carries nothing
but an **approved template**.
Everything you start — a campaign, an order update, a reminder — is a template.

Once one is approved you can put it in a [broadcast](/whatsapp/broadcasts), fire it
from the [API](/api-reference/messages/send-message), or
[send it to a few numbers by hand](/whatsapp/send).

## The three categories

| Category | For | Charged | Reaches an opted-out customer |
| - | - | - | - |
| **Marketing** | Offers, announcements, re-engagement | Every send | No |
| **Utility** | Order confirmations, delivery updates, receipts | Every send | Yes, and must |
| **Authentication** | One-time passwords | Every send | Yes |

Getting the category wrong is the most expensive mistake here. A marketing
template refused for opted-out contacts is correct behaviour, not a bug.

## Already have templates? Import them

If you were using WhatsApp before you came here, your approved templates are
still on your WhatsApp Business Account — and **Import from Meta**, at the top of
the Templates page, brings them in.

They arrive with their wording, their examples, their buttons and their approval
status intact, ready to send. Pressing it again is safe: a template you already
have is refreshed rather than duplicated, which is also how you pick up a status
Meta has changed since.

> [!NOTE]
>
> Only templates on **your own** account are imported. Nothing from anybody
> else's reaches your workspace.

## You need a connected number first

Templates are submitted to **your** WhatsApp Business Account, so until one is
connected there is nothing to submit them to. This page is read-only until then
— you can read what is here and browse the pre-built templates, but writing,
submitting, editing and adding a language all wait.

[Connect WhatsApp](/channels/whatsapp#connecting) is the first thing in the WhatsApp
section of the sidebar, and takes a few minutes.

## Writing one

The editor writes the template and submits it to Meta for approval. Approval
typically takes minutes but is Meta's decision, not ours — see [Template review
and approval](/meta/template-review) for what gets rejected and why.

Placeholders are numbered: `{{1}}`, `{{2}}`. Each one is bound at send time to a
contact field or one fixed string — and a template with a placeholder **cannot
go out with it empty**.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **The header has to be fixed text.** Meta allows a variable there; we do not,
> because nothing in the product can fill it — and a template Meta approves that
> can never be sent is worse than one refused while you are writing it. Put the
> changing part in the body.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Authentication templates are copied, not written for you.** Meta writes and
> localises the wording for one-time passwords itself, and rewording it gets the
> template rejected. The editor copies Meta's text exactly.
>
> Authentication templates are also gated behind business verification.

## Languages and variants

A template name can exist in several languages. When you send, the
[contact's language](/agent/leads#contact-language) decides which variant they
receive.

A contact with no language set receives your default — so adding languages is
always an improvement and never a prerequisite.

> [!TIP]
>
> Competitors generally give you one language per template and leave the
> choosing to you. Per-contact variant selection is the difference between
> "we support Hindi" and "your Hindi-speaking customers get Hindi".

## Buttons

Templates can carry quick replies and link buttons. A link button's blank is
sent separately from the body's blanks — Meta wants it in a different component,
and putting it in the body's list breaks both the words and the link.

A button's label can be up to **25 characters** — WhatsApp's limit. The label
box counts as you type (`12/25`) and stops at 25.

## Carousels

A carousel is a message followed by 2 to 10 swipeable cards, each with its own
picture (or video), text and the same buttons. Two things decide whether Meta
accepts one:

* **Each card's picture must be a direct link to the image itself** — one that
  opens just the picture, usually ending in `.jpg` or `.png`. A Google Drive or
  Dropbox share link opens a web page about the file, not the file, so it is
  refused before anything is sent, and the message names the card.
* **Pick the language the text is written in.** A carousel written in Telugu
  should be a Telugu template; Meta reviews the language you choose against the
  words.
* **It must be a Marketing template.** WhatsApp doesn't allow carousels as
  Utility.
* **It has no footer.** WhatsApp allows nothing above the cards except the
  message itself. A marketing carousel still needs a way out, so end the
  message with a line like "Reply STOP to opt out" (in any language, as long as
  it contains the word STOP in capitals), or give the cards a "Stop promotions"
  quick reply.
* **Its buttons go on the cards.** Leave the Buttons section under the message
  empty; a carousel can't have buttons there.
* **Each card's text is up to 160 characters.** The box counts as you type.

All of these are checked when you save, edit and submit, so you find out here, in
plain words, rather than from Meta.

Each card has **one or two buttons**, and every card has the same ones — a quick
reply, a link or a call. A link button can go somewhere different on each card,
but each card's link is a fixed web address: it can't contain a blank like
`{{1}}`, since nothing fills one in when the carousel is sent.

## Sending one

An approved template's card carries **Send broadcast**. It opens the
[broadcast composer](/whatsapp/broadcasts) with that template already chosen, so
the template you just got approved is one click from reaching somebody.

For a single customer rather than a list, use [Send](/whatsapp/send); from your
own systems, [the messages API](/api-reference/messages/send-message).

## Letting an agent send a template

Your agent can send an approved template **during a call or chat** when a
customer asks for something (a renewal link, your address, a documents list). You
decide which templates it may use.

**1. Open an approved Utility template**

Only **Utility** templates can be sent by an agent. A customer who asked a
question hasn't agreed to marketing, and Meta treats the two differently.

**2. Tick “Agents may send this during a call or chat”**

It applies to every language of that template. Untick it to stop.

**3. Switch the tool on for the agent**

On the agent's **Actions** page, turn on **Send the customer a WhatsApp**. See
[Actions](/agent/actions#reaching-the-customer-on-a-different-channel).

Two things keep a template out:

* **A blank in a link button.** A button like `yoursite.com/{{1}}` needs a value
  for the blank, and an agent can't fill one. Use a fixed link, and put anything
  that changes in the message text.
* **Not being Utility.** Marketing and authentication templates can't be ticked.

New templates start unticked. Templates you already had when this was added were
ticked for you, apart from any with a blank in a link button.

Each message the agent sends is charged like any other template you send, and the
agent may send two an hour in one conversation.

## Forms

A template button can open a **form** — an address, a booking, a return. That is
how you collect structured information from somebody who has not messaged you
recently.

Answers come back into the conversation and are stored against it, so they are
readable in the inbox and available afterwards as structured data rather than as
words in a transcript.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Forms cannot be published until Meta verifies your business.** They build,
> store and preview now; Meta will not publish a flow for an unverified
> business, and an unpublished form reaches nobody.
>
> Forms also cannot be filled from your data — no slot picker showing only free
> slots, no dropdown of that customer's orders.

## Deleting one

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Deleting an AGENT does not delete your templates.** They belong to your
> WhatsApp Business Account rather than to one agent, so they move to whichever
> of your agents is oldest — along with your forms and your broadcasts. The
> delete dialog lists what will move before you confirm.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Deleting removes it from Meta too**, not just from this list. Two
> consequences follow, and both are easier to know beforehand:
>
> * Anything sending that template — a campaign, a sequence, your own code
>   calling the API with its name — **stops working**.
> * Meta will **not let the name be used again for 30 days**. If you are
>   replacing a template, give the replacement a different name rather than
>   waiting a month for the old one.

A draft that was never submitted has neither consequence: Meta has never seen
it, so nothing is using it and the name stays free.

## Template quality

Meta scores every approved template on how people react to it — green, yellow,
red — and tells us when the score changes. **You are warned at yellow**, on the
template and by notification, while there is still something you can do about
it.

Red is not a warning. Meta pauses a red template, and a paused template sends
nothing, so the yellow is the message that matters.

The usual causes are blocks and "report" taps from people who did not expect to
hear from you: a marketing template sent too often, or to a list that never
really opted in.

> [!NOTE]
>
> Your **number** is scored separately, and that one is worse: a flagged number
> has its messaging limit cut, and left flagged it is restricted outright — at
> which point no template works, however healthy. You are warned about that too.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Per-template delivery analytics are not available yet** — how many people
> opened a given template, or tapped its button. Meta reports button taps in
> WhatsApp Manager and we do not yet read them. What you can see today is
> per-campaign delivery and replies on the [campaign
> report](/whatsapp/broadcasts), and the quality score above.


# Brand and domains
Source: https://docs.thinnest.ai/white-label/brand-and-domains

Put your name, logo and colour on everything, serve it from your own domain, and bring your own sign-in check and email sender.

## Your brand

**White label → Brand**: your product name, logo and colour. Every client
workspace wears it — the console, the sign-in page, share links, invitations
and notification email. Change it and every client sees the change.

Upload your logo as a square PNG, JPEG or WebP of up to 2 MB. It is saved as
soon as it uploads; **Remove**, then **Save**, takes it off.

## Favicon and custom CSS

Under **Brand → Favicon and custom CSS**:

* **Favicon** — the icon in your clients' browser tabs. Upload a square PNG,
  JPEG or WebP. Without one, your logo is used, and without a logo, your
  initial on your brand colour. Browsers can take up to an hour to show a new
  one.
* **Custom CSS** — your own styles, added to every page on your domains after
  ours, up to 20,000 characters. Use it for fonts and colours. Console updates
  can change what detailed selectors match, so prefer broad rules over ones that
  depend on a page's exact structure. CSS cannot load other stylesheets or run
  scripts.

## Help and support

Under **Brand → Help and support**, give your clients somewhere to go:

* **Help centre link** — the Documentation button in the console header goes
  here. Use it if you have help pages of your own.
* **Support email** — named wherever your clients are told to contact support,
  including their Billing page.

Leave the help centre link blank and your clients get **your docs** instead
(below). Leave the support email blank and that line is not shown. Your
clients are never sent to us.

## Your docs

Every one of your domains has a documentation site at **/docs** — for example
`https://app.yourcompany.com/docs` — in your name, logo, colours, favicon and
custom CSS. It holds the guides your clients need (agents, knowledge, voice,
WhatsApp, campaigns, the inbox) and a full API reference whose every example
uses your domain, such as `https://app.yourcompany.com/api/v1`. Nothing in it
names us.

* The Documentation button and the guide links in the console open it, unless
  you set a help centre link of your own.
* It leaves out what is only for you as a reseller, such as these white label
  pages.
* It is kept up to date with each release.
* Your clients' API keys, webhooks and AI assistant connections work at your
  domain too, and an AI assistant connected there knows your product by your
  name.

## Your sign-in page

Under **Brand → Sign-in page**, choose how the page your clients sign in on
looks — sign in, sign up and password reset, on all your domains:

* **Side by side** — the form on the left, your picture filling the right half.
* **Centred** — the form in a card over your picture, full screen, on every
  device including phones.
* **Picture with highlights** — your picture fills the screen with your mark at
  the top left and, at the bottom, a headline (up to 80 characters) over up to
  three short points with ticks (up to 40 characters each). The form floats in a
  card on the right. Phones show the form only, without the words.

Upload a picture (PNG, JPEG or WebP, up to 2.5 MB; a landscape photo of about
1920 × 1080 works best). Without one, side by side keeps the default panel, and
centred and picture with highlights use your brand colour. **Remove picture**
goes back to the default. Your headline and points are kept if you switch to
another layout and back.

### Your privacy policy and terms

Under **Brand → Privacy policy and terms**, add links to your own privacy policy
and terms (full `https://` addresses). Sign-up asks your clients to agree to
what you list, and the sign-in page shows the same links beneath the form. They
open in a new tab. Leave both blank and sign-up asks for nothing. Our own
privacy page is never shown on your domains.

**Forgot password?** on the sign-in page sends a reset link in your name, from
your sender if you connected one, that opens on your domain to choose a new
password.

## No domain yet? Use a preview address

Under **White label → Domains → Preview address**, press **Create my preview
address**. You get a free address like `yourname.preview.thinnest.ai`, ready at
once — no DNS to set up.

It works exactly like a connected domain: your brand on every page, sign-in,
invitations to clients, and sign-up if you switch it on. Use it to try your
console, demo it, and start your first clients.

> [!NOTE]
>
> Our name is in a preview address, so connect your own domain before you go
> live with clients. The first visit to a new preview address can take a few
> seconds while its HTTPS certificate is issued.

## Your domain

**White label → Domains** puts the product on your own address, such as
`app.yourcompany.com`.

**1. Add the address**

Type or paste it, and choose which workspace it opens: your main workspace,
or one of your clients.

**2. Publish two DNS records**

The page shows both, ready to copy:

* a **TXT** record that proves the domain is yours;
* an **A** record that points the address at us.

Add them where your domain's DNS is managed (your registrar, Cloudflare and
so on).

**3. Verify**

Press **Verify**. If a record has not appeared yet, the page says which one —
DNS changes can take a while to spread.

**HTTPS is automatic.** The certificate for your address is issued the first
time it is visited after it is verified, and renewed for you. There is nothing
to upload.

> [!NOTE]
>
> An address can open one workspace at a time. One already in use elsewhere
> has to be removed there first; if it is held by a workspace outside your
> account, the page shows the record that proves it is yours.

### Several clients on one domain

Each client can have its own address (`acme.yourcompany.com`,
`beta.yourcompany.com`), or all of them can sign in on one address that opens
your main workspace — from there each person goes to the workspaces they
belong to.

### Letting clients sign up

On an address that opens your **main** workspace you can switch **sign-up**
on. Anyone who creates an account there becomes your client, in a new
workspace of their own. Sign-up cannot be switched on for an address that
opens a client's workspace.

With **Let people sign up here** off, your address is by invitation only. The
sign-up page asks for an invitation instead of a form, and the sign-in page
doesn't offer "Sign up". A person you've invited still signs up from the link
in their invitation, with the email address you invited.

## Sign-in protection

Password sign-in and sign-up are protected by a Cloudflare Turnstile check. On
your domain it has to be **yours**:

1. In Cloudflare, add a Turnstile widget and list your domains in it.
2. Under **White label → Brand → Sign-in protection**, paste its **site key**
   and **secret key**. They are checked with Cloudflare before they are saved.

Until it is connected, people cannot sign in with a password on your domain.

## Email from your domain

Invitations, sign-up and password emails, and notifications to your clients
come from **your** sender once you connect your own Resend account under
**Settings → Notifications**. Until then they are sent in your brand's name
from a neutral address, never from ours.


# Clients
Source: https://docs.thinnest.ai/white-label/clients

Create a workspace for each client, see each client's plan and balance, and fund them by hand if you bill them yourself.

Every client you resell to gets a workspace of its own. It is a full
workspace — agents, channels, contacts, inbox, campaigns, usage — with its own
login and its own people. You manage the list from **White label → Clients**.

## Adding a client

Two ways:

* **Create it yourself.** Under **New client**, give the workspace a name and,
  optionally, the email addresses of the people who should have access. They
  are invited by email, from your sender and in your brand. The workspace
  starts with a first agent ready to set up.
* **Let them sign up.** On your main domain you can switch sign-up on (see
  [Brand and domains](/white-label/brand-and-domains)). Anyone who signs up
  there becomes one of your clients.

> [!NOTE]
>
> You are an admin of every client workspace. Open it from the Clients list to
> set things up for them, and use its own **Members** page to invite or remove
> their people. You and your own team never use one of a client's seats: a
> client on the free trial has one seat, and it is theirs.

## Invitations

Each client row links to the client's **Members** page. Pending invitations
are listed there: **Resend** sends the same invitation email again (in your
name, linking to your domain), and **Revoke** cancels it. An expired invitation
cannot be resent — revoke it and invite the person again.

## Removing a client

**Remove** on a client's row deletes that client's workspace for good — its
agents, contacts, conversations and history. Type the client's name to
confirm. It is refused while the client still:

* holds a phone number or a connected WhatsApp number (release or remove it in
  the client's workspace first — releasing a number is permanent);
* has a paid plan running (cancel it on the client's billing page first);
* has money in its balance (settle it with the client first).

## Each client's plan and call lines

Each client has **its own plan**, just as you have yours with us: it starts on
the free trial you set (see [Prices](/white-label/prices)), then moves to
pay-as-you-go or subscribes to Pro or Scale. Its concurrent call lines are its
plan's own — a busy client never takes lines from another. The Clients list
shows each client's plan.

## Each client's money

Each row shows the client's **balance**, and what it has been charged this
month for usage alongside what that usage **cost you** — the difference is
yours.

* **Add credit** puts money in a client's balance by hand. Use it if you bill a
  client some other way (an invoice, a bank transfer) instead of through your
  Razorpay. Nothing is charged to you when you add credit; you are charged our
  price as the client uses it.
* A client can also add money itself, from its Billing page, once you have
  connected Razorpay. See [Your prices](/white-label/prices).

## One client's own prices

Your markups on **Prices** apply to every client. To give one client
different prices, open **White label → Clients**, click **Prices** on that
client's row, and set any of:

* **Calls** — your markup on every call minute.
* **Phone numbers** — on each number's monthly rental.
* **WhatsApp** — on each message.
* **Replies** — on each AI reply.

Each is a percentage of our price, from 0 to 1000. For calls you can type the
price a minute instead, and the percentage follows; numbers, WhatsApp and replies
are set as a percentage, because our price for them varies. A box left blank uses your
default, shown in the box, and for calls the client's plan's own call markup
if its plan has one. A client with prices of its own shows **Own prices** on
its row. Clear every box to go back to your defaults.

Prices apply from the client's next charge. We still charge you our price, so
the difference is yours, and the client's console shows the prices it pays.

## When your balance runs out

Everything your clients use is charged to **your** balance at our prices. When
your available balance reaches zero, **your clients' calls, campaigns and new
phone numbers stop** — whatever is in their own balances — and their Billing
page tells them service is paused. Agent replies keep answering, as they do on
every plan.

You are warned before it happens: a notice when your balance runs low, and
another when it is empty. Money set aside for phone numbers renewing in the
next few days does not count as available.


# White label
Source: https://docs.thinnest.ai/white-label/overview

Sell AI voice and WhatsApp agents to your clients as your own product — your name, your logo, your domain, your prices.

White label lets an agency resell ThinnestAI under its own brand. Each of your
clients gets a workspace of its own, on your domain, with your name and logo on
every page and every email. Your clients never see ours.

> [!NOTE]
>
> White label comes with **every paid plan** — Pay As You Go, Pro, Scale and
> Enterprise; not the free trial. It is set up from your **main** workspace by
> one of its owners or admins — the **White label** item in the sidebar.

## What you get

> [card] A workspace per client
>
> Each client has its own login, agents, contacts, conversations and usage.
> You can open any of them.

> [card] Your brand
>
> Your product name, logo and colour on every page your clients see, and on
> the email they receive.

> [card] Your domain
>
> `app.yourcompany.com` instead of ours, with HTTPS set up for you.

> [card] Your prices
>
> Your own prices on top of ours, paid into your own Razorpay account. You
> keep the difference.

## How it fits together

1. **You** are on any paid plan. Your main workspace is where you manage
   everything.
2. **Your clients** each get a workspace under yours: up to **3** on Pay As You
   Go, **20** on Pro, **100** on Scale, and more on Enterprise. The Clients tab
   shows how many you have used.
3. **Your clients are like our customers.** Each has its own plan — starting
   on a free trial you set — and its own call lines.
4. **Your clients pay you**, at your prices, through your Razorpay. **We charge
   you** our prices for what they use, from your balance.

## Setting up

The **Overview** tab under White label is a checklist of these steps, and ticks
each one off as you go:

**1. Your brand**

Name, logo and colour. See [Brand and domains](/white-label/brand-and-domains).

**2. Your domain**

Two DNS records, and we check them for you. No domain yet? Start on a free
preview address.

**3. Your sign-in check**

Your own Cloudflare Turnstile, so people can sign in on your domain.

**4. Your email**

Your own Resend sender, so client email comes from your domain.

**5. Your prices**

Connect Razorpay and set your markups. See [Your prices](/white-label/prices).

**6. Your first client**

Create a workspace for them, or let them sign up on your domain. See
[Clients](/white-label/clients).

## What your clients see

* Your name, logo and colour — on the console, the sign-in page, share links
  and every email.
* Your domain in the address bar.
* Their balance, plan and prices **in your prices**, and a Billing page that
  pays you.
* On your domain, sign-in is by email. "Sign in with Google" and LinkedIn are
  not offered there, because their consent screens would name us.


# Your prices
Source: https://docs.thinnest.ai/white-label/prices

Set your own prices on top of ours, get paid into your own payment account, and keep the difference.

You decide what your clients pay. They pay it **to you**, through your own
payment account: Razorpay for a reseller billed in India, Dodo Payments for one
[billed outside India](/workspace/regions). We charge **you** our prices for the same usage, from your
balance, as it happens. The difference is yours, straight away — we never hold
or pass on your clients' money.

Everything is set under **White label → Prices**.

## Connect your Razorpay

No Razorpay account yet? [Create one here](https://rzp.io/rzp/j599idX), then
come back to these steps. The same link is on the **Get paid by your clients**
card until you connect.

**1. Get your keys**

In Razorpay, open **Account & Settings → API keys** and generate a key. You
get a **key id** (`rzp_live_…`) and a **key secret**.

**2. Paste both halves**

Under **Get paid by your clients**, paste them and press **Connect**. They
are checked with Razorpay before they are saved, and the secret is never
shown again.

There is no webhook to set up: every payment is confirmed with Razorpay
directly, and one your client's browser did not report back is picked up within
minutes.

> [!NOTE]
>
> Use your **live** keys — test keys cannot take real payments and are refused.
> You can replace your keys at any time (after regenerating them, for
> instance). While any client pays you a monthly plan, you cannot disconnect
> Razorpay or connect a **different** account: their plans live in this one.

## Paid through Dodo (international)

If you are billed outside India, you connect **your own Dodo
Payments account** under **White label → Prices → Get paid by your clients**.
Your clients then add money on their Billing page into your account. Dodo
Payments is the seller on that checkout, so your clients see your account's
business name on the payment page and on their card statement — not ours.

**1. Get a key**

In Dodo Payments, open **Developer → API keys** and create a key.

**2. Paste it**

Paste it under **Get paid by your clients** and press **Connect**. It is
checked with Dodo Payments before it is saved, and it is never shown again.

A test key takes test cards only; connect your live key before your clients pay.
Prices and payments are in US dollars.

## Without a payment account

If you connect no payment account, your clients are **never stopped for their
own balance**: their usage is charged to **your** balance at our prices as it
happens, and what they owe you shows as their balance, at your prices, for you to
collect however you like. Your own balance still has to cover it. You can still
add money to a client by hand with **Add credit** — see
[Clients](/white-label/clients).

## Usage prices

A **percent on top of our price**, for each kind of usage:

| Usage | Your client pays |
| - | - |
| Voice calls | our per-minute price + your % |
| Phone numbers | our monthly rent + your % |
| WhatsApp messages | our per-message price + your % |
| AI replies | what each reply costs + your % |

Leave a box empty to sell at our price. As you type, the page shows what your
clients will pay against what you pay — for example *Premium voice: ₹2.40 /
min (you pay ₹2.00)*. Every price your clients see — on their Billing page, the
voice picker, phone numbers, broadcast estimates, their usage and history — is
yours.

### The top-up fee

When a client adds money, a fee is added at checkout: **our fee for the
client's plan plus the extra percent you set**. All of it goes to you, with the
rest of the payment.

## Plans

Your clients are customers just like you are ours. Each client has its own
plan — never yours — and can subscribe to **Pro** or **Scale** at your price:
our monthly price plus the amount you set.

Each month a client pays for its plan:

* the client's plan price comes back to it as **usage credit** for that month,
  spent at your prices;
* we charge **you** our monthly price, and give it back to you as credit for
  that client's usage that month — so you are not charged twice for the same
  usage.

A client can cancel from its Billing page; the plan keeps working until the end
of the period it paid for, and the client then moves to pay-as-you-go.

### Yearly
