Tick **Offer yearly billing too** and your clients can also pay for Pro or
Scale a year at a time: our yearly price (twelve months of our monthly price)
plus the amount you set for the year. That amount is separate from the monthly
one, so a yearly discount of your own is up to you.

A year is paid up front, and works like a month, for a year:

* the client gets **the whole year's usage credit** at once, which lasts the
  year;
* we charge **you** our yearly price, and give it back as cover for that
  client's usage for the year.

## Your own plans

Instead of offering Pro and Scale, you can sell plans of your own. Under
**Prices → Your plans**, **Add a plan** and set:

* **Name** and **description** — what your clients see.
* **Built on** — Pro or Scale. This is what we charge you for each month a
  client pays: our monthly price for that plan, and you get the same amount
  back as cover for that client's usage.
* **Price** — what your client pays you each month, into your Razorpay.
* **Price a year** (optional) — sell the plan yearly too. A year gives the
  client twelve months of the plan's usage credit at once, and we charge you
  our yearly price for the plan it is built on. Leave it blank to sell the plan
  monthly only.
* **Usage credit** — what the client gets back each month to spend at your
  prices. It can be more or less than the price.
* **Limits** — agents, team members, calls at once and cloned voices. Each can
  only be lower than the plan it is built on; leave a box blank to keep that
  plan's number. **0 cloned voices** switches voice cloning off.
* **Features** — switch off **Studio voices**, **Projects & teams** (Scale
  only) or **Voice campaigns** for that plan.
* **Call markup** (optional) — your markup on every call for clients on this
  plan, as a percentage of our price a minute, or as the price a minute itself
  (the other box follows). Leave it blank to use your
  default voice markup. A plan with a lower call markup can be cheaper per
  minute for clients who call a lot; a higher one suits plans with more included
  credit. We still charge you our price for each call, so the difference is
  yours. It applies to calls from the moment you save it, and the client's
  Billing page shows the plan's own call rates.

Once you offer a plan, your clients see **only your plans** on their Billing
page, not Pro and Scale. Changing a plan's limits or features reaches every
client on it straight away; a new price or credit applies to new subscriptions.
**Stop offering** hides a plan from new clients; clients already on it keep it
until they cancel.

## Free trial

A new client starts on a **free trial**, as new accounts with us do. You decide
what it includes:

* **Voice minutes** — once per client (ours: 25).
* **AI replies** — each month while the client is on the trial (ours: 200).
* **WhatsApp messages** — once per client (ours: 200).

**You pay our price for every trial minute, reply and message**; the client
pays nothing. Turn the trial off and new clients start on pay-as-you-go
instead. A client leaves the trial when it first adds money (or you add credit
to it), or when it subscribes to a plan. Changes to the trial apply to new
clients and to clients still on their trial.

## Voices your clients can choose

Under **White label → Prices → Voices your clients can choose**, switch either
voice tier off — **Premium** or **Studio** — to hide it from your clients. They
won't see it when choosing a voice, and can't pick one from it. Keep at least
one on.

An agent that already uses a voice from a tier you switch off keeps it, so
nothing stops working. Switching **Studio** off also turns voice cloning off
for your clients, because a cloned voice is a Studio voice.

## What your clients see

Their **Billing** page shows their balance (and, on the trial, what is left of
it), an **Add money** button once you have connected Razorpay, and
pay-as-you-go, Pro and Scale at your prices (or only your own plans, once you
offer any), with a yearly option where you sell one. Checkout opens on **your**
Razorpay account under your name.

Under **Billing → History → Payments**, each client sees every payment it made
to you, top-ups and plan periods, with the amount, the date, your name and the
Razorpay reference. That is its receipt, and it can print the page. A tax
invoice for the sale is yours to issue: we do not raise one for a client.

## When your balance runs out

Your clients' usage — their free trials included — is charged to your balance.
When your available balance reaches zero, **your clients' calls, campaigns,
trials and new phone numbers stop**,
and their Billing page says service is paused. You are warned when your
balance runs low and again when it is empty. Add money to your own balance as
usual and everything resumes.

## Earnings

**White label → Earnings** shows, month by month for the last twelve months:

* **Clients paid you**: their top-ups (what they paid, fee included) and their
  plan payments, into your Razorpay.
* **We charged you**: what left your balance for them: their usage at our
  prices (less what their plan's cover already paid), their free trials, and
  our price for each plan period.
* **Net**: the difference, before Razorpay's own fees and your tax.
* **Usage margin**: their usage at your prices less our price for it, which is
  what your markups earn.

Money your clients have paid but not yet spent is counted when they pay, so the
page also shows how much they hold unspent today. Credit you add to a client by
hand is money you collected yourself: it is not counted as paid, but its usage
is charged to you as it happens. Months run on UTC.

## Good to know

* **Your currency.** Your clients pay in your account's currency. In India
  that is rupees; outside India, US dollars.
* **Tax on your sale is yours** — we add none to what your clients pay you.
  Set your prices with that in mind.
* **History** — your own billing history lists each client's usage and plan
  fees by client name, at our prices; each client's history shows its charges
  at yours.

## Automatic top-up for clients

On their Billing page, a client's owner or admin can switch on **automatic
top-up**: when the balance falls below an amount they choose, the amount they
choose is charged to a card or UPI Autopay they authorise once, into your
Razorpay, at most twice a day. Setting it up takes their first top-up at the
checkout, which is the authorisation. Three failed charges in a row switch it
off and say so on their Billing page.

Automatic charges need **recurring payments** switched on for your Razorpay
account. It is a separate approval from Razorpay, so ask them to enable
recurring (subsequent) payments before your clients rely on it. Automatic top-up
is for rupee accounts only.


# Analytics
Source: https://docs.thinnest.ai/workspace/analytics

Whether the agent did its job — every figure a count you could verify yourself.

Analytics answers one question: **did the agent do its job**. It is deliberately
separate from usage, which is what you owe us. Mixing the two is how a product
starts feeling like a meter.

Nothing here is a forecast, a score, or an invented composite index. Every figure
is a count you could arrive at yourself by reading your own inbox.

## The four numbers

| | |
| - | - |
| **Conversations** | The denominator for everything else |
| **Leads captured** | The outcome the product is sold on |
| **Needed a person** | Where the agent ran out of road |
| **Found an answer** | How often a knowledge search found something |

"Needed a person" is not a failure metric. A business with nobody watching turns
escalation off entirely — it is the number that tells you whether the setup is
working.

## Over time

Conversations and leads per day, drawn as two charts rather than one.

They are deliberately not plotted together. Leads are a small fraction of
conversations — 200 conversations and 9 leads is doing well — so on a shared
axis the line that matters most would sit flat against zero.

## When people write

Conversations by hour of day, in UTC. The question behind it is operational
rather than analytical: when should somebody be near the inbox. An escalation at
09:00 gets answered; the same one at 23:00 is a customer who waited overnight.

## Questions it could not answer

**The most useful page in the product.** These are questions the agent searched
your material for and found nothing on, so it had to say it did not know.

Each row is a page you could write, or a paragraph you could paste into
[Knowledge](/agent/knowledge). Work this list and the "found an answer" number
climbs on its own.

## What people ask most

Grouped by exact wording, so the same question asked two ways appears twice.
Frequently a surprise to whoever wrote the website.


# Your data: erasure and training
Source: https://docs.thinnest.ai/workspace/data-and-erasure

What is deleted when you erase a contact, what is kept on purpose, and when recordings may be used to improve our models.

When a person asks you to forget them, one call to
[`DELETE /contacts/{id}`](/api-reference/contacts/delete-contact) does it. This
page says what that removes, what it deliberately does not, and how recordings
and transcripts are treated for model training.

## Erasing a contact

Erasing a contact removes, together and for good:

* their conversations and every message in them (the transcripts);
* their calls, queued calls, callbacks and calling-campaign entries;
* their form replies, helpdesk tickets and the follow-ups waiting on them;
* **the recordings of their calls**, wherever the audio is kept;
* any duplicate of them that was merged into the contact — the record a merge
  leaves behind still holds a name and an email, so it goes too.

It cannot be undone. To stop messaging someone without forgetting them, set
their consent to `withdrawn` instead.

### Recordings go with the contact

The audio is deleted first, then the call records, so a recording is never left
behind with nothing pointing to it:

| Where the audio is | When it is deleted |
| - | - |
| Stored by us (website calls, and phone calls on a number you brought) | Immediately. |
| The phone provider's copy (calls on a number we rent you) | Immediately, through your workspace's own account with them. |
| A copy made for model training, if the workspace was on pay-as-you-go | Immediately. |

If a file cannot be deleted at that moment — a provider is down, say — the
contact is **still erased**, and the deletion is queued and retried every night
until it succeeds. The response then carries `recordingsPending`, the number of
files still queued:

```json theme={null}
{ "recordingsPending": 1 }
```

Without it (`204`, no body) every file was already gone when the response came
back.

To know when an erasure is **finished**, subscribe a webhook to
[`contact.erased`](/api-reference/webhooks#workspace-events). It is sent once,
with only the contact's id and when it was erased: straight away after a `204`,
or from the nightly retry once the last queued file is gone.

### What is not erased

* **Do-not-call entries are kept, on purpose.** If the person asked never to be
  called again, forgetting the number would let a campaign ring it again. The
  list holds the number and where the request came from, not their history.
* **Webhook payloads we already sent** are kept for retries and then purged
  automatically after 7 days.
* **Copies in your own systems and your vendors'.** Anything your CRM, your
  webhook receiver or your tools stored is yours to delete; erasing a contact
  here does not reach into them.

Recordings you do not erase by hand are deleted on your plan's schedule anyway;
see [Recordings](/workspace/usage#recordings).

## Deleting one call's recording and transcript

To remove what was said on **one** call without erasing the person, call
[`DELETE /calls/{id}/content`](/api-reference/post-call/delete-call-content)
with a full API key.

* **Deleted:** the recording (ours, the phone provider's copy, and any copy
  made for model training), this call's turns in the conversation, its
  summary, the details collected from it, and the summary handed on when the
  call was passed to another agent. Other calls and chats with the same
  person stay.
* **Kept:** the call itself — when it was, how long it lasted, what it cost and
  what it was billed as. Your usage and invoices do not change.

Afterwards [Get Call](/api-reference/calls/get-call) shows the call with no
recording, an empty transcript, `"contentDeleted": true` and when it happened
(`contentDeletedAt`). A recording that cannot be deleted at that moment is
retried every night until it is gone; the answer says how many are still
queued (`recordingsPending`). Asking again is safe. A call that is still
going on, or one booked that has not rung yet, is refused — this is not how
you cancel a call (`DELETE /calls/{id}` still does that).

It cannot be undone.

## How long calls are kept

Your plan keeps call recordings for **30 days** on pay-as-you-go, **49** on
Pro, **75** on Scale and **365** on Enterprise. Transcripts are kept until you
delete them.

To keep less, set `callRetentionDays` with
[`PATCH /workspace`](/api-reference/workspace/update-workspace) — any whole
number of days from 1 up to your plan's limit (a longer one is refused, naming
the limit). Every night, calls older than that lose their recording **and**
their transcript exactly as Delete Call Content removes them, and their billing
record stays. It applies to calls you already have, from the next night.
`null` goes back to your plan's limit for recordings and keeps transcripts.
[`GET /workspace`](/api-reference/workspace/get-workspace) shows your setting
(`callRetentionDays`) and your plan's limit (`planRetentionDays`).

## Model training

**Recordings and transcripts are never used to train models on Pro and above.**

On **pay-as-you-go**, a copy of a call's recording and transcript may be kept to
improve our speech and language models. If you do not want that, ask us and we
will exclude your workspace — and, for a developer, every customer workspace
under it. Exclusion also deletes the copies already made, and a very large backlog is
finished over the following nights. From then on, your calls are not copied. Calls made before the
exclusion, or while it was on, are never copied later, even if the exclusion is lifted.

Write to support from the workspace owner's address and say which workspace.
Erasing a contact deletes its training copies too, whatever the plan.


# Helpdesk
Source: https://docs.thinnest.ai/workspace/helpdesk

Escalations as tickets in Zendesk or Salesforce, with replies coming back.

If your team already lives in a helpdesk, escalations can arrive there as
tickets — and replies typed there reach the customer on the channel they wrote
from.

## Two-way, on WhatsApp

Connect Zendesk or Salesforce and an escalated conversation opens a ticket with
the transcript. When an agent replies in the helpdesk, that reply is delivered
to the customer on WhatsApp.

The customer never learns your helpdesk exists. They asked on WhatsApp; they get
an answer on WhatsApp.

## Connecting

On the agent's **Channels** page, open **Reply from your helpdesk** and connect
the vendor. Credentials are sealed and are not readable from the dashboard.

## Which vendors

| Vendor | Tickets | Replies come back |
| - | - | - |
| **Zendesk** | Yes | Yes |
| **Salesforce** | Yes | Yes |

> [!NOTE]
>
> Ticket numbering differs by vendor and can repeat across accounts, so tickets
> are keyed by connection as well as by number. Two workspaces with the same
> ticket number never cross.

## Salesforce specifics

Salesforce caps a comment at 4,000 **bytes**, not characters — so a long
transcript in a non-Latin script is trimmed on a byte boundary rather than
rejected outright.

## What reaches the ticket

The conversation transcript at the point of escalation, plus a tag identifying
the conversation so replies route back to the right thread.

Internal notes are not included: those are your team's, and a helpdesk ticket is
a different audience.


# Inbox
Source: https://docs.thinnest.ai/workspace/inbox

Every conversation, and how a person takes one over.

The inbox shows every conversation across every channel, as it happens.

## Finding a conversation

Press the search icon at the top of the list and type at least two characters.
The search covers **every conversation in the workspace**, not just the ones
already on screen, so you never have to scroll to load an old thread first.

It matches:

* the customer's **name**, **email** or **phone number** — a number can be typed
  with spaces, dashes or the country code, so `98765 43210` finds `+919876543210`;
* **any message** in the conversation, not just the latest — the matching line is
  shown in the list, so you can see why a conversation was found;
* for calls, the **number the call was with**, including people your calling
  campaigns rang;
* the **teammate** a conversation is assigned to.

Up to 50 matches are shown, newest first. If more conversations match, the list
says so; type more of the name or number to narrow it down. The tabs and filters
still apply to search results.

### Filtering

The filter button beside the search narrows the list by **channel**, **pinned**,
**from an ad** and **who it is assigned to**. Filters look through every
conversation in the workspace, not just the ones already on screen, and work
together with a search.

## Taking over

Anyone on your team can take a conversation over. The moment they do, **the
agent steps out** — it stops replying to that thread entirely.

That is not politeness. Two voices answering the same customer, contradicting
each other, is worse than a slower answer.

When a teammate replies, the agent later sees that reply as its own prior turn,
so it does not re-answer something a person just handled.

## Whose conversation is this?

Assign a thread to a teammate from the picker at the top of it, and it becomes
theirs — they get a **Mine** tab in the inbox listing everything assigned to
them, and everyone else can see at a glance who is dealing with it.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Assigning is not the same as taking over**, and neither one implies the
> other.
>
> Taking over is a fact: somebody replied, so the agent stands down. Assigning
> is a decision about who is responsible, and you can make it before anyone has
> replied — the agent keeps handling the conversation until a person actually
> answers.
>
> So you can hand somebody a thread to keep an eye on without silencing the
> agent, and you can take a thread over without claiming it.

**They are told.** The person you assign a conversation to gets a notification,
and it goes to them alone — nobody else on the team is told which of them is
dealing with a thread. Hand it on later and the next person is told too, so a
thread can move around the team without anyone having to be watching for it.

Assigning one to yourself sends nothing; you already know.

Set it back to **Unassigned** to put it back in the pool. That is how work gets
handed around rather than sitting with whoever happened to open it first.

> [!TIP]
>
> Above about three people sharing an inbox, this is the difference between a
> queue and a pile. Two people answering the same customer is the thing it
> prevents, and it prevents it earlier than taking over does.

## Saved replies

The answers you send twenty times a day — opening hours, refund timings, "could
you share your order number?" — kept in one place so everybody sends the same
sentence.

Open the saved-replies button under the reply box in the inbox. **Add** sits
beside the heading, and opens a form for the shortcut and the reply. Each saved
reply has a pencil to edit it and a bin to delete it, so a typo can be fixed
where you noticed it.

Choosing one adds it to whatever you have already typed rather than replacing
it, so you can write a line of your own and then reach for the policy.

> [!TIP]
>
> Write `{{name}}` where the customer's name should go. It is filled in when you
> insert the reply, so the same saved text reads as though you typed it — and
> for a website visitor who has never given a name it is quietly left out
> rather than sent as `{{name}}`.

> [!NOTE]
>
> Saved replies belong to the **workspace**, not to one person or one agent, and
> anybody on the team can add or edit one. That is the point: the value is that
> the refund policy does not drift between teammates.

## Internal notes

You can leave a note on a conversation that the customer never sees. Notes are
your team talking **about** the customer, not to them, and they are never
replayed to the model — an agent that read one would believe it had said that
out loud.

## What the agent did

**Tools**, at the top of a conversation, lists every tool the agent ran in it, newest first: checking a calendar,
booking, saving a lead, your own actions. A failed one has a red mark and the reason, and opens to show what the
agent sent and what came back. When a customer says the agent promised a booking that never arrived, look here first.
Passwords, keys and codes are never shown, and tool details are kept for 30 days.

## Resetting the agent's memory

**Reset memory**, at the top of a conversation, makes the agent start fresh. Useful when you test from your own
phone, or when a conversation went wrong.

* **This conversation**: the agent no longer reads anything said in it before now.
* **Everything for this number**: every conversation with this contact, on every channel, is forgotten by the agent,
  including what it would otherwise recall from their other chats and calls.

Nothing is deleted. You still see every message, and a note marks the point the agent's memory now starts from.

## Deleting a conversation

**Delete**, at the top of a conversation, removes it for good: every message, its calls and their recordings, and
what the agent ran during it. Only an owner or admin can delete. It cannot be undone.

What was charged stays on the **Usage** page, and the contact is kept: if they write again, a new conversation starts.
A conversation with a call still going cannot be deleted until the call ends. To erase a person entirely, erase the
contact instead ([Data and erasure](/workspace/data-and-erasure)).

## Statuses

| Status | Means |
| - | - |
| **Active** | The agent is handling it |
| **Escalated** | The agent asked for a person |
| **Human handling** | Somebody took over; the agent is silent |
| **Resolved** | Closed |

Assignment sits alongside these rather than among them: a conversation can be
active *and* assigned, or taken over by one person while assigned to another —
which is exactly what happens when somebody covers a colleague's thread.

## Media

## Whether you can reply freely

Above the reply box on a WhatsApp conversation, a line tells you where the
24-hour window stands, so you know before you type whether a free reply or a
form will go through.

| You see | It means |
| - | - |
| **Free replies and forms open · 14h 22m left** | Send anything. The count is in hours and minutes and updates while you have the thread open. |
| **Reply window closes in 42m** (amber) | The last hour. Finish what you are saying; after this only a template reaches them. |
| **WhatsApp closed this conversation 3h ago** | The window ran out. The reply box is replaced by a note; an approved template is the way back in. |
| **This customer hasn't messaged you** | No window has ever opened — you started this conversation with a template, and they have not written back. Forms and free replies open the moment they do. |

The customer messaging you again reopens the window immediately, for another 24
hours from that message.

### Sending a template from the conversation

When the reply box is replaced by one of those notes, **Send a template** sits
beneath it. It opens a list of your approved templates; choose one, fill in any
blanks it has, and it goes to that customer straight from the thread, where it
appears with a line saying it was sent from the inbox.

* **Every blank is yours to fill.** Nothing is pre-filled with the template's
  example values, so a customer is never greeted as somebody else.
* **A template with a picture at the top** uses the one saved with it. If none is
  saved, WhatsApp needs one on every send, so the dialog asks for its address.
* **A marketing template only goes to people who have not opted out.** Send it
  only to somebody who agreed to hear from you.

If you have no approved template yet, the same notes carry **Set up a template**,
which takes you to your Templates page.

## Whether a message arrived

Under each message the workspace sent, the inbox says what WhatsApp did with it.
"Sent" means we handed it to WhatsApp. That is not the same as delivered, and the
difference matters: WhatsApp accepts a message and then decides.

When it cannot deliver one, the message reads **Not delivered**, with WhatsApp's
own reason after it. A number that is no longer on WhatsApp, a picture WhatsApp
could not fetch, an account that is not allowed to start conversations — each
says so in its own words rather than leaving you to guess from silence.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **A message that was not delivered is not charged for.** WhatsApp bills for
> what it delivers, so when a failure comes back, the charge is credited to your
> balance and the line disappears from what you owe. You do not need to ask.

Images sent by customers appear in the thread. On models that can see, recent
images are shown to the agent; older ones stay in the conversation as the
sentence they reduce to, because re-sending every photo on every turn would cost
a great deal for very little.

## Replying on WhatsApp

Inside the 24-hour window you can reply freely. Outside it, only an approved
template will reach the customer — the inbox will tell you which situation you
are in rather than letting you type into the void.


# Notifications
Source: https://docs.thinnest.ai/workspace/notifications

Be told when a call comes in, without logging in — in the console, and by email from your own Resend.

Something happens — your agent answers a call, a template is rejected, Meta
restricts your number — and you find out by opening the console. These settings
change that: choose what you hear about, and have it reach an inbox your team
actually reads.

Find them under **Settings → Notifications**. Anyone in the workspace can see
them; only **owners and admins** can change them.

## Platform notifications

The bell and the feed in the console. Every category is on until you mute it.

| Category | What it tells you |
| - | - |
| **WhatsApp** | Restrictions, bans, review verdicts and sending limits from Meta. Muting these is rarely wise. |
| **Templates** | Approvals, rejections, quality scores and category changes. |
| **Broadcasts and calling campaigns** | When a WhatsApp broadcast or a voice calling campaign finishes, and when an unusual share of it failed. |
| **Calls** | Calls your agent answered or placed, and the ones nobody picked up. |
| **Inbox** | Conversations the agent handed to a person. |
| **Knowledge** | Documents that could not be indexed after repeated attempts. |
| **Plan and usage** | Approaching your included messages, and plan changes. |
| **Connections** | Webhooks, tools, Telegram, voice and your own provider keys failing or being switched off. |
| **Members** | People accepting an invitation to the workspace. |

Muting hides a category from the feed and the bell. Nothing is deleted —
unmuting brings its history back. Anything **critical** is shown regardless: a
muted category cannot hide the news that Meta has banned your account.

### Calls

An answered call and a missed call are different things, so they look different:
an answered call is a record, and a call nobody picked up is a customer who
wanted something. Both inbound and outbound calls are covered.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Calls placed by a calling campaign are not announced one by one.** A
> four-hundred-person campaign would otherwise be four hundred notifications,
> and four hundred emails if you had asked for them. The campaign reports its
> own result when it finishes — see
> [Voice campaigns](/channels/voice-campaigns).

## Receive notifications to email

Notifications can also arrive by email, from **your own Resend account**, at
whatever addresses you choose. That means a shared inbox — `support@` or
`ops@` — rather than the personal addresses people sign in with.

### Connecting Resend

Open the **Receive notifications to email** tab and fill in:

* **Resend API key** — from your Resend dashboard, under API Keys. It is stored
  encrypted and is never shown again.
* **Send from** — an address on a domain you have **verified inside Resend**.
  Resend will refuse anything else.
* **Sender name** — optional; what the recipient sees in their inbox.
* **Send notifications to** — one address per line, up to ten. These do not
  have to belong to people who log in here.

When you press **Connect and send a test**, we send a real message to **every**
address you listed. **Nothing is saved unless Resend accepts it.** A key that
looks right but belongs to an unverified domain fails here, while you are looking
at the screen, rather than weeks later as silence.

"Accepted" is not quite "arrived". A message can still land in a spam folder or
bounce, and we cannot see that from here. If a test does not appear within a
minute, check that address's **spam** folder first, then open **Emails** in your
Resend dashboard — it shows each message as *Delivered*, *Bounced* or *Delayed*.
If one address works and another does not, the problem is that address, not your
setup.

> [!TIP]
>
> Give Resend a key with **full access** if you want it to be easy to diagnose
> this yourself. A key restricted to "sending access" is the safer choice and works
> perfectly for notifications — it just means we cannot look at delivery status for
> you.

### Choosing what is emailed

Once an account is connected, each category above gets a choice:

| Choice | You get emailed |
| - | - |
| **No email** | Never. The default for every category. |
| **Only urgent** | Only the ones that mean messages are not reaching customers. |
| **Every one** | Everything in that category. |

To be told about every call, set **Calls** to *Every one*.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Nothing is emailed until you ask.** A workspace that has never opened this
> page receives no notification email. That is stricter than before — urgent
> Meta alerts used to arrive uninvited — so if you rely on those, set **WhatsApp**
> to *Only urgent*.

### If you would rather not connect Resend

You do not have to. With nothing connected, anything you switch on still reaches
your owners and admins, sent by us. Connecting your own account only changes who
it comes from and where it goes.

### If your account stops working

If Resend starts refusing — a revoked key, a lapsed domain — the connection shows
the recent failures and the reason on the settings page. Notifications keep
arriving in the console. An account that has never had a successful test is never
used, and mail goes out through ours instead of being lost.

**Disconnect** removes the stored key entirely. Your choices about what to hear
about are kept.


# Where you are billed
Source: https://docs.thinnest.ai/workspace/regions

One app for every country: what changes with the country your business is billed in.

ThinnestAI is one app, at `app.thinnest.ai`, for every country. When you
create a workspace it asks which country your business is billed in. That
answer sets what you pay in and a few things you can use.

| | India | Everywhere else |
| - | - | - |
| You pay in | Rupees (₹), with a GST invoice | US dollars (\$) |
| Phone numbers | Buy an Indian number from us, or bring your own | Buy a United States number from us, or bring your own |
| Phone calls are charged | In half-minute steps | In whole minutes, at the same rate a minute |
| API address | `app.thinnest.ai/api/v1` | `app.thinnest.ai/api/v1` |

## Choosing

The sign-up page starts the country on where your network says you are. Change
it if your business is billed somewhere else. It is set when the workspace is
created, and a workspace stays in the market it was created in.

> [!NOTE]
>
> An agent, a wallet or a balance cannot be moved from one workspace to
> another. If you need a workspace in the other market, create a new one and
> set it up again.

A few countries we cannot take payments from yet. If yours is one of them, the
sign-up page says so before it creates anything.

## What you pay in

A workspace billed outside India is billed in **US dollars**. Prices, your
wallet, invoices and the WhatsApp message rates on the [Usage](/workspace/usage)
page all appear in dollars, never converted from rupees. A workspace billed in
India is billed in rupees only.

## Voices

A workspace billed outside India has one voice tier, **Studio**, with the whole
voice library. Ten British voices — five women and five men, chosen for
answering the phone for a business — come first, and new agents start on the
first of them. On the Playground, **Browse voices** opens the library: search
it, filter by language, accent, gender, age and tag, and select. Studio voices
have no sample to play; use **Test a call** to hear one. Or choose through the API's [List Voices](/api-reference/voices/list-voices)
and the agent's `voice` setting. See [Voice](/channels/voice).

## Phone numbers

A workspace billed outside India can buy a **United States** local number from
us, or bring a number it already owns from any country and point it at the agent.
A United States number from us calls the United States and Canada only; see
[United States numbers](/channels/phone-numbers#united-states-numbers).
Whichever market you are in, give every number with its country code. See [Phone
numbers](/channels/phone-numbers#country-codes).

## Phone calls

A phone call on a workspace billed outside India is charged in **whole minutes**,
rounded up: a 20-second call is one minute, a 61-second call two. The rate a
minute is the same as anywhere else on your plan. A workspace billed in India is
charged in half-minute steps. Web calls are charged by the second in both.

## WhatsApp

Messages are priced from Meta's own published rates for the country they go to,
in your workspace's currency. You pay Meta directly for messages sent from your
own WhatsApp account; what we add is our platform fee. See [WhatsApp
windows and pricing](/meta/windows-and-pricing).

## Resellers

A [white-label](/white-label/overview) reseller billed outside India sets
prices in dollars and connects **its own Dodo Payments account** to be
paid by its clients. See [Your prices](/white-label/prices#paid-through-dodo-international).


# Usage
Source: https://docs.thinnest.ai/workspace/usage

What your agents did, what it cost, and every call you can open and listen to.

**Usage** is the workspace-wide record: how much your agents worked, what that
cost, and a line for every call. It sits in the main sidebar, not under an
agent, because it covers all of them at once.

Analytics answers *how well is my agent doing*. Usage answers *what did it do,
and what am I paying for* — and they are different questions.

## The last thirty days

The chart at the top is activity over time: replies your agents sent and calls
they handled, on the same thirty-day grid so you can see them against each
other. A spike in calls the week you ran a campaign should look like one.

Useful for the thing dashboards rarely tell you: **when** your customers
actually get in touch. If the line rises every evening after six, that is when
somebody should be reachable.

## WhatsApp

WhatsApp is billed per message, and it is broken out here in full — marketing,
utility, authentication and service counted separately, by country, because they
cost very different amounts.

The figure against each line is **what you were charged**, in your own currency,
so it reconciles against your balance and against your own record of what you
sent. Everything the workspace sends is counted the same way, whether it came
from a campaign, a sequence, the Send Message page or the API.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **A message that was not delivered is not charged for.** WhatsApp bills for
> what it delivers. When a failure comes back the charge is credited, so a line
> you see here is a message that arrived.

> [!NOTE]
>
> Until 1 October 2026, an open 24-hour window makes two things free: the
> agent's own replies, and any utility template you send while it is open.
> Templates that start a conversation are charged, and so is authentication in
> or out of a window. If a number looks higher than you expected, the split here
> usually shows why — see
> [Windows and what gets charged](/meta/windows-and-pricing).

## Instagram

Instagram has no per-message fee of its own, so there is no Instagram cost
breakdown the way there is for WhatsApp. Your agent's replies to Instagram DMs
and comments count in **Replies** at the top of this page, the same as replies
on any other channel.

For what your Instagram accounts did (DMs received, replies by your agent and
your team, comments answered), open **Instagram > IG Dashboard**. See
[Instagram](/channels/instagram#ig-dashboard).

## Calls

Every call the workspace answered or placed, newest first: when, who, which
agent, whether it connected, how long it ran, and what it cost.

Open one to read the transcript. If the call was recorded, the recording is
there too.

**Tools** shows every tool the agent ran on the call, in order: booking a slot, saving a lead, a
custom action. A failed one is marked in red with the reason, and opens to show what the agent sent and what came
back. It is the first place to look when an agent said it did something and did not. Passwords, keys and codes are
never shown. Tool details are kept for 30 days.

**Export** gives you the same list as a file that opens in Excel or any
spreadsheet: when each call started, its direction, the agent, the other
person's number, which of your numbers it rang from (calls the agent placed),
how it ended, its length and its cost. After those come **what the call was
about**: its summary, and one column for each detail the agent collected, such
as the caller's name or the reason they called. A call that did not collect a
detail has an empty cell under it.

To get the caller's name and the reason in the file, add them as details on the
agent's Actions page under **Collect details here**, and keep **Summarise each
call** on, on the Playground. A call whose recording and transcript you deleted
shows no summary or details.

A call on [OpenAI GPT-Live-1](/channels/voice#speech-to-speech-openai-gpt-live-1) shows the model by that name and is
billed at its own flat rate a minute rather than on a voice plan: its cost is the charge for the
call, with no per-minute rate beside it.

> [!NOTE]
>
> A call that shows as **failed** never connected — a wrong number, a line that
> rang out, a caller who hung up before the agent spoke. Failed calls cost
> nothing and are kept so the list is honest about what was attempted.

### How a call went

An opened call also shows how it went, in numbers, and whether anything broke:

* **How the call went** — how long the caller waited for each reply (the typical
  wait, the slow end, and the slowest), how many pauses of 10 seconds or more
  there were (or your agent's own "are you still there?" time, if it has one),
  how often the caller spoke over the agent, and how many replies the agent could
  not produce or a backup had to produce. A call that was never measured, such
  as one that never connected, has no figures.
* **Where the time went in each turn** — open it under **How the call went**.
  One row per turn: when the first word of the actual answer was heard, when the
  first sound of any kind was (a thinking line or an acknowledgement that plays
  first is not the answer, and the row says so), how long the turn took to be
  decided, Ear's check, the model's first sentence and the voice. A dash means
  the step did not happen on that turn. A leading **≈** means a thinking line
  spoke first and the answer's start is worked out from the audio queued behind
  it, not heard directly.
* **Problems on this call** — shown only when something went wrong while the
  call was live: the agent could not answer, your own model key failed, a reply
  took more than 5 seconds to start, or the voice connection failed.

Through the API the numbers are `quality` on
[Get Call](/api-reference/calls/get-call) (`answerMs` is the time to the first
word of the actual answer, and `knowledgeTurns` the turns that looked something
up in the agent's knowledge), every turn's timing is
[Get Call Timeline](/api-reference/calls/get-call-timeline), and every problem is sent as a
`call.problem` [webhook](/api-reference/webhooks#problems-on-a-live-call) while
the call is still going on, so you can alert somebody before it ends.

## Recordings

Recording is off unless you turn it on, per agent, on that agent's
**Playground**, in the **Sound and recording** card. When it is on, the calls that agent answers or places — on your website,
and by phone on a number you took from us — are recorded and appear here.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Recordings are deleted when your plan says** — after 30 days on
> pay-as-you-go, 49 on Pro and 75 on Scale. Download anything you need to keep before
> then. Once it is deleted it is gone and we cannot get it back.

A caller on your website sees *This call is recorded* as the call connects. See
[Recording calls](/channels/voice#recording-calls) for which phone calls can be.

Telling people they are being recorded is your responsibility, not ours. In most
places it has to be said at the start of the call, and the wording that satisfies
your regulator is not something we can write for you. Put it in your agent's
first words.

## Plan credit

Pro and Scale give you usage credit every billing period. It is spent **before**
your own balance, so money you topped up is not touched until the credit is used.

**Unused credit rolls over for up to 3 months while your paid subscription
remains active.** Each period's credit expires at the end of its own 3-month
window: credit granted for the period starting 1 January can be spent until
1 April, and the credit granted for February has its own window after that. When
you spend, the oldest credit goes first, so what would expire soonest is used
before newer credit.

* **If you cancel,** what is left lasts until the end of the period you have paid
  for, then expires.
* **On a yearly plan** the whole year's credit is granted at once, and it lasts
  the year plus two months.
* **Money you topped up never expires.** Only the plan's credit does.

Your balance on the billing page shows the credit and your own money together.
Through the API, [Get Usage](/api-reference/usage/get-usage) returns `creditMicro`
(the credit you hold) and `creditExpiresAt` (the earliest date any of it
expires, or `null` when there is none).

## What is not here

> [!WARNING]
>
> * **Per-customer spend.** Usage is per workspace and per channel, not per
>   contact.
> * **Live figures to the second.** Costs settle when a call ends and when Meta
>   confirms a send, so the most recent minutes can lag slightly.
> * **Your invoice.** This is what you used. What you owe is on
>   **Settings → Billing**, and the two are presented differently on purpose.

> [!TIP]
>
> **Registered for GST in India? Put your GSTIN in Settings → General, under
> Billing details.** It is recorded on every invoice we issue you from the
> moment you save it, which is what makes those invoices usable by your
> accountant. Only an owner or admin can set it, and it takes effect on invoices
> issued afterwards — so it is worth doing before your first payment rather than
> after. The GST number is asked of workspaces billed in rupees only.

**Invoices in a different name.** If your invoices should carry your company's
legal name rather than the workspace name, set a **Billing name** in Settings →
General, under Billing details. Left empty, invoices use the workspace name.
